Title: Specific heat capacity
Aim: Determine the specific heat capacity of a solid block (e.g. aluminium or copper).
Key variables: IV: energy supplied (J). DV: temperature (°C). Control: mass of block, insulation.
Method: 1. Place immersion heater in central hole of the metal block; place thermometer in second hole with a drop of oil. 2. Wrap block in insulation and record starting temperature. 3. Connect heater via joulemeter (or ammeter + voltmeter + stopwatch) to a low-voltage supply (12 V). 4. Switch on; record temperature every 60 s for 10 min. 5. Switch off; continue recording until temperature peaks (thermal lag).
Measurements: Energy input E (J), temperature rise ΔT (°C), mass m (kg).
Analysis: c = E / (m × ΔT). Plot E against ΔT; gradient = m·c. Compare to accepted value.
Safety: Hot metal — allow to cool before handling. Check insulation for damage. Low voltage only.
Data skills: Linear plot; gradient → constant; % difference from accepted value.
Common errors / improvements: Heat lost to surroundings → measured c too high. Improve with insulation, oil in thermometer hole, and continue recording after switch-off to capture peak T (thermal lag). Thermometer reads block surface not core — wait for equilibrium. Check joulemeter zero before starting.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: 1 aluminium block (pre-drilled with 2 holes, ~1 kg), 1 × 12 V immersion heater, 1 low-voltage PSU, 1 joulemeter (or ammeter + voltmeter), 1 thermometer with oil in hole, insulating material (bubble wrap or foam). Check joulemeters zero correctly. Wrap blocks in insulation before lesson. Set out on heat-proof mats. Ensure heater fits snugly in hole — wrap with PTFE tape if loose.

Title: Resistance of a wire
Aim: Investigate how the length of a wire affects its electrical resistance.
Key variables: IV: length of wire (cm). DV: resistance (Ω). Control: wire material, diameter, temperature.
Method: 1. Set up circuit: cell, ammeter in series with crocodile clips and a metre of constantan wire taped to a metre rule; voltmeter across the test length. 2. Connect crocodile clips at 10 cm; close switch only long enough to record V and I. 3. Repeat at 20, 30, 40… 100 cm. 4. Open switch between readings to avoid heating.
Measurements: Voltage V (V), current I (A) at each length L (cm).
Analysis: R = V/I. Plot R against L; expect straight line through origin. Gradient = resistance per unit length.
Safety: Wire gets hot if current flows continuously — open switch between readings. Low voltage supply only.
Data skills: Linear plot; gradient → constant; line through origin = direct proportion.
Common errors / improvements: Wire heating → resistance drifts up during readings. Close switch only momentarily. Crocodile-clip contact resistance → take L from inside edge of each clip. Kinks in wire change effective length — straighten before taping. Connect voltmeter directly across the test length, not at the supply.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: 1 m constantan wire (SWG 28) taped to a metre rule, crocodile clips × 2, ammeter, voltmeter, 1.5 V cell or low-voltage PSU. Pre-tape wire to metre rules, ensuring wire is straight with no kinks. Check wire continuity with a multimeter. Provide switch in circuit to avoid overheating. Replace wire between classes if it has kinked or been heated excessively.

Title: I–V characteristics
Aim: Investigate the current–voltage characteristics of a filament lamp, a fixed resistor and a diode.
Key variables: IV: potential difference (V). DV: current (A). Control: component.
Method: 1. Set up circuit with variable power supply, ammeter in series, voltmeter across component. 2. Vary V from 0 to ~6 V in steps; record I. 3. Reverse connections to get negative values. 4. Repeat for filament lamp, fixed resistor, and diode (with protective resistor).
Measurements: V and I for each component, positive and negative.
Analysis: Plot I vs V. Resistor: straight line. Lamp: S-curve. Diode: threshold then steep rise; no reverse current.
Safety: Disconnect between changes. Diode requires protective resistor.
Data skills: Non-linear curves; gradient = 1/R varies with V (lamp); curve shape identification.
Common errors / improvements: Filament lamp: not letting it cool → upward drift. Take ascending and descending sweeps and average. Diode without protective resistor → blows. Too few points near knee — take closer-spaced readings 0–2 V. Swap leads at the component (not just the supply) for negative V.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: variable PSU (0–6 V), ammeter, voltmeter, filament lamp (MES, 6 V 0.06 A), fixed resistor (10 Ω), signal diode (1N4001) + 100 Ω protective resistor, connecting leads, switch. Pre-wire circuits or provide circuit diagram. Check lamps — replace any blown bulbs. Diodes: mark anode/cathode with marker pen.

Title: Density of solids and liquids
Aim: Determine the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids.
Key variables: Measure mass and volume independently.
Method: Regular solid: measure dimensions with callipers / micrometer; mass on balance. Irregular solid: mass on balance; volume by displacement in eureka can. Liquid: mass empty then full measuring cylinder; read volume from scale.
Measurements: Mass m (g), volume V (cm³).
Analysis: ρ = m / V. Compare with tabulated values.
Safety: Glassware on stable surface. Wipe spills.
Data skills: % difference from tabulated value; absolute uncertainty from instrument resolution.
Common errors / improvements: Eureka can not pre-filled to spout → first displaced water fills spout. Air bubbles on irregular solid → tap to release. Parallax reading meniscus — eye level, bottom of meniscus. Measure each dimension 3 times and average.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: top-pan balance (0.1 g), 30 cm ruler, vernier calipers, measuring cylinder (100 cm³), string, selection of regular and irregular solids (e.g. metal cylinder, stone, wooden block), water. Check balances are zeroed. Ensure measuring cylinders are clean and dry. Pre-select objects of varied densities including at least one that floats.

Title: Force and extension (Hooke's law)
Aim: Investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
Key variables: IV: force (N). DV: extension (mm). Control: spring.
Method: 1. Hang spring from a clamped stand; attach pointer and vertical metre rule. 2. Record unloaded pointer position. 3. Add 1 N (100 g) masses one at a time; record pointer position. 4. Continue past limit of proportionality. 5. Remove masses; check spring returns.
Measurements: Force F (N) and extension x = position − unloaded position.
Analysis: Plot F vs extension. Straight line through origin → k = gradient. Mark limit of proportionality.
Safety: G-clamp stand. Eye protection. Stand back near limit — spring may snap.
Data skills: Linear plot; gradient → k; identification of limit of proportionality; line through origin test.
Common errors / improvements: Plotting position not extension → doesn't go through origin. Parallax: ruler not vertical — clamp vertically and read at eye level. Including plastic-region points in gradient calculation — linear region only. Mass hanger weight (~1 N) forgotten — count as first load.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: retort stand, boss, clamp, spring (Hooke's law spring, k ~25 N/m), slotted masses (10 × 100 g) + hanger, metre rule, pointer (paper arrow taped to spring bottom). Set up stands on bench edge so masses hang freely. Check springs are not permanently stretched from previous use — replace if coils touch at rest. Provide a G-clamp to secure retort stand base.

Title: Acceleration (varying F and m)
Aim: Investigate the effect of varying force and mass on the acceleration of a trolley.
Key variables: IV: force (Part A) or mass (Part B). DV: acceleration.
Method: 1. Dynamics trolley on friction-compensated tilted ramp with pulley; string to hanging mass. 2. Two light gates measure acceleration. 3. Part A: keep total mass constant; transfer masses from trolley to hanger. 4. Part B: keep hanger mass constant; add masses to trolley.
Measurements: Light gate times → velocities → acceleration. Force = weight of hanging mass.
Analysis: Part A: a ∝ F (straight line through origin). Part B: plot a vs 1/m for straight line.
Safety: Catch trolley at bottom. Cushion floor below hanger.
Data skills: Linearisation (a vs 1/m); direct vs inverse proportion; intercept → friction.
Common errors / improvements: Friction not compensated → positive x-intercept on a vs F graph. Total mass must include hanging mass. Card not perpendicular to light gates → false time. Use low-friction pulley and light string.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Per group: dynamics trolley, runway (inclined ~5°), light gate × 2 + datalogger or ticker-tape timer + power supply, slotted masses + pulley + string, ruler, protractor. Check light gates connect to datalogger and produce readings. Set runway incline to compensate for friction (trolley should roll at constant speed without masses). Ensure ticker tape feeds smoothly and carbon paper is fresh.

Title: Waves on a string and in water
Aim: Measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves on a string and in water.
Key variables: v = fλ.
Method: Water: ripple tank with straight dipper at known f; strobe to freeze; measure λ from shadow. String: vibration generator + pulley + hanging mass; vary f until standing wave; measure node spacing (= λ/2).
Measurements: Frequency f (Hz), wavelength λ (m).
Analysis: v = fλ. Compare water wave speed at different depths.
Safety: Mop ripple-tank spills. Stroboscope warning for photosensitive students.
Data skills: Substitution; uncertainty in λ (ruler resolution vs fringe spacing).
Common errors / improvements: Measure λ in centre of ripple tank not near edges. Measure across multiple wavelengths and divide. Loop between nodes = λ/2, not λ. Strobe at half-frequency makes waves appear stationary at wrong λ.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Ripple tank: fill to ~1 cm depth with clean water, check lamp working, ensure white paper on bench under tank. For string waves: per group: signal generator (1–20 Hz), vibration generator, length of string, pulley, slotted masses. Adjust string tension so clear standing wave visible at ~5 Hz. Dry tank thoroughly between classes.

Title: Light — refraction and reflection
Aim: Investigate reflection and refraction of light.
Key variables: IV: angle of incidence. DV: angle of reflection / refraction.
Method: Reflection: ray box → mirror on plain paper; trace rays; measure angles. Refraction: ray box → rectangular glass block; trace rays through block.
Measurements: Angles of incidence, reflection, refraction.
Analysis: Reflection: θᵢ = θᵣ. Refraction: plot sin θ₁ vs sin θ₂; gradient = refractive index n.
Safety: Ray box gets hot — handle with care.
Data skills: Linearisation (sin θ plots); gradient → refractive index n.
Common errors / improvements: Thick ray lines → ambiguity. Use sharp pencil, mark crosses along ray and join. Measure angles from normal, not surface — draw normal first. Outline block in pencil before rays and don't move it. Take ≥5 angle values.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: rectangular glass block, ray box + single-slit, protractor, plain white paper, ruler, pencil. Check ray boxes work and slits are clean. Provide fresh white paper sheets — enough for 3–4 per group. Ensure room blinds are available (darker room gives clearer rays).

Title: Infrared emission (Leslie cube)
Aim: Investigate how infrared emission depends on surface type.
Key variables: IV: surface (matt black / shiny silver etc.). DV: detector reading.
Method: 1. Fill Leslie cube with boiling water; let temperature stabilise 1 min. 2. Hold IR detector at fixed distance from one face. Record reading. 3. Rotate cube; repeat for each face.
Measurements: Detector reading for each surface.
Analysis: Matt black emits most; shiny silver least.
Safety: Boiling water — pour carefully, use heatproof mat.
Data skills: Categorical comparison; controlling distance; ranking.
Common errors / improvements: Cube cools between faces → take readings in fixed time order then reverse and average. Clamp detector at fixed distance or use a spacer block. Shield from background IR.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group or per 2 groups: Leslie cube (pre-filled with near-boiling water by teacher at lesson start), infrared detector (thermopile or IR thermometer), ruler, stopwatch. Fill cube with boiling water just before lesson — do not pre-fill as it cools. Ensure all 4 faces are clean: one black matt, one white matt, one shiny, one dull. Handle cube with oven gloves — warn students surfaces are hot.

Title: Period of a pendulum
Aim: Investigate how the period of a simple pendulum depends on its length.
Key variables: IV: length L (m). DV: period T (s).
Method: 1. Clamp string between two wooden splints (defines pivot). 2. Measure L from pivot to centre of bob. 3. Displace <10°; time 20 oscillations; T = time/20. 4. Repeat for L = 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 cm.
Measurements: Length L, time for 20 oscillations → T.
Analysis: T = 2π√(L/g). Plot T² vs L; gradient = 4π²/g.
Safety: G-clamp stand.
Data skills: Linearisation (T² vs L); gradient → g; reaction-time uncertainty reduced by timing many oscillations.
Common errors / improvements: Timing 1 oscillation → reaction time ~20% error. Time 20–50 and divide. Time using fiducial marker at equilibrium not at turning point. Angle >10° invalidates T = 2π√(L/g). Measure L to centre of bob.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: clamp stand, string (1.5 m), bob (100 g mass), stopwatch, ruler. Pre-cut strings at 100 cm, 80 cm, 60 cm, 40 cm lengths. Tie bobs securely. Check clamps hold securely — pendulum must swing in a consistent plane.

Title: g by free fall (electromagnet)
Aim: Determine g using a free-fall apparatus.
Key variables: IV: drop height h (m). DV: fall time t (s).
Method: 1. Electromagnet releases steel ball; millisecond timer starts on release, stops on trapdoor. 2. Measure h from bottom of ball to trapdoor. 3. Repeat 3× at each h. Vary h from 0.2 to 1.0 m.
Measurements: Fall height h, fall time t (averaged).
Analysis: h = ½gt². Plot h vs t²; gradient = g/2.
Safety: Catch tray below. Stand clear of falling ball.
Data skills: Linearisation (h vs t²); gradient → g; non-zero intercept reveals systematic timing error.
Common errors / improvements: Residual magnetism delays release → systematic t overestimate. Use minimum holding current. Plot h vs t² not h vs t. Measure h from bottom of ball. Check apparatus vertical with spirit level.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: electromagnet + 12 V PSU, ball-bearing (steel), electronic timing gate or spark timer, metre rule clamped vertically. Check electromagnet releases cleanly when switched off. Adjust drop height so time is measurable (recommended 0.5–1.5 m). Test timing gate triggers reliably.

Title: Young modulus of a wire
Aim: Determine the Young modulus of a metal wire.
Key variables: IV: load F (N). DV: extension x (mm).
Method: 1. Clamp ≥2 m wire; pulley at free end; small pre-load to straighten. 2. Measure L and diameter d (micrometer, ≥3 positions). 3. Add 1 N loads; record extension at each. 4. Unload to verify elastic behaviour.
Measurements: Load F, extension x, original length L, diameter d.
Analysis: σ = F/A, ε = x/L. Plot σ vs ε; gradient = E.
Safety: Wire may snap — safety screen, goggles, lab coat. Cushion floor.
Data skills: Stress–strain plot; gradient → E; % uncertainty in d² dominates; elastic limit identification.
Common errors / improvements: Diameter uncertainty is squared in A → dominant error. Take ≥3 readings at different angles. Wire not initially straight → curved base of graph; use pre-load. Wire ≥1.5 m essential — short wire gives tiny extension. Only use linear region for E.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min. Per pair: long (~2 m) copper or steel wire mounted on board between two clamps, micrometer screw gauge, metre rule, slotted masses (up to 5 kg), vernier scale or travelling microscope. Pre-measure wire diameter in 3 places — record for class. Load wire gently before lesson to remove kinks. Warn: do not exceed elastic limit (wire should return to zero when masses removed).

Title: Wavelength by diffraction grating
Aim: Determine the wavelength of laser light using a diffraction grating.
Key variables: IV: grating spacing d. DV: order angle θ.
Method: 1. Laser → grating → screen ~1.5 m away. 2. Mark positions of orders 0, ±1, ±2. 3. Measure grating-to-screen distance D; fringe positions; compute θ.
Measurements: Grating spacing d = 1/N, angles θ, order n.
Analysis: d sin θ = nλ. Solve for λ.
Safety: Never look into laser beam. Class 2 only. Remove jewellery.
Data skills: Trigonometric calculation; small-angle limitation; uncertainty in d (grating pitch tolerance).
Common errors / improvements: Grating not perpendicular → asymmetric orders; rotate to equalise and average ±n. Use full sin θ not small-angle tan θ approximation. Measure ±n distance and halve for better accuracy. Use higher orders (n=2, 3) for larger angles and better λ precision.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: diffraction grating (300 or 600 lines/mm), spectrometer or metre rule setup, sodium lamp or laser + screen, ruler. Switch sodium lamps on 10 min before lesson (warm-up required). Lasers: check <1 mW, class 2. Provide beam stops and safety goggles. Gratings: handle by edges only — fingerprints destroy them.

Title: Stationary waves on a string
Aim: Verify v = √(T/μ) for transverse waves on a string.
Key variables: IV: tension T or frequency f. DV: wavelength λ.
Method: 1. Vibration generator + signal generator drives string over pulley with hanging mass. 2. Adjust f until clear standing wave; measure node spacing (= λ/2). 3. Repeat for different tensions. Determine μ by weighing known length of string.
Measurements: T, f, λ, μ.
Analysis: v = fλ = √(T/μ). Plot v² vs T; gradient = 1/μ.
Safety: Cushion floor below hanging mass.
Data skills: Linearisation (v² vs T); gradient → 1/μ; comparison with directly measured μ.
Common errors / improvements: Measure between interior nodes not at the driver clamp. Find fundamental first then tune to higher harmonics. Weigh ≥1 m of string for reliable μ. Use low-friction pulley.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: signal generator (20–200 Hz), vibration generator, long string, pulley, slotted masses, stroboscope (optional), metre rule. Pre-set signal generator range. Check vibration generator connections. Provide strings pre-cut to ~2 m.

Title: EMF and internal resistance
Aim: Determine the EMF and internal resistance of a cell.
Key variables: IV: current I. DV: terminal pd V.
Method: 1. Cell + rheostat in series with ammeter; voltmeter across cell. 2. Vary resistance; record V and I over widest feasible range. 3. Disconnect between readings.
Measurements: V, I.
Analysis: V = ε − Ir. Plot V vs I; intercept = ε, gradient = −r.
Safety: Disconnect between readings. Old cells may leak.
Data skills: Linear plot; intercept → EMF; gradient → −r; range of I important.
Common errors / improvements: Fresh cell: r ≈ 0.1 Ω → barely visible gradient. Use partially-used cell. Cell heats with continuous current → r drifts. Use high-impedance voltmeter. Vary I over widest possible range for a clean gradient.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: 2–3 identical cells (AA), cell holder, variable resistor (0–10 Ω, wire-wound), digital voltmeter, ammeter, connecting leads, switch. Measure and record actual EMF of cells with a high-resistance voltmeter — tape value to each cell holder. Check variable resistor sweeps smoothly. Replace cells that are below 1.4 V.

Title: Resistivity of a metal wire
Aim: Determine the resistivity of constantan wire.
Key variables: IV: length L. DV: resistance R. Also measure diameter d.
Method: 1. Constantan wire taped to metre rule. 2. Measure d at ≥5 positions with micrometer. 3. Record V and I at lengths 10–100 cm in 10 cm steps.
Measurements: L, R = V/I, cross-sectional area A = πd²/4.
Analysis: R = ρL/A. Plot R vs L; gradient = ρ/A; ρ = gradient × A.
Safety: Open switch between readings.
Data skills: Linear plot; gradient × A → ρ; % uncertainty propagation (d² dominates).
Common errors / improvements: Diameter uncertainty doubled in A = πd²/4 → dominant error. Check micrometer zero. Oxidised wire → high contact resistance at clips. Use clean fresh wire. Quote ρ with propagated uncertainty and state temperature.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: 1 m of resistance wire (various gauges: SWG 28, 32, 36) taped to metre rule, micrometer, ammeter, voltmeter, low-voltage PSU, crocodile clips. Pre-measure diameter of each wire with micrometer — post on bench. Check wires are not kinked. Use switch to prevent overheating.

Title: Capacitor discharge (RC time constant)
Aim: Investigate capacitor discharge and determine RC.
Key variables: DV: voltage V across capacitor over time t.
Method: 1. Charge capacitor C (≈1000 μF) through SPDT switch from supply V₀. 2. Switch to discharge through R (≈100 kΩ); record V every 5 s. 3. Use data logger if available.
Measurements: V, t.
Analysis: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC). Plot ln V vs t; gradient = −1/RC.
Safety: Discharge capacitor fully before handling.
Data skills: Log-linear plot (ln V vs t); gradient → 1/RC; exponential decay.
Common errors / improvements: Electrolytic capacitor tolerance ±20% → don't compare directly to R×C. Use high-impedance digital voltmeter (≥10 MΩ) to avoid loading the circuit. Data logger for short RC; ln V vs t gives far better precision than reading t at V₀/e.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: electrolytic capacitor (1000–4700 µF, 16 V rated), fixed resistor (10–100 kΩ), digital voltmeter (high impedance), stopwatch or datalogger, 9 V battery and switch. Check capacitor polarity is marked. Ensure resistor value gives time constant of 30–120 s for easy manual logging. Fully discharge capacitors before issue.

Title: Force on a current-carrying conductor
Aim: Investigate F = BIL using a top-pan balance.
Key variables: IV: current I. DV: force F (balance reading).
Method: 1. Magnadur magnets on yoke sitting on tared balance. 2. Stiff copper wire through field, clamped independently of balance. 3. Vary current 0–5 A; record balance reading (mass × g = force).
Measurements: Current I, mass reading m → F = mg.
Analysis: F = BIL. Plot F vs I; gradient = BL. Measure L → B.
Safety: Wire heats at high I — keep current on briefly. Magnets brittle.
Data skills: Linear plot; gradient → BL; unit conversion (g to N).
Common errors / improvements: Wire must not touch balance — use independent stand. Wire perpendicular to B — use set square. Keep current-carrying length inside central uniform field region. Re-tare between readings.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: current-carrying conductor (stiff wire on holder), horseshoe magnet or pair of magnets on yoke, top-pan balance, ammeter, variable PSU (0–6 A). Check balance reads zero with wire in place and no current. Adjust wire position so it sits centrally between magnet poles. Ensure PSU can supply at least 4 A reliably.

Title: Electromagnetic induction (dropping magnet)
Aim: Investigate factors affecting induced EMF in a coil.
Key variables: IV: drop height (→ speed) or number of turns N. DV: peak EMF.
Method: 1. Drop bar magnet through coil; record EMF trace with data logger or oscilloscope. 2. Vary drop height. 3. Vary N using different coils. 4. Compare peak EMF and pulse duration.
Measurements: Drop height, turns N, peak EMF, pulse area.
Analysis: ε = −N dΦ/dt. EMF increases with speed and N. Area under EMF–t = NΔΦ.
Safety: Catch magnet — strong magnets brittle.
Data skills: Area under curve (numerical integration); peak EMF vs integrated flux linkage.
Common errors / improvements: Use a guiding tube for axial fall. Must use data logger or oscilloscope — peaks last milliseconds. Only vary N if coil geometry is identical. Area under entry and exit pulses should be equal in magnitude — if not, energy is lost.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: copper or aluminium pipe (~1 m, 25 mm bore), strong neodymium cylinder magnet (fits inside pipe with ~1 mm clearance), stopwatch, ruler. For quantitative version: connect coil at bottom to oscilloscope. Check magnet size — must fall freely, not jam. Have a foam pad at base to catch magnet.

Title: Specific latent heat of fusion of ice
Aim: Determine the specific latent heat of fusion of ice.
Key variables: IV: energy supplied E. DV: mass of ice melted m.
Method: 1. Two identical funnels of ice; one with heater, one control. 2. Wait until both dripping steadily at 0 °C. 3. Heater on for 10 min; collect meltwater in pre-weighed beakers. 4. Meltwater from heater funnel minus control = mass melted by heater alone.
Measurements: Energy E (joulemeter), mass m (balance).
Analysis: L = E/m. Compare to 334 kJ/kg.
Safety: Low voltage only. Wipe spills.
Data skills: Control subtraction technique; % difference from accepted value.
Common errors / improvements: Control funnel essential — room-temperature melting otherwise included in m. Start only when ice is dripping steadily (at 0 °C). Pack ice tightly around heater. Weigh beakers promptly to avoid evaporation loss.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: crushed ice (pre-made), beaker, immersion heater (25 W, 12 V), joulemeter or ammeter + voltmeter, thermometer, balance. Prepare ice by crushing and draining excess water just before lesson. Calibrate joulemeters. Set up collection beakers. Keep ice in insulated container until needed.

Title: Boyle's law
Aim: Verify PV = constant at constant temperature.
Key variables: IV: pressure P. DV: volume V.
Method: 1. Boyle's law apparatus (oil-sealed tube + pressure gauge + foot pump). 2. Pump slowly; wait ≥30 s after each step for T equilibration; record P and V. 3. Cover atmospheric to ~3× atmospheric.
Measurements: P, V at each step.
Analysis: PV = constant. Plot P vs 1/V; straight line through origin.
Safety: Pressure vessel — do not exceed rating. Eye protection.
Data skills: Linearisation (P vs 1/V); PV product as constancy check.
Common errors / improvements: Compression heats gas → wait for T equilibration before reading. Check whether gauge reads absolute or gauge pressure and correct. Release pressure slowly to avoid oil rising into gas column.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: Boyle's law apparatus (sealed air column + pressure gauge), ruler, pump. Check seals are airtight — pump up to max pressure, release, observe pressure return to atmospheric. Calibrate pressure gauge against atmosphere.

Title: SHM (pendulum and mass-spring)
Aim: Investigate factors affecting period of SHM.
Key variables: IV: length L (pendulum) or mass m (spring). DV: period T.
Method: Pendulum: time 50 oscillations; vary L from 20 to 100 cm. Mass-spring: time 20 oscillations; vary m from 50 to 500 g.
Measurements: L or m; time for many oscillations → T.
Analysis: Pendulum: T² ∝ L, gradient = 4π²/g. Spring: T² ∝ m, gradient = 4π²/k.
Safety: G-clamp stand.
Data skills: Linearisation (T² vs L or m); gradient → g or k; effective mass of spring correction.
Common errors / improvements: Spring effective mass = m_load + m_spring/3 — include for light masses. Time many oscillations early; late oscillations are slower due to damping. Keep pendulum angle <10° for SHM assumption to hold.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per pair: pendulum (as GCSE-10 but longer), mass-spring system (100 g mass on spring, clamp stand), stopwatch, ruler, motion sensor + datalogger (optional). Pre-measure spring constant (see MAT-01). Ensure pendulum length can be varied easily.

Title: Inverse-square law for gamma radiation
Aim: Verify the inverse-square law for gamma radiation.
Key variables: IV: distance d from source. DV: corrected count rate C.
Method: 1. Measure background count over 5 min; no source present. 2. Place sealed gamma source using tongs. Record count over 60 s at d = 5, 10…50 cm. 3. Subtract background count rate.
Measurements: Distance d, corrected count rate C.
Analysis: C ∝ 1/d². Plot C vs 1/d² → straight line; or 1/√C vs d → intercept gives distance offset.
Safety: Sealed source: tongs, minimise exposure, log usage, lock away after.
Data skills: Background subtraction; Poisson uncertainty (σ = √N); linearisation (1/√C vs d) for offset.
Common errors / improvements: Source is not a point — true separation is between effective centres; fit 1/√C = (d+d₀)/k. Background dominates at large d without subtraction. Count ≥60 s per point; longer at large d.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. RADIATION SOURCE — consult CLEAPSS/local rules. Per setup (teacher-supervised): sealed gamma source (e.g. Co-57, 5 µCi max), Geiger-Müller tube + counter/ratemeter, metre rule with source holder, lead absorbers, lead brick behind source. Record background count for at least 5 min before lesson. Source must be signed in/out per school policy. Do not leave unattended. Return to locked storage immediately after.

Title: Black body radiation (Stefan's law)
Aim: Investigate black-body radiation from a filament lamp.
Key variables: IV: lamp voltage → filament temperature T. DV: emitted power.
Method: 1. Variable supply → lamp; measure V and I → power P = VI. 2. Estimate T from resistance ratio (R/R₀) for tungsten. 3. Measure relative radiated power with light meter at fixed distance.
Measurements: V, I, R, light meter reading.
Analysis: P ∝ T⁴. Plot log P vs log T; expect gradient ≈ 4.
Safety: Lamp very hot — do not touch.
Data skills: Log-log plot; gradient → power-law exponent.
Common errors / improvements: Temperature estimate from R uses single α over huge T range — quote as estimate. Light meter misses IR and UV — relative, not absolute, power. Fix detector distance precisely. Expect gradient 3–5; discuss systematics not just 'agreement'.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per setup: Leslie cube or black-body approximation lamp, Stefan-Boltzmann sensor or calibrated thermopile, variable PSU (0–12 V), ammeter, voltmeter, ruler. Warm up sensor 10 min before lesson. Check PSU gives stable voltage at all set points.

Title: Measuring speed with light gates
Aim: Measure the instantaneous speed of a moving object using a light gate and interrupt card.
Key variables: Card length d (m), blocking time t (s); v = d/t.
Method: 1. Attach interrupt card of known length d to trolley. 2. Light gate connected to interface; set to measure time blocked. 3. Release trolley at different positions; record t. 4. Repeat ≥3× per run and average.
Measurements: Card length d, blocking time t.
Analysis: v = d/t. Quote Δv/v = Δd/d + Δt/t. Shorter card → more instantaneous but higher % Δd.
Safety: Trolley off bench — fit end stop.
Data skills: % uncertainty propagation; trade-off: shorter card → more instantaneous vs higher % error in d.
Common errors / improvements: Card not perpendicular to gate beam → effective length wrong; check alignment. Long card measures average v not instantaneous — use shortest card giving readable t (>1 ms). Trolley still accelerating as card passes if card is long relative to deceleration distance.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: 2 × light gates on stands, datalogger or interface, dynamics trolley or falling mass on string, card interrupt (10 cm wide). Set light gates at known separation (measure precisely). Check datalogger records both gates and calculates speed correctly. Test with a known object before class.

Title: Acceleration down a ramp
Aim: Measure acceleration of a trolley on an inclined ramp and compare with g sin θ.
Key variables: IV: ramp angle θ. DV: acceleration a.
Method: 1. Two light gates separated by distance s on ramp. Release trolley from rest. 2. Interface computes a = (v₂² − v₁²)/(2s). 3. Vary θ by raising end on books; measure θ from ramp dimensions.
Measurements: s, v₁, v₂, angle θ.
Analysis: Expect a = g sin θ − μg cos θ. Plot a vs sin θ; gradient ≈ g, y-intercept → friction.
Safety: Clamp ramp securely. Catch trolley at bottom.
Data skills: Linearisation (a vs sin θ); gradient → g; intercept → kinetic friction coefficient.
Common errors / improvements: Friction makes a < g sin θ — use a vs sin θ plot, not single-point comparison. Trolley wheels dirty → jerky motion; clean axles. Release without initial push — use a pin-release mechanism. Check sin θ formula with a sketch to avoid using complement angle.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: inclined runway (adjustable angle), dynamics trolley, 2 × light gates + datalogger, protractor, ruler, G-clamp. Adjust friction compensation before lesson: trolley should roll at constant speed on slight incline. Check light gates at measured separation.

Title: Newton's second law (air track)
Aim: Verify F = ma quantitatively using a linear air track.
Key variables: IV: F (Part A) or m (Part B). DV: acceleration a.
Method: 1. Air track levelled with bubble level. Glider with double-card; two light gates give a. 2. Part A: keep m_total constant; transfer masses between glider and hanging hanger. 3. Part B: keep F constant; add masses to glider.
Measurements: Hanger mass, glider mass, velocities at both gates.
Analysis: a vs F: straight line through origin, gradient = 1/m. a vs 1/m: straight line, gradient = F.
Safety: Fit end stops to track. Air-track compressor noise.
Data skills: Two-stage linearisation; gradient comparison; identifying zero-intercept conditions.
Common errors / improvements: Pulley friction and string mass → F ≠ hanger weight exactly; include string mass in m_total for high precision. Track not level → a varies with direction; re-level and verify with unpowered constant-v glide. Hanger oscillating → tension not constant; let it settle before releasing glider.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Per pair: linear air track + blower, two gliders (equal mass), light gates × 2 + datalogger, velcro bumpers for elastic collision, wax/pin for perfectly inelastic. Run blower for 5 min before lesson to reach steady state. Check gliders slide without touching track.

Title: Terminal velocity in glycerol
Aim: Measure terminal velocity of steel balls in glycerol; determine viscosity η.
Key variables: IV: ball radius r. DV: terminal velocity v_t.
Method: 1. Long measuring cylinder of glycerol; mark two reference lines well below surface (~30 cm apart). 2. Drop ball gently; time between two lines. 3. Verify terminal: add a third line — times(1→2) and (2→3) should be equal. 4. Repeat for different ball sizes.
Measurements: r (micrometer), fall time t, line separation s → v_t = s/t.
Analysis: Stokes' law: 6πηrv_t = (4/3)πr³(ρ_ball − ρ_liq)g. Plot v_t vs r²; gradient → η.
Safety: Glycerol slippery if spilled. Tall cylinder — clamp it securely.
Data skills: Linearisation (v_t vs r²); checking terminal condition; systematic wall-effect correction.
Common errors / improvements: Ball not at terminal v at first line — use third line to verify. Wall effect: if r_ball/r_cylinder >0.05, Stokes underestimates drag. Use wide cylinder. Reaction time dominates for fast small balls — use video analysis. Viscosity of glycerol changes ~7%/°C — record and quote temperature.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: tall measuring cylinder (500 cm³) filled with glycerol, ball bearings of different diameters (3–8 mm), stopwatch, ruler, micrometer, balance. Fill cylinders the day before to allow bubbles to clear. Keep glycerol at room temperature — viscosity is highly temperature-dependent.

Title: Projectile motion (horizontal launch)
Aim: Verify independence of horizontal and vertical motion; measure launch speed.
Key variables: IV: launch height h. DV: horizontal range x.
Method: 1. Ball rolls off horizontal track at bench edge. Carbon paper on floor marks landing. 2. Measure h (bench to floor) and x (horizontal from launch point). 3. Repeat ≥5 heights; ≥5 landings per height (average x).
Measurements: h, x (averaged from carbon-paper marks).
Analysis: t = √(2h/g); v = x/t = constant (same launch track). Plot x² vs h; gradient = 2v²/g → v.
Safety: Ball landing area — keep feet clear. Ball bouncing under furniture.
Data skills: Quadratic linearisation (x² vs h); using gradient to find launch speed v independently of g.
Common errors / improvements: Ball must leave track horizontally — add a short flat section at the end. Measure x from the actual launch point, not from the edge of the bench top. Average 5+ landing marks per height; spread indicates random error. Use steel ball, not ping-pong — air resistance matters for light balls.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: ramp, ball bearing, carbon paper, plain white paper on floor, clamp and stand, ruler, plumb line. Test setup — ensure ball lands on carbon paper. Carbon paper: dull side up. Replace carbon paper between groups.

Title: Conservation of momentum (air track)
Aim: Verify conservation of linear momentum in elastic and inelastic collisions.
Key variables: Masses and velocities of two gliders before and after collision.
Method: 1. Air track with two gliders, each with double-card and light gate. 2. Elastic: magnetic bumpers; record v₁, v₂ before and v₁', v₂' after. 3. Inelastic: Velcro pads; gliders stick; record combined v after. 4. Weigh each glider assembly.
Measurements: Masses m₁, m₂; velocities from light gates.
Analysis: Verify Σmv before = Σmv after. Compute % discrepancy. Check KE: elastic → conserved; inelastic → lost.
Safety: Fit end stops. Don't leave air track unattended.
Data skills: Vector sign conventions; fractional discrepancy; KE audit to classify collision type.
Common errors / improvements: Assign positive direction first — all velocities as signed scalars. Place gates close to collision point — friction between gates changes momentum. Include mass of card and bumpers in glider mass. Quote uncertainty in p_before and p_after before claiming 'verified'.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min — see MECH-03 for air track setup. Additional: equal and unequal mass gliders, velocity cards (10 cm). Check datalogger records and calculates momentum.

Title: Impulse and change in momentum
Aim: Verify the impulse-momentum theorem: J = ∫F dt = Δ(mv).
Key variables: F(t) trace from force sensor; v before and after from light gates.
Method: 1. Glider on air track collides with spring buffer attached to force sensor. 2. Data logger records F(t) at ≥1 kHz; light gates record v in and v out. 3. Compute impulse = area under F–t (trapezium / built-in integration). 4. Compute Δp = m(v_out − v_in) (with sign).
Measurements: Mass m, v_in, v_out, F(t) trace.
Analysis: Compare J = ∫F dt with Δp = mΔv. Both in N·s.
Safety: Force sensor rated for peak expected. Glider end stops.
Data skills: Numerical integration (area under F–t); vector sign of Δv; matching two independent measurements.
Common errors / improvements: Force sensor saturation → clipped peak → underestimated impulse. Verify peak < sensor rating. Sampling rate ≥1 kHz for collisions lasting ~10 ms. Δv is signed — if rebound, v_out is negative: Δv = v_out − v_in, not v_out + v_in. Zero force sensor offset before each run.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: force sensor + datalogger, dynamics trolley, rubber bumper or elastic. Calibrate force sensor before lesson. Check datalogger records area under F-t curve.

Title: Friction (static and kinetic)
Aim: Measure coefficients of static (μ_s) and kinetic (μ_k) friction.
Key variables: IV: normal force N. DV: friction force F.
Method: Horizontal pull: block on surface; string over pulley to mass hanger. μ_s: add masses slowly until block just slips; F = m_hanger·g at that point. μ_k: find mass giving steady motion after a gentle push. Vary block mass to get several (F, N) pairs. Tilted ramp option for μ_s: raise until slip; μ_s = tan θ.
Measurements: Hanger mass at slip (μ_s) and at constant motion (μ_k); block mass.
Analysis: Plot F vs N; gradient = μ. Compare μ_s and μ_k.
Safety: Cushion floor below hanger. Clamp tilted ramp.
Data skills: Gradient (F vs N) → μ; ratio μ_s/μ_k; equilibrium analysis on inclined plane.
Common errors / improvements: Clean surfaces with IPA — oil/dust changes μ significantly. Kinetic measurement: block moves in stick-slip bursts — quote average. Keep string horizontal by placing pulley at block-string height. Surface area should not affect μ (Amonton–Coulomb) — investigate this as extension.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: block of wood, spring balance or force sensor, masses to add on top, ruler, various surface materials (sandpaper, smooth board, fabric). Ensure spring balance is zeroed and calibrated.

Title: Centre of mass (irregular lamina)
Aim: Locate the centre of mass of an irregular lamina using plumb lines.
Key variables: Intersection of plumb lines from ≥3 suspension points.
Method: 1. Cut irregular shape from stiff card; punch ≥3 holes near edge. 2. Suspend from pin through one hole; attach plumb line. Wait until still. 3. Mark plumb-line direction on card (two crosses, join with ruler). 4. Repeat from two more holes. 5. Intersection = centre of mass. Test by balancing on pin tip.
Measurements: Geometric positions of plumb lines.
Analysis: Three lines should meet at a single point. Optionally predict for an L-shape lamina (sum of rectangles).
Safety: Pin sharp — handle carefully.
Data skills: Geometric construction; principle of moments; predicting vs measuring.
Common errors / improvements: Plumb line still swinging → wait until stationary. Friction at pin holds card at slight angle from true vertical hang — make holes slightly larger than pin. Mark line with two crosses then join — tracing along string (which has thickness) gives offset.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: irregular card shapes (pre-cut, ~A5), plumb line, pin-board, pins, ruler. Pre-cut irregular laminas. Ensure pin-boards are available.

Title: Moments and equilibrium of a metre rule
Aim: Verify the principle of moments.
Key variables: Clockwise and anticlockwise moments about a pivot must balance.
Method: 1. Balance metre rule on knife-edge; find unloaded balance point (rule's own centre of mass). 2. Hang mass m₁ at distance d₁; adjust m₂ at d₂ until balanced horizontally. 3. Repeat for ≥5 (m₁, d₁) combinations.
Measurements: Masses m₁, m₂; distances d₁, d₂ from pivot.
Analysis: Verify m₁d₁ = m₂d₂. Compute % discrepancy. Extension: solve for unknown mass.
Safety: Masses can fall — cushion floor.
Data skills: Equilibrium equations; including rule's own weight when pivot ≠ centre of mass.
Common errors / improvements: Pivot at rule's unloaded balance point eliminates rule's own moment. String loops slide along rule — read d to the centre of the loop. Rule not horizontal when 'balanced' — slight tilt means moments aren't equal. Parallax reading distance on scale.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: metre rule with hole at centre, pivot (pencil on block), slotted masses × 4 pairs, ruler. Check metre rule balances at 50 cm on pivot. Sand edges if needed.

Title: Centripetal force (rubber bung)
Aim: Investigate the relationship between centripetal force and angular velocity.
Key variables: IV: hanging mass M (→ F = Mg). DV: period T for fixed radius r.
Method: 1. Rubber bung on string through glass tube; hanging mass provides tension. 2. Swirl bung so paper marker holds just below tube (T = Mg). 3. Time 20 revolutions; T = time/20. 4. Repeat for 4–5 different hanging masses.
Measurements: Hanging mass M, period T, radius r (string length above tube), bung mass m.
Analysis: F = mω²r = m(2π/T)²r. Plot F vs 1/T²; gradient = 4π²mr.
Safety: Clear space — bung can fly off. Goggles. Inspect string for fraying.
Data skills: Linearisation (F vs 1/T²); gradient comparison with theory; identifying friction at tube as systematic error.
Common errors / improvements: Friction at tube top → T < Mg (effective force underestimated). Lubricate tube rim. Paper marker drifts → radius changes mid-run; practise before recording data. Bung path not horizontal → actual radius = r sin θ; correct for tilt. Time ≥20 revolutions. Let hanging mass settle before counting.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: rubber bung on string (~50 cm), glass tube (as guide), slotted masses as centripetal force, stopwatch, ruler, tape marker on string. Check string is not fraying. Tape safety note — do not let bung fly at face.

Title: Damping of a mass-spring oscillator
Aim: Investigate how oscillation amplitude decays with time under different damping conditions.
Key variables: IV: drag-card area. DV: amplitude decay over time.
Method: 1. Vertical mass-spring system; attach drag card to mass. 2. Pull mass ~5 cm and release; record amplitude at each cycle using motion sensor or by eye on ruler. 3. Try: no card, small card, large card. Take ~30 cycles for light damping.
Measurements: Amplitude A_n at each cycle n, period T.
Analysis: Light damping: A_n = A₀ e^(−γn). Plot ln A vs n; gradient = −γ. Quality factor Q ≈ π/γ.
Safety: Clamp stand securely. Ensure mass oscillates vertically only.
Data skills: Log-linear plot (ln A vs n); exponential decay; Q-factor from gradient.
Common errors / improvements: Read amplitude at peak — use motion sensor or video for accuracy. Lateral swing contaminates data — guide oscillation vertically. Restrict exponential fit to region where A >> reading uncertainty. Distinguish underdamped (oscillates with decaying amplitude) from overdamped (no oscillation) for large card.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: mass on spring (as AL-12), damping material options (cardboard vanes of different sizes), ruler, stopwatch or motion sensor. Ensure spring is not overloaded.

Title: Resonance (driven mass-spring)
Aim: Investigate amplitude of a driven oscillator as a function of driving frequency.
Key variables: IV: driving frequency f. DV: steady-state amplitude A.
Method: 1. Mass on spring driven by vibration generator (signal generator). 2. At each f, wait ≥30 s for steady state; measure peak-to-peak amplitude. 3. Sweep f through f₀ in small steps (≤1% near peak). 4. Repeat with and without drag card.
Measurements: f, A.
Analysis: Plot A vs f. Peak at f₀ = (1/2π)√(k/m). Q = f₀/Δf (FWHM).
Safety: Secure clamp stand. Large amplitude at resonance — restrain travel range.
Data skills: FWHM analysis; Q-factor; effect of damping on peak amplitude and width.
Common errors / improvements: Wait for steady state before recording — transient inflates amplitude near f₀. Use fine frequency steps near f₀ or miss the actual peak. Keep driver amplitude small to avoid mechanical clipping. Distinguish f₀ of free oscillation from resonant driving frequency (they differ under heavy damping).
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min — see MECH-12. Additional: signal generator + vibration driver to drive the system. Check signal generator frequency range covers resonant frequency of system.

Title: Spring constant (static and dynamic methods)
Aim: Determine the spring constant k by both static (Hooke's law) and dynamic (SHM period) methods; compare.
Key variables: Static: IV = force F, DV = extension x. Dynamic: IV = mass m, DV = period T.
Method: Static: load spring in 10 g steps from 0 to 300 g; record extension. Plot F vs x; gradient = k. Dynamic: time 20 oscillations for each of 5–6 masses (50–400 g); T = time/20. Plot T² vs m; gradient = 4π²/k.
Measurements: Static: F (N), extension x (m). Dynamic: mass m (kg), period T (s).
Analysis: Static k from gradient of F vs x. Dynamic k from gradient of T² vs m = 4π²/k. Compare the two values; any discrepancy reflects spring mass effect in dynamic method.
Safety: G-clamp stand. Eye protection. Stand back near elastic limit.
Data skills: Two independent gradient methods for same constant; effective mass correction; % agreement between methods.
Common errors / improvements: Static method: parallax on ruler — clamp rule vertically, read at eye level with fiducial marker. Dynamic method: must add m_spring/3 to each hanging mass for accurate k — without this, k appears too low at small m. Using too few masses in dynamic method (only 2–3 points) → noisy gradient; use ≥6 masses. Spring oscillating laterally — guide with a straw or use a stiffer spring.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: spring (known k), slotted masses + hanger, clamp stand, ruler, stopwatch. Identical to GCSE-05 but with quantitative k determination. Provide at least 2 different springs of different stiffness.

Title: Springs in series and parallel
Aim: Verify theoretical rules for combined spring constants: series (1/k_tot = Σ1/kᵢ) and parallel (k_tot = Σkᵢ).
Key variables: IV: spring configuration. DV: effective spring constant k_eff.
Method: 1. Measure k of each individual spring by static loading (F vs extension). 2. Connect two springs in series (end to end); measure k_series by same method. 3. Connect in parallel (side by side, same attachment points); measure k_parallel. 4. Compare measured k with predicted values.
Measurements: Individual k₁, k₂; combined k_series, k_parallel.
Analysis: Predict k_series = k₁k₂/(k₁+k₂); k_parallel = k₁+k₂. Check % agreement.
Safety: G-clamp stand. Eye protection.
Data skills: Predicted vs measured comparison; % discrepancy; propagated uncertainty through 1/k formula.
Common errors / improvements: Springs in series must hang freely and not rub against each other — mount with small gap. Parallel springs must be exactly the same length unstretched, or one takes all the load at first. Contact at the join in series → effective k is higher than predicted (springs compress against each other). Weigh the spring-connector mass and include it as load on the lower spring in series.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min — see MAT-01. Additional: 2 identical springs for series and parallel arrangements. Pre-rig series and parallel mounts.

Title: Elastic and plastic deformation of a wire
Aim: Distinguish elastic and plastic deformation by loading and unloading a metal wire; identify elastic limit.
Key variables: IV: load (N). DV: extension (mm) on loading and unloading.
Method: 1. Clamp a ~60 cm copper wire (SWG 26); attach a marker and vernier/mm scale. Small pre-load to straighten. 2. Add masses in 100 g steps; record marker position. Continue well past the expected elastic limit (~4–6 N). 3. Remove masses in same steps; record marker position at each unloading point. 4. Plot loading and unloading extension on the same axes.
Measurements: Load F (N), extension on loading, extension on unloading.
Analysis: Plot F vs extension for both load and unload curves. Elastic region: loading and unloading curves coincide; permanent deformation shown by non-zero extension at zero load. Area between curves = energy dissipated (hysteresis).
Safety: Wire may snap — goggles, safety screen. Cushion floor.
Data skills: Hysteresis loop area (energy dissipated); identifying elastic limit from divergence of curves; permanent set.
Common errors / improvements: Elastic limit and limit of proportionality are NOT the same — proportionality limit is where F vs x deviates from a straight line; elastic limit is where permanent deformation begins (detected only on unloading). Loading and unloading must be at the same positions — add / remove one mass at a time and wait for creep to settle (~10 s each). Wire creep in the plastic region means extension increases with time even at constant load — wait longer at high loads. Short wire gives small extensions → large % uncertainty; use ≥50 cm.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min. Per pair: long (~2 m) copper wire on board (as AL-02), masses up to 5 kg, vernier or travelling microscope to measure extension. Note: wire yields irreversibly at elastic limit — replace wire between classes if overloaded.

Title: Elastic hysteresis (rubber band)
Aim: Investigate elastic hysteresis in a rubber band; calculate energy stored and dissipated.
Key variables: IV: load. DV: extension on loading and unloading.
Method: 1. Hang rubber band from clamp; attach mass hanger. Record unloaded length. 2. Load in 100 g steps to ~800 g; record length at each. 3. Unload in same steps; record length. 4. Check rubber band returns to original length (if not, it was over-stretched).
Measurements: Force F (N), extension x (m) on loading and unloading.
Analysis: Plot F vs x for loading and unloading on same axes (hysteresis loop). Area under loading curve = energy stored. Area under unloading curve = energy returned. Difference = energy dissipated as heat.
Safety: Masses can fall. Overstretching rubber snaps suddenly — goggles.
Data skills: Hysteresis loop area by counting squares or trapezium rule; energy stored vs dissipated; comparison with metal spring (no hysteresis).
Common errors / improvements: Rate of loading matters for rubber — load slowly and consistently; fast stretching increases hysteresis artificially. Temperature rises as rubber is stretched (Gough-Joule effect) — allow to cool before unloading for standard comparison. Rubber doesn't obey Hooke's law — don't try to extract a 'spring constant'. Wide rubber bands are easier to handle than thin ones but give smaller extension.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: rubber band, clamp stand, ruler, slotted masses up to 500 g. Use same rubber bands throughout — natural rubber, not silicone. Provide fresh band for each group as rubber fatigue affects hysteresis.

Title: Stress-strain curves for different materials
Aim: Compare stress-strain behaviour of mild steel, copper and nylon wires; identify key features of each curve.
Key variables: IV: stress σ. DV: strain ε.
Method: 1. For each wire (~1 m, SWG 26): clamp, measure L and d (micrometer, ≥3 readings). Pre-load to straighten. 2. Add loads in 200 g steps; record marker position. Continue to fracture (or until clearly plastic). 3. Unload part-way at a point in the plastic region; show permanent set. 4. Plot σ vs ε for each material on the same axes.
Measurements: Load F, diameter d, original length L, extension x at each load.
Analysis: σ = F/A, ε = x/L. Identify from graph: proportionality limit, elastic limit, yield point, UTS, fracture. Young modulus E = gradient of linear region.
Safety: Wire may fracture suddenly — safety screen, goggles, lab coat. Cushion floor. Mark floor exclusion zone.
Data skills: Stress–strain plot with labelled features; gradient → E; comparing three curves on same axes; identifying ductile vs brittle behaviour.
Common errors / improvements: Mild steel shows a clear yield point (load drops suddenly) — many students miss this because they're loading continuously. Pause and observe. Nylon shows significant creep — wait at least 30 s at each load for stable reading. Fracture is sudden and wire recoils — never lean over the apparatus at high loads. Diameter varies along the wire (necking in plastic region) — measure d before the experiment, not after deformation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: tensile test samples (copper, polythene, glass fibre, rubber strips), force sensor + datalogger or hanging masses, ruler, micrometer. Pre-cut strips to uniform width. Measure cross-sectional area before class.

Title: Viscosity: comparing liquids (falling ball)
Aim: Compare the viscosity of different liquids (or glycerol/water mixtures) using Stokes' law.
Key variables: IV: liquid viscosity (different solutions). DV: terminal velocity v_t of ball.
Method: 1. Prepare 4 glycerol/water mixtures (0%, 30%, 60%, 100% glycerol by volume). 2. For each, drop a 3 mm steel ball and time fall between two marks (verify terminal velocity with third mark). 3. Record v_t for each mixture. Measure liquid density ρ with density bottle or specific gravity bottle.
Measurements: v_t, ball radius r, liquid density ρ_liq, ball density ρ_ball.
Analysis: η = 2r²(ρ_ball − ρ_liq)g / (9v_t). Plot η (calculated) against glycerol concentration; verify exponential rise with concentration.
Safety: Glycerol spills are very slippery. Tall cylinders — clamp firmly.
Data skills: Stokes' law application; wall-effect correction; viscosity calculation from multiple variables; % uncertainty propagation.
Common errors / improvements: As MECH-04 (terminal velocity) — all the same pitfalls apply. Liquid density must be measured, not assumed — glycerol/water mixtures differ from tabulated pure values. Temperature sensitivity: run all liquids at the same temperature, or correct using tabulated T-dependence. Air bubbles trapped in glycerol lower apparent viscosity — stir gently and let stand overnight.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: tall cylinders filled with glycerol, water, cooking oil; ball bearings of known diameter; stopwatch; ruler; micrometer. See MECH-04 for glycerol filling instructions. Prepare 3 cylinders per group.

Title: Surface tension (thin wire loop / capillary rise)
Aim: Demonstrate surface tension and estimate its value for water and surfactant solutions.
Key variables: IV: liquid (water, soapy water, various concentrations). DV: force to pull loop from surface / capillary rise height.
Method: Wire-loop method: 1. Attach a thin wire loop (~5 cm diameter) to a force sensor. 2. Lower loop onto liquid surface; slowly raise. Record maximum force F just before film breaks. 3. Surface tension γ = F / (2 × perimeter) = F / (2 × 2πr) for a circular loop. 4. Repeat for water, soapy water, ethanol. Capillary rise method (alternative): Insert a capillary tube in liquid; measure rise height h; γ = ρghr / (2 cos θ).
Measurements: Force F (wire-loop), or rise height h and capillary radius r.
Analysis: γ (N/m) for each liquid. Compare with tabulated values: water ≈ 0.073 N/m; ethanol ≈ 0.023 N/m.
Safety: Force sensor is fragile — do not overload. Glassware on stable surface.
Data skills: Surface energy concept; force per unit length; capillary rise calculation; distinguishing demo from quantitative experiment.
Common errors / improvements: Wire-loop method: film must form cleanly — the loop wire must be very clean (degrease with IPA). Force sensor resolution limits precision — γ differences between similar solutions may be undetectable. Capillary rise: contact angle θ is assumed 0° for water on glass; verify with tabulated value. Draft from air-con or windows causes surface ripples and inconsistent film formation — perform in still air.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per setup: fine capillary tubes (different bores), trough of water + dye, ruler, wire loops on handle (for surface tension). Have coloured water (food dye) ready. Ensure capillary tubes are clean and dry before experiment.

Title: Fluid flow: Poiseuille / volume flow rate
Aim: Investigate how volume flow rate Q depends on the pressure head Δh for water through a tube.
Key variables: IV: pressure head Δh (height of water above outlet). DV: volume flow rate Q.
Method: 1. Clamp a tube (~2 cm diameter, 30 cm long) vertically; fill reservoir above it. 2. Set height of water surface above outlet h; collect outflow in measuring cylinder for 30 s. 3. Q = volume / time. Repeat for 5–6 values of h.
Measurements: h (m), volume collected V (mL), time t (s) → Q = V/t.
Analysis: Q ∝ Δh for laminar flow (Poiseuille). Plot Q vs h; expect straight line through origin. Extension: vary tube diameter or length to verify Q ∝ r⁴/L.
Safety: Mop spills. Clamp reservoir securely — water is heavy.
Data skills: Linear plot Q vs h; gradient proportional to r⁴; laminar vs turbulent flow discussion.
Common errors / improvements: Flow may be turbulent (Re > 2000) for a wide tube at high head — Q vs h becomes nonlinear. Use a narrow tube (≤5 mm diameter) for laminar flow at school pressures. Meniscus formation at outlet drips rather than streams → measure during steady flow. Air bubbles in tube reduce effective cross-section — prime tube before measuring. Level the bench and check reservoir height is measured vertically, not along a slanted pipe.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: tube of known bore, funnel + reservoir, ruler, stopwatch, measuring cylinder, clamp stand. Fill reservoir before lesson. Flush tubes to remove air bubbles.

Title: Bernoulli principle (Venturi tube / aerofoil)
Aim: Demonstrate the Bernoulli principle using a Venturi tube or flow-past-an-aerofoil setup.
Key variables: IV: cross-sectional area of tube at different points. DV: pressure (manometer height difference).
Method: Venturi: 1. Water flows through constricted tube connected to a manometer at wide and narrow sections. 2. Higher flow rate → greater manometer difference. 3. Measure h at wide and narrow section; compare with ½ρv² + ρgh = const prediction. Aerofoil demo: pass air over an aerofoil model; observe tissue paper / smoke deflection.
Measurements: Manometer height h, tube diameters (known), flow rate Q.
Analysis: Bernoulli: P + ½ρv² = const. Pressure lower where v higher (narrow section). Quantitative: ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²); v from Q and area.
Safety: Water spills — mop promptly. Ensure reservoir clamped.
Data skills: Application of continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) and Bernoulli equation; qualitative and quantitative versions.
Common errors / improvements: Students confuse Bernoulli (steady, incompressible, no viscosity) with everyday lift explanations. The 'equal transit time' myth for aerofoil lift — correct carefully. Manometer readings fluctuate with flow pulsation — average over several readings. Venturi works best with steady laminar flow — avoid turbulence by having a smooth entry region.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per setup: Venturi tube + manometer, aerofoil on stand, air supply. Check all joints sealed. Calibrate manometer. Adjust air supply to give measurable pressure differences without flooding manometer.

Title: Conical pendulum
Aim: Investigate circular motion using a conical pendulum; verify T = 2π√(L cos θ / g).
Key variables: IV: string length L or rotation speed (period T). DV: angle θ or radius r.
Method: 1. Suspend a mass on a string from a pivot; spin it in a horizontal circle. 2. Measure the angle θ the string makes with the vertical using a protractor, or from r and L geometrically. 3. Time 20 revolutions; T = time/20. 4. Repeat for different lengths and rotation speeds.
Measurements: String length L, radius r, period T, angle θ.
Analysis: T = 2π√(L cos θ / g). Also: tan θ = ω²r/g = 4π²r/(gT²). Plot r vs T²; gradient = g/4π². Or plot cos θ vs T²; gradient = g·L/4π².
Safety: Clear space — mass can fly outward if string breaks. Goggles. Inspect string before use.
Data skills: Trigonometric geometry; two equivalent linearisations (r vs T², or cos θ vs T²); identifying centripetal condition.
Common errors / improvements: Angle θ hard to read accurately while mass is spinning — photograph from the side or measure r and L geometrically and compute θ = arcsin(r/L). Pivot friction causes string to wrap — use a smooth bearing or a hook with low friction. Period measurement: count revolutions from a fixed reference point; 20 revolutions minimum. At small angles r is small → difficult to measure r accurately; work at θ > 15°.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min — see MECH-11. Extend string length to ~80 cm. Provide protractor to measure half-angle.

Title: Atwood machine (g determination)
Aim: Use an Atwood machine to measure g by controlling net force and total mass.
Key variables: IV: mass difference Δm (net force). DV: acceleration a.
Method: 1. Hang equal masses m on either side of a low-friction pulley (Atwood's machine). 2. Add a small rider mass δm to one side; release from rest. 3. Light gates or ticker tape give acceleration a. 4. Vary δm (keeping 2m + δm constant).
Measurements: Masses m, δm; acceleration a from light gates.
Analysis: a = δm·g / (2m + δm). For small δm: a ≈ δm·g/(2m). Plot a vs δm; gradient = g/(2m). Solve for g.
Safety: Masses falling — soft pad below. Keep fingers clear of moving string.
Data skills: Linear plot (a vs δm for fixed 2m); gradient → g; systematic error from pulley friction and string mass.
Common errors / improvements: Pulley friction is the dominant systematic error — use a low-friction pulley (ball-bearing or air bearing). String mass not negligible if string is heavy — use thin nylon thread. δm must be small compared to 2m for the linear approximation to hold; otherwise use full formula. Rider mass δm must be placed symmetrically or it causes a pendulum oscillation. Acceleration is small (~0.1–0.5 m s⁻²) — light gates give better precision than ticker tape here.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: Atwood machine (pulley over clamp stand), slotted masses (2 × 200 g + extra 10 g rider), light gate + datalogger or ticker-tape timer. Check pulley rotates freely — oil if stiff. Ensure masses can drop at least 50 cm.

Title: Torque and couples (beam balance)
Aim: Investigate torques and couples using a balanced beam; verify the couple = Fd relationship.
Key variables: IV: force separation d. DV: couple magnitude.
Method: 1. Support a uniform beam (metre rule) at its centre on a pivot. 2. Apply two equal but opposite forces at different separations d using spring balances or force sensors. 3. Verify equilibrium: Σtorques = 0. 4. Vary F and d; for a couple, measure turning effect with a torque sensor or infer from equilibrium condition.
Measurements: Forces F₁, F₂; distances d₁, d₂ from pivot.
Analysis: Couple C = F·d. Verify C = F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ for equilibrium. Extension: measure reaction at the pivot (should be zero for a pure couple).
Safety: Spring balances can spring back if released — handle gently.
Data skills: Couple vs single torque distinction; principle of moments applied to beam; zero pivot reaction for a pure couple.
Common errors / improvements: Students confuse couple (two equal opposite forces, no net force) with a single torque (one force about a pivot). Spring balances must be read perpendicular to the beam — angled forces reduce the effective moment. Beam must be truly horizontal — use spirit level and adjust pivot position. Measure d between the lines of action of the forces, not the length of the beam between attachment points.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: see MECH-10. Add: forcemeter to apply couples. Ensure pivot is frictionless.

Title: Angular momentum and gyroscope (demo)
Aim: Demonstrate conservation of angular momentum and gyroscopic precession qualitatively.
Key variables: Qualitative: spinning wheel resists change in orientation; precession rate increases as spin slows.
Method: 1. Spin a bicycle wheel rapidly using the string pull. 2. Suspend axle from one end by a string — wheel precesses rather than falling. 3. Observe precession direction relative to spin direction (right-hand rule). 4. Quantitative extension: time precession rate ω_p = τ/L = mgd/(Iω_spin). Measure mass of wheel m, distance d from string to centre of mass, spin period T_spin.
Measurements: Precession period T_prec, spin period T_spin, mass m, d.
Analysis: ω_p = τ / L = mgd / (Iω). Verify precession slows as wheel slows.
Safety: Keep fingers away from spokes. Wheel can swing outward suddenly — clear area around apparatus.
Data skills: Vector cross-product (L = Iω direction); precession rate formula; qualitative angular momentum conservation.
Common errors / improvements: Students expect the wheel to fall — the surprise of precession is the teaching point. Discuss before the demo. Quantitative precession rate measurement is difficult because spin decays continuously due to friction. Precession itself causes the wheel to slowly descend (nutation) — this is normal and can be shown. Right-hand rule for angular momentum must be established before demo or the direction of precession seems arbitrary.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. DEMO ONLY. Gyroscope (large spinning top or bicycle wheel gyroscope). Spin up with motor or by hand. Check bearings are free. Ensure safe space — gyroscope may precess unexpectedly.

Title: Ohm's law verification
Aim: Verify that current through a resistor is directly proportional to voltage (Ohm's law).
Key variables: IV: voltage V across resistor. DV: current I through resistor.
Method: 1. Connect fixed resistor (e.g. 10 Ω, 22 Ω, 47 Ω) in series with ammeter; voltmeter in parallel with resistor. 2. Variable supply (or potential divider) from 0 to 6 V in 0.5 V steps; record I at each V. 3. Reduce V back to 0; record descending values (check for heating drift). 4. Repeat for two more resistor values.
Measurements: V (V), I (A) for each resistor.
Analysis: Plot I vs V for each resistor; expect straight line through origin with gradient = 1/R. Verify R = V/I is constant at each point (tabulate). Compare gradient with marked resistance value.
Safety: Low voltage only. Check component ratings.
Data skills: Linear plot through origin; gradient = 1/R; constant ratio R = V/I test; % difference from marked value.
Common errors / improvements: Heating of resistor at high current → resistance drifts upward; I vs V curve curves slightly. Use low wattage (≤1 W) or switch off between readings. Ammeter resistance adds to circuit resistance — for accurate R, use four-terminal (Kelvin) connection or correct for ammeter V drop. Potentiometer (potential divider) gives access to V = 0; simple variable supply does not — this matters for verifying the line passes through origin.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: variable PSU (0–6 V), ammeter, voltmeter, various fixed resistors (10–1000 Ω), switch, connecting leads. Check all instruments are working. Test PSU output with a multimeter.

Title: I–V characteristics: thermistor and LDR
Aim: Investigate how current through a thermistor and an LDR varies with voltage; relate to resistance change with temperature and light.
Key variables: IV: voltage V. DV: current I. Secondary IV: temperature (thermistor) or light level (LDR).
Method: Thermistor: 1. Same I–V circuit as GCSE-03. Immerse NTC thermistor in water bath; vary temperature 20–80 °C. 2. At each temperature, sweep V 0–6 V and record I; plot I–V curve. 3. Calculate R = V/I at a fixed V for each temperature. Plot R vs T. LDR: 1. Cover LDR with card (dark); sweep V and record I. 2. Illuminate at fixed, increasing light levels (measured with lux meter); repeat sweep at each. 3. Plot R vs illuminance.
Measurements: V, I, temperature T (thermistor) or illuminance E (LDR).
Analysis: I–V curves become steeper as T rises (thermistor) or light increases (LDR) — resistance falls. For thermistor: plot ln R vs 1/T (Kelvin); expect straight line (Arrhenius behaviour).
Safety: Water bath — electrical insulation of thermistor leads. Beware hot water.
Data skills: Family of I–V curves; R vs T or R vs E secondary plot; ln R vs 1/T linearisation (Arrhenius).
Common errors / improvements: NTC thermistor heats itself if current is large → self-heating error; use low V or a high series resistor to limit I. LDR: ambient light leaking around the cover changes the 'dark' reading — use a light-tight box. Comparing I–V curves at different T: axes must be consistent across all curves. Kelvin not Celsius in ln R vs 1/T — common exam error.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: as ELEC-01 plus thermistor (NTC, 10 kΩ at 25 °C), LDR, water bath or Bunsen for temperature variation, torch. Pre-wire circuits. Ensure thermistors are not cracked.

Title: Potential divider circuits
Aim: Investigate how output voltage of a potential divider depends on the ratio of resistances.
Key variables: IV: resistance ratio R₁/(R₁+R₂). DV: output voltage V_out.
Method: 1. Set up potential divider: two resistors R₁ and R₂ in series across a fixed supply V_in. 2. Measure V_out across R₂ with a high-impedance voltmeter. 3. Vary R₁ and R₂ (keep R₁+R₂ roughly constant for fair comparison); record V_out. 4. Extension: replace R₂ with an LDR or thermistor; show V_out changes with light/temperature.
Measurements: R₁, R₂, V_in, V_out.
Analysis: V_out = V_in × R₂/(R₁+R₂). Plot V_out vs R₂/(R₁+R₂); expect straight line through origin with gradient V_in.
Safety: Low voltage. Check component ratings.
Data skills: Linear proportionality; voltmeter loading effect; application to sensor circuits.
Common errors / improvements: Voltmeter resistance loads the circuit — V_out drops below the predicted value. Use a high-impedance digital voltmeter. Show loading effect explicitly by connecting a low-value load resistor across V_out. Students often confuse which resistor is 'top' and which is 'bottom' — draw and label the circuit first. Variable resistor (rheostat) as R₁: resistance varies non-linearly with the slider unless it's a linear-taper type — verify with ohmmeter.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: 2 fixed resistors (e.g. 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ), voltmeter (high impedance), 9 V battery or PSU, connecting leads. Provide range of resistors so students can build different ratio dividers.

Title: Series and parallel circuits (Kirchhoff verification)
Aim: Verify Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) and voltage law (KVL) in simple series and parallel networks.
Key variables: Currents at junctions (KCL); voltages around loops (KVL).
Method: 1. Series circuit: 3 resistors in series across a fixed supply. Measure V across each resistor and across the supply; measure I (single ammeter, then move to each branch). Verify: V_total = ΣVᵢ; I same throughout. 2. Parallel circuit: 3 resistors in parallel. Measure I through each branch and total I; measure V across each (should all equal supply V). Verify: I_total = ΣIᵢ; V same across all branches.
Measurements: V and I at each component in both configurations.
Analysis: KVL: ΣV around any loop = 0. KCL: ΣI into a node = ΣI out. Compute % discrepancy; explain any systematic offsets (meter resistance, contact resistance).
Safety: Low voltage. Check component ratings.
Data skills: Algebraic loop equations; node equations; systematic vs random error discussion.
Common errors / improvements: Ammeter in the wrong position (parallel instead of series) blows the fuse or shorts the component — always series. Voltmeter takes a small current — for parallel circuits this alters branch currents slightly; use high-impedance meter. Loose connections give variable contact resistance → voltages don't add up. Check all connections. Including battery internal resistance in KVL — supply voltage is terminal pd, not EMF; measure V_supply with voltmeter in circuit.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: 2–3 lamps or resistors, ammeters × 3, voltmeter, PSU, leads. Pre-check all lamps work. Mark junction points clearly on circuit boards if using them.

Title: Capacitor charging (RC circuit)
Aim: Investigate capacitor charging through a resistor; compare time constant with discharge.
Key variables: DV: voltage V_C across capacitor over time t during charging.
Method: 1. Same RC circuit as AL-07 but switch to charging position. 2. From V_C = 0, switch to charge; record V_C every 5 s (or use data logger). 3. Plot V_C vs t; also plot ln(V_in − V_C) vs t. 4. Compare τ_charge with τ_discharge from AL-07 (should be equal = RC).
Measurements: V_C, t during charging; V_in.
Analysis: V_C = V_in(1 − e^(−t/RC)). Rearrange: ln(V_in − V_C) = −t/RC + ln(V_in). Plot ln(V_in − V_C) vs t; gradient = −1/RC.
Safety: Discharge capacitor before reconnecting. Check capacitor polarity.
Data skills: Log-linear linearisation; comparing charge and discharge τ; systematic error if V_in not steady.
Common errors / improvements: V_in must be stable during charging — use a regulated supply; a battery is ideal. Voltmeter loading (finite impedance in parallel with C) shortens apparent τ — same issue as AL-07. V_C approaches V_in asymptotically — hard to see the tail; ln(V_in − V_C) plot reveals it clearly but small errors in V_in cause large errors in ln(V_in − V_C) near full charge. Stop recording before V_C reaches 95% V_in (the log plot becomes unreliable in the last 5%).
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min — see AL-07. Connect datalogger to record voltage vs time automatically if available. Check datalogger sample rate is at least 1 Hz.

Title: Transformer investigations
Aim: Investigate the relationship between turns ratio and voltage ratio in a transformer; measure efficiency.
Key variables: IV: turns ratio N_s/N_p. DV: voltage ratio V_s/V_p.
Method: 1. Laminated iron-core transformer kit with interchangeable coil formers. 2. Set primary coil N_p = 200 turns; vary secondary N_s = 50, 100, 200, 400 turns. 3. Apply 2 V AC to primary; measure V_p and V_s with AC voltmeter. 4. Efficiency: connect a load resistor across secondary; measure I_p, I_s, V_p, V_s. Efficiency η = P_out/P_in = (I_s V_s)/(I_p V_p).
Measurements: N_p, N_s, V_p, V_s, I_p, I_s (with load).
Analysis: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. Plot V_s vs N_s; expect straight line through origin with gradient = V_p/N_p. Efficiency ≈ 90–98% for a good laminated core.
Safety: AC supply — check all connections before switching on. Low voltage only.
Data skills: Linear proportionality (V_s vs N_s); efficiency calculation; power in vs power out; AC vs DC distinction.
Common errors / improvements: DC supply gives no output — transformer works on AC only; students try DC and report 'no result'. Core not fully laminated → eddy current losses inflate I_p and reduce efficiency. Measuring AC voltages with a DC voltmeter — must use true-RMS AC meter or oscilloscope. Load resistance too low → I_s too high → large copper loss; efficiency drops sharply. Use R ≥ 10× the secondary winding resistance.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: laminated iron-core transformer (demountable), AC signal generator or 6 V AC supply, 2 × voltmeters, connecting leads. Wind secondaries with different turn ratios before lesson if using demountable transformer. Check for short-circuits in windings.

Title: Power and efficiency of an electric motor
Aim: Measure the electrical power input and useful mechanical power output of a small electric motor; calculate efficiency.
Key variables: IV: supply voltage V (or load). DV: input power P_in, output power P_out.
Method: 1. Connect small DC motor to variable supply with ammeter and voltmeter. 2. Motor lifts a known mass m through height h in time t using a cotton reel drum. 3. P_in = V × I. P_out = mgh/t (useful mechanical power). 4. Vary V (or load mass) and record P_in and P_out at each setting. 5. Efficiency η = P_out/P_in × 100%.
Measurements: V, I, m, h, t.
Analysis: P_in = VI. P_out = mgh/t. η = P_out/P_in. Plot η vs P_in; efficiency peaks at a particular load — too light or too heavy reduces it.
Safety: Motor can jam and overheat — don't stall under load for >5 s.
Data skills: Power calculation; efficiency; energy loss pathways; optimal load concept.
Common errors / improvements: Motor stalls at too high a load → I spikes, P_in large, P_out zero → η = 0%; this is realistic but students sometimes think they've made an error. Cotton reel must wind evenly — if string slips or jams, h is wrong. Use a thin, light string. Measuring h: the mass may not rise vertically — check cotton reel is directly above start point.
