No-load current is non-zero (overcomes bearing friction) — this is a fixed loss, visible as P_in offset even at P_out = 0.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: small electric motor on stand, string + mass (as load), joulemeter or ammeter + voltmeter + stopwatch, ruler, stopwatch. Check motor runs smoothly. Set load mass so motor lifts it clearly but doesn't stall.

Title: Investigating electric heating
Aim: Investigate the relationship between electrical power dissipated in a resistor and the temperature rise of water.
Key variables: IV: power P = VI. DV: rate of temperature rise dT/dt.
Method: 1. Immerse a resistor (or immersion heater, ~10 Ω) in a polystyrene cup of water (100 mL). 2. Apply fixed voltage; record T every 30 s for 5 min. 3. Repeat for 3 different voltages (giving 3 different powers). 4. For each run: plot T vs t; gradient = dT/dt. 5. Plot dT/dt vs P; expect straight line.
Measurements: V, I → P = VI; T vs t gradient for each P.
Analysis: P = mc·(dT/dt). Plot dT/dt vs P; gradient = 1/(mc). Infer c of water (known ≈ 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).
Safety: Water and electricity — keep leads away from water surface. Use a low-voltage supply.
Data skills: Rate of change (gradient of T vs t); proportionality between P and dT/dt; deriving c from gradient.
Common errors / improvements: Heat loss to surroundings makes dT/dt decrease over time (not constant) — use gradient from first 2 min only. Poor thermal contact between resistor and water — stir water or use an immersion heater that is fully submerged. Resistor value changes with temperature → P = V²/R isn't constant; measure I directly. Polystyrene cup absorbs some heat — for accurate c, account for heat capacity of cup and resistor (or use as a systematic error discussion).
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: immersion heater (12 V, 25 W), beaker of water, thermometer, joulemeter or ammeter + voltmeter + stopwatch, balance. Calibrate joulemeters. Fill beakers with a consistent volume of water.

Title: Magnetic field mapping around a wire and coil
Aim: Map the magnetic field pattern around a long straight wire and a flat circular coil using a plotting compass or Hall probe.
Key variables: IV: position relative to wire/coil. DV: field direction (compass) or field strength B (Hall probe).
Method: Straight wire: 1. Pass a large DC current (≥3 A) through a vertical wire through a horizontal card. 2. Sprinkle iron filings on card, or use a plotting compass to trace field lines at several radii. 3. Hall probe: measure B at radii r = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 cm from wire. Coil: 4. Lay flat circular coil on card; repeat mapping inside and outside coil.
Measurements: Field direction at each position; B (mT) at each r (Hall probe).
Analysis: Straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr). Plot B vs 1/r; expect straight line through origin with gradient = μ₀I/(2π). Coil: field strongest at centre, weakens away from axis.
Safety: Large current — check wiring before switching on. Hall probe is fragile — don't bend.
Data skills: 1/r dependence (linearisation B vs 1/r); gradient → μ₀; field-line pattern interpretation.
Common errors / improvements: Iron filings give a snapshot — disturbing the card changes the pattern. Photograph before moving. Earth's magnetic field adds to the measurement at low currents — use large I (≥3 A) so B_wire >> B_earth, or subtract a background reading with current off. Hall probe orientation critical — must be perpendicular to field for maximum reading; rotate to find peak. Residual magnetism in iron-core components near the wire distorts the field — use non-magnetic bench clamps.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: plotting compasses × 10, long straight wire on stand + DC supply (2–5 A), slinky spring or coil, plain paper. Check plotting compasses all point same direction. Ensure wire is insulated. Use heavy-duty leads for 5 A.

Title: Motor effect (force on conductor, varying angle)
Aim: Extend AL-08 to verify F = BIL sin θ by varying the angle between wire and field.
Key variables: IV: angle θ between wire and magnetic field. DV: force F.
Method: 1. As AL-08 but mount the wire on a rotating holder so θ can be varied from 0° to 90°. 2. At each angle, record the balance reading (force). 3. Keep I constant throughout.
Measurements: Angle θ, balance mass reading → F.
Analysis: F = BIL sin θ. Plot F vs sin θ; expect straight line through origin; gradient = BIL.
Safety: Wire heats at high I — keep current on briefly. Magnets brittle.
Data skills: Sin θ linearisation; gradient = BIL; identifying θ = 90° as maximum and θ = 0° as zero force.
Common errors / improvements: Difficulty in reading angle accurately — protractor mounted rigidly on rotating holder. At θ = 0°, there should be zero force — if not, there's a misalignment offset; treat as systematic error. Rotating the wire moves its position relative to the field — verify it stays within the uniform field region throughout rotation. At angles far from 90°, the force is small and the balance reading noisy; weight the fit toward the θ = 45°–90° range.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min — see AL-08. Provide protractor for angle measurement.

Title: Lenz's law (falling magnet through tube)
Aim: Demonstrate Lenz's law: induced currents oppose the change causing them, creating a braking force.
Key variables: Qualitative: a strong magnet falls slowly through a conducting (copper/aluminium) tube compared to free fall.
Method: 1. Drop a strong neodymium magnet through a copper tube (~1 m); time the fall. 2. Drop the same magnet beside the tube (free fall); compare times. 3. Repeat with aluminium tube; compare braking effect. 4. Extension: use a non-conducting (PVC) tube — no braking, fall time matches free fall.
Measurements: Fall time through conducting tube vs free fall time.
Analysis: Fall time through copper tube >> free fall time; aluminium > copper in fall time (lower conductivity). Eddy currents in tube produce a field opposing magnet's motion (Lenz's law).
Safety: Strong magnets — keep away from pacemakers, computers, credit cards.
Data skills: Qualitative Lenz's law reasoning; induced current direction from Lenz; eddy current braking.
Common errors / improvements: Effect is most dramatic with neodymium (NdFeB) magnets, not alnico or ferrite — use neodymium. Tube must have no longitudinal slit (a slit breaks the eddy current path, eliminating the effect) — seamless tube only. Students sometimes think the magnet is 'attracted' to the tube — the force is purely repulsive/braking. Quantitative extension: measure terminal velocity by timing between two marks; compare to theoretical from Lenz + Stokes drag.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min — see AL-09. For quantitative measurement, wind a search coil and connect to datalogger.

Title: Eddy currents (braking pendulum)
Aim: Demonstrate eddy current braking using a metal pendulum swinging between magnet poles.
Key variables: IV: material of pendulum plate (copper / slotted copper / aluminium / card). DV: rate of amplitude decay.
Method: 1. Suspend a flat copper plate as a pendulum; swing it through the gap between two strong magnets. 2. Count oscillations to half-amplitude; repeat with slots cut in the plate. 3. Repeat with aluminium plate, then card (no eddy currents). 4. Note that slots disrupt eddy current paths and reduce braking.
Measurements: Number of oscillations to half-amplitude for each plate.
Analysis: Solid plate decays fastest; slotted plate slower; card slowest (like free swing). Slots interrupt eddy current loops → smaller induced currents → less braking force.
Safety: Strong magnets — keep away from electronics and cards. Plate can swing out of gap — fit guides.
Data skills: Eddy current path analysis; qualitative Lenz's law; application to induction cooktops and maglev braking.
Common errors / improvements: Magnet gap must be just wider than the plate or braking is dominated by mechanical friction on the sides. Slots must be cut parallel to the plate's motion direction to maximally interrupt horizontal eddy current loops. Effect is highly dependent on magnet strength — use the strongest available pair. This is a classic 'explain the observation' exam question — ensure students predict before observing.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per setup: copper pendulum bob on string, powerful horseshoe magnet, clamp stand. Non-slotted vs slotted (comb-cut) pendulum bob to demonstrate eddy current effect. Ensure magnet pole gap matches pendulum swing path.

Title: Magnetic flux linkage (search coil and oscilloscope)
Aim: Investigate how the EMF induced in a search coil depends on the rate of change of flux linkage.
Key variables: IV: frequency f of AC in primary coil. DV: induced EMF in search coil.
Method: 1. Wind a search coil (≈200 turns, small area) on a former. 2. Place inside a large solenoid connected to a signal generator at low AC voltage. 3. Measure peak EMF in search coil with oscilloscope at frequencies 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 Hz. 4. Vary orientation of search coil (0°, 30°, 60°, 90° to solenoid axis).
Measurements: Frequency f (Hz), peak EMF ε (V), coil orientation θ.
Analysis: ε = NABω = NAB(2πf). Plot ε vs f; straight line through origin, gradient = 2πNAB. Orientation: ε ∝ cos θ (field perpendicular to coil gives maximum EMF).
Safety: AC supply — check connections before switching on.
Data skills: Linear plot (ε vs f); gradient → NAB; cosine dependence on orientation; flux linkage vs rate of change distinction.
Common errors / improvements: Search coil too close to edge of solenoid where field is non-uniform — position in the central third. Oscilloscope set to wrong time-base scale → waveform too compressed or too expanded to read peak accurately. EMF is proportional to dΦ/dt, not Φ — students confuse these; at higher f the flux is the same but EMF is larger. Solenoid field not uniform across its cross-section — centre of search coil should coincide with solenoid axis.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: search coil (pre-wound, ~50 turns, known area), large solenoid + AC PSU, oscilloscope. Check oscilloscope triggers correctly. Measure and tape coil area on each search coil.

Title: Rectification (half-wave and full-wave)
Aim: Investigate half-wave and full-wave rectification of AC using diodes; observe effect of smoothing capacitor.
Key variables: Input: AC signal from signal generator. DV: output waveform on oscilloscope.
Method: 1. Half-wave: single diode in series with a resistor load. Apply 6 V AC at 50 Hz; display input and output on oscilloscope (dual channel). 2. Full-wave: bridge rectifier (4 diodes) with same load. Compare waveforms. 3. Smoothing: add capacitor (100–1000 μF) in parallel with load; observe ripple voltage. 4. Vary capacitor value; observe how ripple changes.
Measurements: Oscilloscope waveforms: V_in and V_out amplitude and shape.
Analysis: Half-wave: output is every other half-cycle. Full-wave: output is every half-cycle, doubled frequency. Smoothing: ripple V_r ≈ V_peak/(fCR); larger C or R → less ripple.
Safety: Check diode polarity before switching on. AC supply — secure all connections.
Data skills: Waveform interpretation; frequency doubling in full-wave; ripple formula; time constant RC in smoothing.
Common errors / improvements: Oscilloscope DC-coupled vs AC-coupled — must use DC-coupled to see rectified output correctly; AC-coupling removes the DC offset and shows only ripple. Diode in wrong direction → no output for half-wave, or bridge shorts for full-wave. Capacitor polarity: electrolytic must match the polarity of the rectified DC — reverse polarisation damages it. Ripple frequency: full-wave = 2 × AC frequency; students often predict it equals AC frequency.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: signal diode × 2 (or bridge rectifier), signal generator (50 Hz), oscilloscope, smoothing capacitor, load resistor. Pre-wire half-wave circuit. Check oscilloscope time-base settings give clear display at 50 Hz.

Title: Oscilloscope investigations (AC/DC, frequency, phase)
Aim: Use an oscilloscope to measure AC voltage amplitude, frequency, and phase difference between two signals.
Key variables: Inputs: signal generator output(s). Oscilloscope as measuring instrument.
Method: 1. Connect signal generator to oscilloscope; adjust timebase and Y-gain to display 2–3 clear cycles. 2. Read peak voltage V_p; calculate V_rms = V_p/√2. Compare to AC voltmeter reading. 3. Read period T from timebase; f = 1/T. Compare to signal generator dial. 4. Phase difference: connect two signals from the same generator (one phase-shifted by RC circuit) to channels 1 and 2. Measure horizontal offset between peaks; phase difference φ = (Δt/T) × 360°.
Measurements: V_p, T, Δt from oscilloscope graticule.
Analysis: V_rms = V_p/√2; f = 1/T; φ = (Δt/T) × 360°. Verify V_rms with AC voltmeter; f with signal generator frequency.
Safety: AC supply. Oscilloscope screen — do not touch with sharp objects.
Data skills: Peak-to-rms conversion; period → frequency; phase difference calculation; instrument calibration verification.
Common errors / improvements: Y-gain and timebase must be read from the knob setting (V/div, ms/div) — not just counting boxes. Reading peak-to-peak and forgetting to halve for V_p. Phase measurement: use cursors if available; if reading by eye, use crossing-point of the waveform with the zero line (midpoint of rising or falling edge) rather than the peaks — less ambiguous. Trigger not set correctly → waveform drifts or flickers; set trigger to channel 1 at 0 V rising edge.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: oscilloscope, signal generator, connecting leads. Set oscilloscopes to auto-trigger before class. Check time-base and gain controls work. Provide at least 2 different signal frequencies for comparison.

Title: Investigating the Hall effect (optional/A-Level extension)
Aim: Use a Hall probe to investigate how Hall voltage V_H varies with current and magnetic field strength.
Key variables: IV: current I through Hall slice, or magnetic field B. DV: Hall voltage V_H.
Method: 1. Set up Hall slice (semiconductor, e.g. InAs or packaged Hall probe) in a known magnetic field (between magnadur magnets). 2. Vary current I through the slice; record V_H at each I. 3. Use an electromagnet with variable current to vary B; record V_H for fixed slice current.
Measurements: Current I, field B, Hall voltage V_H.
Analysis: V_H = IB/(ned) → V_H ∝ I (fixed B); V_H ∝ B (fixed I). From gradient: n = IB/(eV_H·d) → charge carrier density n.
Safety: Hall probe is fragile — do not bend or overheat.
Data skills: Two-variable proportionality (V_H ∝ I and V_H ∝ B separately); carrier density calculation from gradient.
Common errors / improvements: Misalignment of Hall slice relative to B gives an offset voltage even at I = 0 — zero the reading with current off and B on, or use the 'offset subtract' feature. Temperature affects n for semiconductors — keep slice current low to avoid self-heating. Polarity of V_H identifies carrier type (electrons vs holes) — establish a sign convention before the experiment. Magnadur magnets give a limited, non-uniform field — measure B with a separate Hall probe before using it as the 'known' field.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per setup: Hall probe + datalogger or galvanometer, large horseshoe magnet or solenoid, DC power supply, ammeter. Calibrate Hall probe before lesson.

Title: Magnetic field along a solenoid axis
Aim: Measure how the magnetic field along the axis of a solenoid varies with position and current.
Key variables: IV: position along solenoid axis x; or current I. DV: field B.
Method: 1. Wind a solenoid (~500 turns, 20 cm long, 3 cm diameter) on a cardboard former. 2. Connect to a variable DC supply with ammeter. 3. Hall probe on a sliding mount along the axis; record B at positions from −15 to +15 cm from centre, in 1 cm steps. 4. Part B: fix probe at centre; vary I from 0 to 3 A; record B.
Measurements: Position x, field B at each position; current I, B at centre.
Analysis: B = μ₀nI at centre (n = turns per unit length). Plot B vs x: field uniform in centre, falls toward ends. Plot B vs I at centre: straight line; gradient = μ₀n.
Safety: DC supply at up to 3 A — check connections before switching on. Solenoid gets warm at high I.
Data skills: Linear plot B vs I (gradient → μ₀n); field uniformity profile; end-effect discussion.
Common errors / improvements: Hall probe orientation — must be perpendicular to the solenoid axis at each position. Earth's magnetic field is non-negligible at low I — subtract background reading (I = 0) at each position. Solenoid wound non-uniformly (gaps or bunches) → B profile is irregular; wind carefully or use a pre-wound solenoid. At the ends, the field is approximately B_centre/2 — use this as a sanity check.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: solenoid (known turns per metre), DC supply + rheostat, Hall probe or plotting compass array, ruler. Supply solenoid specifications (n, length, diameter) on a label.

Title: Ripple tank — wave properties
Aim: Use a ripple tank to investigate reflection, refraction and diffraction of water waves.
Key variables: IV: wave frequency f, barrier geometry. DV: wavelength λ, direction of refracted/diffracted waves.
Method: 1. Set up ripple tank; use straight-bar dipper for plane waves. Adjust signal generator to 5–20 Hz. 2. Reflection: place a straight barrier at an angle; photograph shadow pattern; verify θᵢ = θᵣ. 3. Refraction: place a flat glass plate (shallow region) in tank; observe wavelength change; measure λ in deep and shallow regions. 4. Diffraction: place two barriers leaving a gap; vary gap width relative to λ; observe spreading.
Measurements: Wavelength λ from shadow spacing, frequency f from signal generator, angles from photographs.
Analysis: v = fλ in each region. Refraction: v decreases in shallow water, λ decreases, f unchanged. Snell's law analogy: sin θ₁/sin θ₂ = v₁/v₂ = λ₁/λ₂. Diffraction: greatest spreading when gap width ≈ λ.
Safety: Mop spills immediately. Stroboscope warning for photosensitive students. Electrical equipment near water — low-voltage only.
Data skills: Wave speed from v = fλ; Snell's law ratio; qualitative diffraction condition (gap ≈ λ).
Common errors / improvements: Measuring λ from shadows: meniscus at edges distorts wavefronts — measure only in central region. Measure across several wavelengths and divide for better precision. Shallow-region glass plate must be perfectly horizontal or waves refract at an angle even straight-on. Frequency drift on signal generator changes λ mid-experiment — verify f with a stroboscope or check generator stability.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per setup: ripple tank, white paper on bench, dipper (straight and circular), stroboscope, lamp. Fill to 1 cm depth with clean water — add a drop of washing-up liquid to reduce surface tension effects. Dry tank between classes. Replace paper.

Title: Measuring the speed of sound (echo / resonance tube)
Aim: Measure the speed of sound in air by two methods: echo timing and resonance tube.
Key variables: Echo method: distance d, echo time t. Resonance tube: frequency f, resonant length L.
Method: Echo method: 1. Stand ~50 m from a large flat wall. Clap two wooden boards together rhythmically until claps and echoes synchronise. 2. Time 20 clap intervals; time for one = 2d/v. Resonance tube: 1. Hold a tuning fork (known f) over a tube dipping into a cylinder of water; raise tube until first resonance (loudest sound). 2. Measure tube length L₁ (first resonance: L₁ ≈ λ/4). Lower tube to find second resonance L₂ (L₂ ≈ 3λ/4). 3. λ = 2(L₂ − L₁); v = fλ. Use several tuning forks.
Measurements: Echo: d (measured with tape), time for 20 echoes. Resonance: f (from tuning fork), L₁ and L₂.
Analysis: Echo: v = 2d × 20 / (total time for 20 echoes). Resonance: λ = 2(L₂ − L₁); v = fλ. Plot λ vs 1/f; gradient = v. End correction: actual L₁ = λ/4 − e (where e ≈ 0.3× tube diameter); using L₂ − L₁ cancels this.
Safety: Echo method outdoors — road traffic awareness. Tuning forks: don't strike on bench — use a rubber mallet.
Data skills: End-correction cancellation; linear plot λ vs 1/f; agreement between two independent methods.
Common errors / improvements: Echo method: clapping rhythm drifts → synchronisation breaks down. Practise before timing. Resonance tube: not finding the second resonance (only first) → λ is ambiguous because of end correction. Always find both L₁ and L₂. Wind and temperature affect v_sound (v ≈ 331 + 0.6T m/s where T is °C) — record temperature and correct. Tuning fork frequency varies with temperature and age — verify against a known reference.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: long corridor or hallway (for echo method) or resonance tube (50 cm closed tube), signal generator, speaker, microphone + datalogger, ruler. Resonance tube: fill with water; check tube is clean and clear. Signal generator: set to ~500 Hz starting point.

Title: Critical angle and total internal reflection
Aim: Measure the critical angle for glass (or perspex) and determine its refractive index.
Key variables: IV: angle of incidence (inside the medium). DV: angle of refraction (in air); observe TIR onset.
Method: 1. Place a semicircular glass (or perspex) block with its flat face on a ray-tracing sheet. 2. Direct a ray box beam through the curved face (no refraction at curved surface) toward the flat face at increasing angles. 3. Observe refracted ray in air; as angle increases, refracted ray bends toward 90°. 4. Find the critical angle θ_c where refracted ray just disappears (lies along the flat face). 5. Repeat for 5+ different angles to build a sin θ₁ vs sin θ₂ graph.
Measurements: Angles of incidence θ₁ (inside glass), refraction θ₂ (in air).
Analysis: n = sin θ₂ / sin θ₁ = 1/sin θ_c. Plot sin θ₁ vs sin θ₂; gradient = 1/n. From critical angle: n = 1/sin θ_c.
Safety: Ray box gets hot — handle with care. Bright light — avoid looking directly into beam.
Data skills: Sin θ plot; gradient = 1/n; critical angle as special case where θ₂ = 90°; TIR condition derivation.
Common errors / improvements: Semicircular block must be centred so the ray enters through the exact centre of the curved face — otherwise refraction occurs at entry. Critical angle is the angle at which the refracted ray just vanishes — it's easier to find by approaching from above (TIR already occurring) and slowly decreasing the angle. Thick block edges scatter light — use thin perspex blocks or a ray box with a sharp single slit. Only 5 data points is barely enough for a reliable gradient — take ≥8 angles spread across the full range.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min — see GCSE-08. Add: ray box with narrow slit, semicircular glass block, protractor. Check ray box slits are clean. Room blinds improve ray visibility.

Title: Young's double-slit experiment
Aim: Measure the wavelength of light using Young's double-slit interference.
Key variables: IV: slit separation a, screen distance D. DV: fringe spacing w.
Method: 1. Mount double-slit slide (slit separation a ≈ 0.5 mm) perpendicular to a laser or monochromatic source. 2. Project fringes onto a screen 1–2 m away. 3. Measure fringe spacing w across ≥10 fringes and divide. 4. Vary D (2–3 distances); verify w ∝ D. 5. Verify w ∝ 1/a by using slits of different separation.
Measurements: Fringe spacing w, slit separation a, screen distance D.
Analysis: λ = aw/D. Plot w vs D; gradient = λ/a → λ.
Safety: Laser: never look into beam. Class 2 only. Remove reflective jewellery.
Data skills: Linear plot (w vs D); gradient → λ/a; comparison between two slit spacings; small-angle validity.
Common errors / improvements: Measuring only one fringe spacing → large reading uncertainty. Measure across ≥10 fringes and divide. Slit not perpendicular to incident beam → asymmetric fringe pattern; check alignment. Central maximum not at centre of screen — tilt screen until fringes are symmetric. Using a white-light source gives coloured fringes at the edges; only the central fringe is white — identify it first before measuring w.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: class 2 laser (<1 mW) on stand, double-slit slide (slit separation labelled), screen (at least 1 m from slits), ruler, vernier calipers. LASER SAFETY: check class rating, provide warning signs, ensure beam stop at end. Measure and label each slit separation — record values on equipment. Do not point lasers at students.

Title: Microwave diffraction and interference
Aim: Investigate diffraction and interference of microwaves (λ ≈ 3 cm) using a transmitter and receiver.
Key variables: IV: gap width or slit separation. DV: receiver signal strength.
Method: 1. Set up microwave transmitter pointing at receiver; maximise signal. 2. Diffraction through a single gap (metal plates): vary gap width; observe signal vs angle. 3. Double-slit (two gaps in a metal plate): move receiver across the beam; record signal at each position; identify maxima and minima. 4. Measure wavelength using standing waves (receiver between transmitter and a metal reflector; count nodes).
Measurements: Gap width or slit separation, receiver position, signal strength.
Analysis: Maxima at d sin θ = nλ. Measure node spacing (= λ/2) for wavelength. Compare λ from standing waves with λ from manufacturer spec (≈ 3 cm).
Safety: Microwave transmitter — do not point at eyes or stand in direct beam path. Keep >20 cm from transmitter.
Data skills: Diffraction maxima/minima condition; standing wave node counting; λ comparison between two methods.
Common errors / improvements: Receiver must be in the far field (Fraunhofer regime) — place it ≥1 m from the slits for 3 cm microwaves. Metal plate edges must be clean (not jagged) or stray diffraction from the edges confuses the pattern. Receiver probe sensitive to orientation — keep it consistently vertical (or horizontal) throughout. Room reflections from walls and bench create spurious maxima — work away from metal surfaces or absorb with foam.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per setup: microwave transmitter and receiver (10.5 GHz), metal plates for slits, metre rule. Check transmitter and receiver are working before lesson. Set slit width to ~3 cm for clear diffraction pattern. Warn: avoid prolonged direct exposure of microwave beam.

Title: Polarisation of light and microwaves
Aim: Investigate polarisation by verifying Malus's law: I = I₀ cos² θ.
Key variables: IV: angle θ between polariser and analyser. DV: transmitted intensity I.
Method: Light method: 1. Pass light from a lamp through a linear polariser; rotate an analyser through 360°. 2. Measure transmitted intensity with a light meter at each angle (0° to 360° in 10° steps). Microwave method: 1. Microwave transmitter (plane-polarised); rotate receiver by 0° to 90°; record signal at each angle.
Measurements: Angle θ between polariser and analyser, intensity I.
Analysis: I = I₀ cos² θ (Malus's law). Plot I vs cos² θ; expect straight line through origin. Or plot √I vs cos θ; expect straight line.
Safety: Do not stare into bright lamp. Microwave — keep away from transmitter beam.
Data skills: Cosine-squared plot linearisation; I vs cos² θ; verification of Malus's law; distinction between polarised and unpolarised light.
Common errors / improvements: Unpolarised light source gives I = I₀/2 (not zero) even when analyser is crossed — only laser or polaroid-filtered light polarises fully. Background light adds to I at all angles, shifting the curve up — measure background (with beam blocked) and subtract. Protractor must be centred on the polaroid axis, not the mount — rotate polaroid not the whole holder. Microwave: the transmitter is already plane-polarised — rotating receiver 0°–90° is sufficient; beyond 90° repeats.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: 2 × polarising filters, light source, microwave set (as WAVE-05) for microwave polarisation. Check filters are labelled with polarising axis direction.

Title: Doppler effect (demonstration)
Aim: Demonstrate the Doppler effect qualitatively using a moving sound source; estimate speed from frequency shift.
Key variables: Moving buzzer on string changes perceived pitch as it approaches and recedes.
Method: 1. Attach a battery-powered buzzer (single frequency, ~1000 Hz) to a string (~1 m). 2. Swing in a horizontal circle; listeners at the side hear frequency shift. 3. Quantitative: record sound with a smartphone frequency analyser app; measure f_approach and f_recede. 4. Calculate source speed v_s from Doppler formula and compare to measured string speed.
Measurements: f_approach, f_recede (from spectrum analyser), source frequency f₀.
Analysis: f_obs = f₀(v ± v_obs)/(v ∓ v_s). From f_approach and f_recede: v_s = v(f_a − f_r)/(f_a + f_r). Compare to string speed v_s = 2πr/T (time period of rotation).
Safety: Swinging buzzer — clear area of people. String must be secure.
Data skills: Doppler shift formula; observed vs emitted frequency; calculating source speed from two observed frequencies.
Common errors / improvements: Circular motion means the maximum shift occurs only when the source moves directly toward/away from the listener — at angles the shift is less. Buzzer frequency must be stable — use a battery well above depletion. Smartphone frequency analyser: must be far enough from the source that the signal isn't distorted by proximity. Students often confuse approach/recede with higher/lower amplitude — emphasise it's the frequency (pitch) that shifts, not the volume.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. DEMO: Sound source (buzzer or speaker on trolley or rotating on a string), stopwatch. Alternatively: tone generator + moving speaker demonstration. Pre-test in room to ensure Doppler shift is clearly audible.

Title: Lens focal length (converging lens)
Aim: Determine the focal length of a converging lens using object and image distances.
Key variables: IV: object distance u. DV: image distance v.
Method: 1. Place a lit object (illuminated cross-wire or LED) on an optical bench. 2. Place converging lens; move a screen until a sharp image forms; record u and v. 3. Repeat for 6–8 object distances (from just outside f to ~5f). 4. Plot 1/v vs 1/u; gradient = −1, intercept on each axis = 1/f.
Measurements: Object distance u, image distance v (both from lens).
Analysis: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (real-is-positive convention). Plot 1/v vs 1/u: straight line, gradient = −1, y-intercept = 1/f. Or: plot v vs u; use graph to read f = intercept/gradient.
Safety: Optical bench — secure the lamp housing. Hot lamp — allow to cool.
Data skills: Reciprocal plot (1/v vs 1/u); gradient check = −1; intercept → f; power of lens P = 1/f (in dioptres).
Common errors / improvements: Object distance measured from wrong reference (front of lens vs principal plane) — always measure from optical centre. Image not sharp when u < f (virtual image — no real image on screen); restrict u > f. Parallax: eye not on the axis of the bench — ensure bench is straight and eye is at the level of the image. Dirty or scratched lens scatters light → bright halo, hard to focus sharply; use clean optics.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Per group: converging lens (various focal lengths: 10, 15, 20 cm), optical bench or metre rule, illuminated object (mounted bulb), screen, ruler. Label lenses with power (dioptre) or focal length. Check bulbs work.

Title: Concave and convex lens comparison
Aim: Determine focal length of a concave (diverging) lens using a combination method; compare image formation in converging vs diverging lenses.
Key variables: Converging lens alone: u, v. Combination: u_combo, v_combo; then isolate f of diverging lens.
Method: 1. First measure f of a strong converging lens (as WAVE-08). 2. Place diverging lens in contact with it; measure combined focal length f_combo. 3. 1/f_div = 1/f_combo − 1/f_conv → f_div (negative — confirms diverging). 4. Qualitative: observe how converging and diverging lenses form images of the same object; note upright/inverted, magnified/diminished.
Measurements: f_conv, f_combo, calculated f_div.
Analysis: Lensmaker's combination: 1/f_combo = 1/f_conv + 1/f_div. Power: P_combo = P_conv + P_div.
Safety: Optical bench — secure lamp housing. Allow lamp to cool.
Data skills: Reciprocal focal length combination; sign convention (negative f for diverging); power addition.
Common errors / improvements: Diverging lens cannot form a real image on a screen alone — students try and report 'no image'; the combination method is necessary. Lenses must be in close contact for the combination formula to apply accurately — use a lens holder that keeps them touching. Sign of f_div is negative — if calculation gives positive, the lenses are in wrong order or f_conv was mis-measured. Focal length of diverging lens measured this way has double the uncertainty of f_conv — propagate uncertainties explicitly.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min — see WAVE-08. Add diverging lens. Label concave and convex clearly.

Title: Image formation and magnification
Aim: Investigate the relationship between object distance, image distance and magnification for a converging lens.
Key variables: IV: object distance u. DV: image distance v, image height h_i.
Method: 1. Use optical bench with illuminated object of known height h_o. 2. For each u (5–8 values), find v (sharp image) and measure image height h_i on screen. 3. Calculate linear magnification m = h_i/h_o = v/u.
Measurements: u, v, h_o (fixed), h_i at each u.
Analysis: m = v/u = h_i/h_o. Plot m vs v/u; expect gradient = 1. Also: plot m vs u; observe m decreases as u increases; m = 1 when u = 2f.
Safety: Secure lamp housing. Hot lamp.
Data skills: Magnification as a ratio; two equivalent definitions (h_i/h_o and v/u); position of unit magnification at u = 2f.
Common errors / improvements: Image height measured to outer edge of image — if image has blurred edges, measure the central sharp region. Magnification >1 for u < 2f; m = 1 at u = 2f; m < 1 for u > 2f — plotting these three regimes clearly shows the relationship. Inverted image: measure h_i as a positive number (magnitude only) unless sign convention is used consistently. At u close to f, image distance v becomes very large and the image falls off the bench — use a longer optical bench or accept reduced range.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min — see WAVE-08. Ensure optical bench rulers are clear and legible.

Title: Telescope construction and investigation
Aim: Build a simple refracting telescope; measure angular magnification.
Key variables: IV: objective and eyepiece focal lengths. DV: angular magnification M.
Method: 1. Select two convex lenses: objective (long focal length f_obj, e.g. 50 cm) and eyepiece (short focal length f_eye, e.g. 5 cm). 2. Mount in a cardboard tube (or on optical bench) separated by f_obj + f_eye for parallel (infinity) focus. 3. Observe a distant object (≥10 m); compare angular size with and without telescope. 4. Measure M directly: place a metre rule 2 m away; count how many divisions are visible through the eyepiece vs the naked eye.
Measurements: f_obj, f_eye, apparent vs actual object size.
Analysis: M = f_obj / f_eye. Compare calculated M with measured M from ruler method.
Safety: Do not look at the Sun. Handle lenses carefully — fragile.
Data skills: Ratio of focal lengths; angular vs linear magnification distinction; telescope in normal adjustment.
Common errors / improvements: Telescope not in normal adjustment (image at infinity) → eye strain and incorrect M. Adjust tube length until the image is comfortable (relaxed eye, parallel rays from eyepiece). Measuring M with a ruler: one eye through telescope, other eye looking alongside at the ruler — requires some practice. f_obj must be much greater than f_eye for useful M — the other way round gives M < 1 (actually a microscope layout in reverse). Chromatic aberration (coloured fringes on bright objects) — normal for simple single-element lenses; mention as a limitation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: two converging lenses (one large diameter f=25 cm as objective, one short f=5 cm as eyepiece), lens holders, optical bench, distant object (e.g. printed chart on far wall). Set up distant target at least 3 m away.

Title: Optical fibre demonstration
Aim: Demonstrate total internal reflection in an optical fibre; show light guided around bends.
Key variables: Qualitative: light transmitted through bent optical fibre; bright spot at exit regardless of fibre path.
Method: 1. Shine a bright LED or laser into one end of a plastic optical fibre bundle. 2. Bend the fibre through various angles (including >90°); observe that light exits the other end with little loss. 3. Compare with a straight glass rod (no TIR constraint). 4. Extension: introduce a sharp bend beyond the fibre's acceptance angle; observe light leaking out.
Measurements: Qualitative: light transmission vs bend angle.
Analysis: Explain TIR condition (n_core > n_cladding; angle > critical angle). Numerical aperture: NA = √(n_core² − n_clad²); acceptance cone half-angle = arcsin(NA).
Safety: Laser or bright LED — do not look into fibre end. Class 2 laser only.
Data skills: TIR condition; numerical aperture concept; application to communications.
Common errors / improvements: Students often think the glass itself glows — it's just scattered light from imperfections. The key point is the end-to-end transmission. Sharp bends cause light to hit the core-cladding interface at less than the critical angle → TIR fails → light leaks out; demonstrate this deliberately. For a quantitative extension, measure attenuation (in dB/m) using a light meter at different fibre lengths.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. DEMO: Optical fibre kit or fibre bundle, laser or LED source, light sensor. Check fibre ends are clean — polish if cloudy. Ensure light path is visible in a dimmed room.

Title: Stationary waves: microwaves and sound
Aim: Observe and measure stationary waves in sound (Kundt's tube) and microwaves; determine speed from node spacing.
Key variables: IV: frequency (sound) or position (microwaves). DV: node positions.
Method: Sound (Kundt's tube): 1. Pour fine powder (cork dust or lycopodium) into a horizontal glass tube. 2. Draw a resined rod (or use a loudspeaker + signal generator) along the tube to produce a standing wave. 3. Powder collects at nodes; measure node spacing (= λ/2); v = fλ. Microwaves: 1. Transmitter faces a metal reflector; receiver on a rail moves between them. 2. Record signal minima (nodes) and maxima; node spacing = λ/2.
Measurements: Node positions (ruler), frequency f.
Analysis: λ = 2 × node spacing. v = fλ. For Kundt's tube: compare measured v_sound with 331 + 0.6T.
Safety: Kundt's tube powder is irritant — avoid inhaling. Microwave transmitter — don't stand in direct beam.
Data skills: Node spacing → λ; v = fλ; comparison with expected value; standing wave formation conditions.
Common errors / improvements: Kundt's tube: powder heap spacing gives node positions, but heaps have a width — measure centre-to-centre. Microwave: room reflections add to the pattern and shift node positions — minimise by working along a clear line away from walls. Microwave receiver response is nonlinear — use it to locate minima (most reliable) rather than maxima. Temperature correction for v_sound — measure lab temperature and apply 0.6T correction.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: microwave transmitter + receiver (WAVE-05), metal reflector plate. For sound stationary waves: signal generator + speaker + microphone + datalogger, flat wall. Mark nodes with tape on bench before lesson.

Title: Resonance tubes (closed and open pipes)
Aim: Investigate resonance in closed and open pipes; verify harmonics and end correction.
Key variables: IV: frequency f (tuning forks or signal generator). DV: resonant lengths L.
Method: 1. Closed pipe (tube dipping in water): find first (L₁ ≈ λ/4) and second (L₂ ≈ 3λ/4) resonances. 2. Open pipe: find resonance with signal generator; measure length L (L ≈ λ/2 for fundamental). 3. Repeat for ≥4 different tuning fork frequencies. 4. Plot λ vs 1/f (closed) or L vs 1/f (open); gradient = v_sound / constant.
Measurements: Frequencies f, resonant lengths L₁ and L₂ for each f.
Analysis: Closed pipe: λ = 2(L₂ − L₁) (cancels end correction). v = fλ. Open pipe: L = λ/2 − 2e (e = end correction ≈ 0.3d). Plot λ vs 1/f; gradient = v_sound.
Safety: Water — mop spills. Tuning forks struck with rubber mallet only.
Data skills: End correction technique; linear plot λ vs 1/f; gradient → v_sound; comparison of harmonics in open vs closed pipes.
Common errors / improvements: Using only L₁ (first resonance) → end correction e makes the result inaccurate. Always use L₂ − L₁ to cancel e for closed pipe. Tuning fork decays — hold over tube immediately after striking and measure quickly. Water level: for closed pipe, the air column length L is measured from the water surface to the open end, not from the bottom of the tube. Overtones in closed pipe are odd harmonics only (f, 3f, 5f...); open pipe has all harmonics — a testable prediction.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: closed resonance tube (as WAVE-02) + open-ended tube, signal generator, speaker, microphone + datalogger, ruler. Fill closed tube with water — check no leaks.

Title: Speed of light (Foucault / time-of-flight demo)
Aim: Demonstrate or simulate the measurement of the speed of light; discuss historical methods.
Key variables: Conceptual and calculation exercise; demonstration if equipment available.
Method: If Foucault apparatus available: 1. Rotating mirror deflects a laser beam; image shifts as mirror rotates. Δx = 4ωd²/(cD). If not available (typical for schools): 2. Use a microwave oven method: remove turntable; place chocolate bar; heat ~15 s; measure distance between melt spots (= λ/2); f stamped on back of oven; c = fλ. 3. Class discussion of Rømer, Bradley, Foucault, Michelson methods.
Measurements: Microwave oven: λ from melt spots, f from oven label.
Analysis: c = fλ. Expected ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s. Error analysis: λ measured to ±5 mm (two melt spots); f given to 3 sig fig.
Safety: Microwave oven: don't run empty for >30 s. Hot chocolate — allow to cool before touching.
Data skills: Order-of-magnitude estimation; c = fλ; sources of systematic error in historical methods.
Common errors / improvements: Microwave oven method: the melt spots are antinodes (maximum E field), not nodes — separation is λ/2 not λ. Turntable must be removed or it rotates the chocolate away from the standing-wave antinodes. Some ovens use non-uniform field distribution — result varies across the tray; average several spots. This method gives c to ~10% — more than adequate as a demonstration; don't over-claim precision.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: DEMO ONLY — specialist equipment. Foucault wheel or commercial time-of-flight kit. Set up and test before lesson. Alternatively: show video of Michelson's experiment.

Title: Diffraction with single slit
Aim: Investigate the single-slit diffraction pattern; measure slit width from the pattern.
Key variables: IV: slit width a. DV: positions of minima.
Method: 1. Shine a laser through a single slit (variable or fixed widths 0.1–0.5 mm) onto a screen 1–2 m away. 2. Measure distance between first-order minima (2y₁) on screen; D = distance to screen. 3. Repeat for 3–4 different slit widths.
Measurements: Slit width a, screen distance D, position of first minima y₁.
Analysis: Minima at a sin θ = mλ. For first minimum: sin θ₁ ≈ λ/a. a = λD/y₁. Plot y₁ vs D for fixed a; gradient = λ/a → a.
Safety: Laser: never look into beam. Class 2 only.
Data skills: Inverse slit-width relationship (y₁ ∝ 1/a); gradient → a; distinguishing single-slit from double-slit pattern.
Common errors / improvements: Wider slit → narrower central maximum (inverse relationship) — counter-intuitive to most students; verify explicitly. Central maximum is twice the width of side maxima — measure carefully; students sometimes measure the first side maximum. Intensity of side maxima much lower than central — need a dark room to see them clearly. For very narrow slits (<0.1 mm) the central maximum is very wide and fringes merge — stay within 0.1–0.5 mm range.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min — see WAVE-04. Replace double slit with single slit of adjustable width. Provide multiple slit widths.

Title: Spectroscopy (diffraction grating with white light / emission spectra)
Aim: Use a diffraction grating to observe emission spectra and measure wavelengths of spectral lines.
Key variables: IV: spectral line order n. DV: angle θ to each line.
Method: 1. Set up spectrometer (or improvised grating + protractor) with a diffraction grating (600 lines/mm). 2. Illuminate with a gas discharge tube (hydrogen, helium, or sodium). 3. Measure angle θ to each visible spectral line in first and second orders. 4. Calculate λ = d sin θ/n for each line; compare with tabulated values.
Measurements: Grating spacing d, angles θ to spectral lines, order n.
Analysis: d sin θ = nλ. Identify hydrogen Balmer series lines: red (656 nm), blue-green (486 nm), violet (434 nm). Extension: from hydrogen wavelengths, verify 1/λ = R_H(1/2² − 1/n²) (Balmer formula).
Safety: Gas discharge tubes run at high voltage (few kV) — use only with proper holders; do not touch terminals. UV from mercury lamp — avoid prolonged direct exposure.
Data skills: Grating equation; spectral line identification; Balmer series verification; R_H from multiple lines.
Common errors / improvements: Spectrometer collimator must be focused on the slit — if the lines appear blurry, adjust the collimator. Zero-order (white central) must be identified before measuring angles — all θ measured from this. Second-order lines of short wavelengths overlap with third-order of long wavelengths at high angles — only use clean, non-overlapping orders. Vernier scale on spectrometer: read the vernier coincidence, not just the main scale.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: diffraction grating (600 lines/mm), sodium lamp + discharge tube kit (He, H, Hg), spectrometer or metre rule, ruler. Switch discharge tubes on 5 min before lesson. Keep spectrometers pre-focused on slits. Gratings: handle by edges only.

Title: Redshift demonstration (Hubble's law activity)
Aim: Demonstrate redshift using an analogy (stretched rubber band with marked points) and/or spectral data; verify Hubble's law.
Key variables: Qualitative demonstration + data-analysis activity.
Method: Rubber-band analogy: 1. Mark equally spaced dots on a rubber band; measure separations. Stretch uniformly; re-measure. 2. From any dot's perspective, all others recede; recession speed ∝ distance (Hubble's law analogy). Data activity: 3. Provide students with spectra of distant galaxies (printed or projected); measure apparent wavelength of a known spectral line (e.g. Hα). 4. z = (λ_obs − λ_rest)/λ_rest. v = zc (for z << 1). Plot v vs distance (given); gradient = H₀.
Measurements: Spectral line wavelengths, distances (provided).
Analysis: Hubble's law: v = H₀d. From gradient: H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc.
Safety: None beyond normal lab safety.
Data skills: Doppler redshift formula; Hubble's law; H₀ from gradient; distinction between recession and proper motion.
Common errors / improvements: Rubber-band analogy: students must understand no dot is 'special' (no centre of expansion) — any dot sees all others receding. Redshift ≠ Doppler shift for large z (cosmological redshift is due to space expansion) — at school level, treat v = zc as valid for small z only. H₀ value from student data will scatter widely (distances to galaxies are uncertain) — treat as order-of-magnitude. Students sometimes calculate z using the wrong rest wavelength — provide it clearly on the worksheet.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 5 min. Data activity — print or project Hubble's velocity-distance data. Provide graph paper or access to spreadsheet.

Title: Measuring wavelength of sound (signal generator and CRO)
Aim: Measure the wavelength and speed of sound directly using a signal generator, two microphones and an oscilloscope.
Key variables: IV: separation between two microphones Δx. DV: phase difference φ.
Method: 1. Signal generator drives a loudspeaker at a fixed frequency (e.g. 1000 Hz). 2. Two microphones connected to dual-trace oscilloscope; one fixed (reference), one moveable. 3. Move second microphone away from speaker; measure distance for one full wavelength (phase returns to in-phase after λ). 4. Repeat for 3–4 frequencies.
Measurements: Microphone separation Δx, frequency f.
Analysis: λ = Δx per complete phase cycle. v = fλ. Plot λ vs 1/f; gradient = v_sound.
Safety: Speaker at high volume — keep reasonable distance. Loudspeaker can overheat — don't run at maximum volume for extended periods.
Data skills: Phase comparison; linear plot λ vs 1/f; gradient → v_sound; end-correction-free method.
Common errors / improvements: Moving microphone must stay on axis with the speaker to avoid angle effects. Reflections from walls create standing-wave nodes and antinodes that can be confused with phase-shift progression — use absorbing foam behind the setup. At high frequencies (>5 kHz) the microphone directional response varies — stay below 3 kHz for reliable results. Oscilloscope phase readout: note in-phase appears as identical waveforms; out-of-phase by λ/2 appears as mirror image.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min — see WAVE-02 (resonance tube version). Pre-set signal generator and CRO to appropriate ranges.

Title: Newton's rings (optional A-Level / extension)
Aim: Observe Newton's rings (thin-film interference); measure the radius of curvature of a plano-convex lens.
Key variables: IV: ring number m. DV: ring radius r_m.
Method: 1. Place a plano-convex lens (long focal length, ≈1 m) on a flat glass plate; illuminate from above with monochromatic light (sodium lamp or filtered). 2. Observe circular interference rings through a travelling microscope; measure ring diameters. 3. Tabulate r_m² vs m.
Measurements: Ring number m, ring radius r_m (measured with travelling microscope).
Analysis: r_m² = mλR. Plot r_m² vs m; gradient = λR. With λ known (sodium: 589 nm), calculate R. Or: use two wavelengths to determine λ if R is known independently.
Safety: Sodium lamp: UV emission — do not stare directly. Travelling microscope — fragile objective.
Data skills: Linear plot (r² vs m); gradient → λR; phase change on reflection at the denser medium.
Common errors / improvements: Central spot should be dark (destructive interference from phase inversion at lower glass surface) — if it is bright, there is a dust layer separating the surfaces. Clean both surfaces. Lens must rest only on its own weight — pressing it distorts the air gap and moves ring centres. Travelling microscope: always approach the sample from the same direction (avoid backlash). Rings are compressed at the top if the plate is tilted — tilt the lens stage until rings are circular.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per setup: sodium lamp, flat glass plate, plano-convex lens (large radius of curvature), travelling microscope. Clean glass surfaces thoroughly — dust causes false rings. Set up in vibration-free location.

Title: Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water
Aim: Determine the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water by electrical heating.
Key variables: IV: energy supplied E. DV: mass of water evaporated m.
Method: 1. Bring ~200 mL of water in an insulated container to a rolling boil using an immersion heater. 2. Once boiling steadily, start the joulemeter and tare the balance simultaneously. 3. Record mass lost (steam driven off) every 2 min for 10 min. 4. Switch off; record final E and Δm. 5. Run a control (no heater, same apparatus boiling on a hotplate) to estimate ambient evaporation rate; subtract.
Measurements: Energy E (J), mass lost Δm (kg).
Analysis: L_v = E / Δm. Compare with accepted value (2.26 MJ/kg at 100 °C).
Safety: Boiling water — use heatproof gloves when handling. Steam burns. Low-voltage heater only.
Data skills: Control subtraction; % difference from accepted value; systematic loss from ambient evaporation.
Common errors / improvements: Evaporation from the surface (not boiling) contributes a background mass loss — the control experiment corrects for this. Steam condensing on the inside of the container returns water — do not include condensed drops in Δm. Ensure steam escapes freely. Joulemeter zero must be checked before starting; balance must be re-tared to zero before the timed run. Heat loss through container walls means not all E goes into vaporisation → L_v measured too high; insulate well.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: boiling tube of water + immersion heater, joulemeter, thermometer, balance, insulated flask. Fill boiling tubes with pre-measured water. Calibrate joulemakers.

Title: Cooling curve experiment
Aim: Investigate how a substance cools with time; identify phase changes from a cooling curve.
Key variables: IV: time t. DV: temperature T.
Method: 1. Melt stearic acid (or similar, m.p. ~55–70 °C) in a boiling tube in a water bath. 2. Remove from bath; insert thermometer; record T every 30 s as it cools from ~80 °C to ~40 °C. 3. Plot T vs t; identify the plateau (phase change at melting point). 4. Extension: repeat with salol (m.p. 43 °C) to observe supercooling before crystallisation.
Measurements: Time t (s), temperature T (°C) at each step.
Analysis: Plot T vs t. Plateau at melting point = latent heat being released at constant T. Gradient before/after plateau gives specific heat capacity of liquid and solid respectively.
Safety: Hot water bath — heatproof mat, tongs. Stearic acid fumes — ventilate the room.
Data skills: Identifying phase transitions from gradient changes; qualitative latent heat concept; supercooling discussion.
Common errors / improvements: Plateau may not be perfectly flat — temperature can drift slightly if cooling is too fast or thermometer has slow response. Stearic acid takes time to fully solidify — the plateau ends when the last liquid solidifies, not when the outside looks solid. Thermometer must be in the liquid/solid, not in the air above it — reposition if the substance contracts. For salol: supercooling is more pronounced when the tube is very clean — a scratch or dust particle acts as a nucleation site.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: substance (naphthalene or stearic acid, ~50 g in test tube), water bath at 90 °C, thermometer, stopwatch, clamp stand. CLEAPSS check: naphthalene is harmful vapour — use stearic acid as safer alternative. Pre-melt solid by heating water bath. Ensure thermometer inserted into substance not water.

Title: Thermal conductivity (bar method)
Aim: Compare thermal conductivity of different metals using a heated bar and wax pegs or temperature probes.
Key variables: IV: material (copper, iron, glass). DV: distance along bar where wax melts, or temperature profile.
Method: Wax-peg method: 1. Clamp identical bars of different materials horizontally; attach wax-coated match-sticks at equal intervals along each. 2. Heat one end of each bar simultaneously with Bunsen/electric heater. 3. Record time for each peg to drop (wax melts); the more pegs that drop = higher conductivity. Temperature-profile method (quantitative): 4. Drill holes along a bar; insert thermocouples or temperature probes at each position. 5. Record steady-state T at each position; gradient dT/dx = −P/(kA).
Measurements: Position x, temperature T at steady state; or time for wax pegs to fall.
Analysis: Wax method: ranking of conductivities. Quantitative: k = P / (A × dT/dx). Plot T vs x; gradient → k.
Safety: Hot bar — tongs and heatproof mat. Bunsen — standard precautions.
Data skills: Steady-state heat conduction; linear T gradient → k; comparison of materials; ranking conductivities.
Common errors / improvements: Steady state takes time — the temperature profile keeps changing unless you wait until all probes are stable (can take 15+ min). Record only steady-state values. Bar must be well-insulated along its length (lagging) or heat losses to air make the T profile nonlinear. Wax-peg method is purely qualitative — it shows which conducts better but not by how much. Contact resistance at the heater–bar junction can dominate for metal bars — use a proper heat-sink compound.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Per setup: conducting bar (brass, aluminium, steel — same dimensions), multiple thermistors or thermocouples at equal intervals along bar, datalogger, Bunsen or hot plate. Ensure good thermal contact between sensors and bar (thermal grease or clamps).

Title: Thermal insulation comparison
Aim: Compare the effectiveness of different insulating materials by measuring the rate of cooling of a hot liquid.
Key variables: IV: insulating material. DV: rate of cooling (dT/dt).
Method: 1. Fill identical beakers (or tin cans) with 200 mL of hot water (~70 °C). 2. Wrap each in a different insulating material (cotton wool, bubble wrap, newspaper, foam, nothing). 3. Record temperature every 1 min for 15 min. 4. Plot T vs t for each material on the same axes; compare gradients.
Measurements: Time t, temperature T for each material.
Analysis: Gradient dT/dt ∝ (T − T_room) for Newtonian cooling (exponential decay). Better insulator → smaller gradient → slower cooling. Extension: plot ln(T − T_room) vs t; straight line confirms Newton's law of cooling; gradient = −1/τ (time constant).
Safety: Hot water — heatproof mat. Don't lean over beakers.
Data skills: Gradient comparison; Newton's law of cooling; log-linear plot (ln(T − T_room) vs t); time constant τ.
Common errors / improvements: Water level must be the same in each beaker — different volumes change the heat capacity and confound comparisons. Lid or no lid must be consistent — evaporation adds a large systematic cooling effect. Use identical covers on all. Thermometer not at same depth in each beaker → different readings. For the exponential fit, T_room must be accurately known and stable — measure it at the start and end.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: identical cans (one bare, one wrapped in insulating material), thermometers or temperature probes, hot water, stopwatch. Fill cans with equal volumes of hot water (60 °C) simultaneously just before measuring.

Title: Charles's law (V ∝ T at constant pressure)
Aim: Verify that the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure is proportional to its absolute temperature.
Key variables: IV: temperature T (K). DV: volume V (length of trapped air column).
Method: 1. Trap a column of air in a glass capillary tube sealed at one end with a small sulfuric acid plug (or oil drop) — the plug provides constant pressure. 2. Immerse tube in a water bath; vary temperature from ~10 °C to ~80 °C in ~10 °C steps. 3. At each temperature (wait for equilibrium), measure the length of air column L with a ruler. L ∝ V.
Measurements: Temperature T (°C → K), air column length L (mm).
Analysis: V ∝ T (Kelvin). Plot L vs T(K); expect straight line through origin (or extrapolate to L = 0 at T = 0 K). Extrapolated x-intercept ≈ −273 °C = 0 K (experimental determination of absolute zero).
Safety: Concentrated sulfuric acid plug — teacher preparation only; do not let students handle acid. Hot water bath — heatproof mat, tongs.
Data skills: Kelvin vs Celsius distinction; extrapolation to absolute zero; linear regression with x-intercept interpretation.
Common errors / improvements: Using Celsius not Kelvin → line does not pass through origin and the result is meaningless. Always convert. Acid plug must move freely — if it sticks (tube too narrow or wet), pressure is not constant and the law is not being tested. Waiting for equilibrium at each temperature is critical — the air column continues to expand for ~30 s after stirring. The extrapolated intercept is sensitive to the slope — a poor fit over a narrow T range gives a large uncertainty in absolute zero.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: capillary tube sealed at one end with air column above oil plug, ruler, thermometer, water bath (adjustable to 80 °C), clamp. Pre-measure and record initial air column length. Check oil plug is intact — no leaks.

Title: Pressure–temperature law (Gay-Lussac's law)
Aim: Verify that pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume is proportional to absolute temperature.
Key variables: IV: temperature T (K). DV: pressure P.
Method: 1. Seal a volume of air in a flask connected to a pressure gauge (Bourdon or electronic). 2. Immerse flask in water bath; vary temperature from ~10 °C to ~80 °C. 3. Record P at each T (wait for thermal equilibrium each step).
Measurements: Temperature T (°C → K), pressure P (kPa).
Analysis: P ∝ T (Kelvin). Plot P vs T(K); straight line; extrapolate to x-intercept ≈ 0 K. Combine with Boyle's law to discuss ideal gas law PV = nRT.
Safety: Pressure vessel — do not exceed gauge rating. Hot water bath — heatproof mat.
Data skills: Linear plot P vs T(K); extrapolation to absolute zero; combining gas laws discussion.
Common errors / improvements: Flask volume must include the volume of the connecting tube to the gauge — systematic error if this is not negligible. Electronic pressure gauges give absolute pressure; Bourdon gauges give gauge pressure — add atmospheric pressure to get absolute P. Waiting for equilibrium: the air inside the flask equilibrates more slowly than the water bath — stir and wait ≥2 min. Plot should not extrapolate to exactly 0 K due to real-gas effects at low T — discuss as a limitation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: sealed flask of air with pressure gauge (or Bourdon gauge), water bath (0–100 °C), thermometer. Check seals. Allow flask to equilibrate at each temperature for 3 min before reading.

Title: Ideal gas law investigation (combined)
Aim: Investigate PV = nRT simultaneously by varying P, V, and T in a controlled way.
Key variables: IV: any two of P, V, T. DV: third variable.
Method: 1. Use a syringe sealed with a pressure sensor and a temperature-controlled water jacket. 2. Vary volume (piston position) at constant T: verify PV = constant (Boyle). 3. Vary T at constant V: verify P ∝ T (Gay-Lussac). 4. Compute nR from each dataset; verify consistency. 5. Plot PV vs T; gradient = nR.
Measurements: P, V, T at each condition.
Analysis: PV = nRT. Plot PV vs T (fixed n): straight line, gradient = nR. Calculate n from mass of trapped gas (if known) and verify R ≈ 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Safety: Sealed syringe under pressure — do not exceed 3× atmospheric. Hot water — standard precautions.
Data skills: PV product as combined variable; gradient → nR; verification of R; real gas deviations at high P.
Common errors / improvements: Syringe friction gives hysteresis in V reading — push and pull and average, or use a frictionless piston. Gas in dead volume of sensor tube not accounted for → V is systematically underestimated. nR should be the same from all three approaches — if not, identify which assumption (constant n, V, or T) broke down. At high T the syringe may leak — use PTFE tape on the piston seal.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Per group: as THERM-05 and THERM-06 combined, plus Boyle's law tube. Check all three setups before lesson.

Title: Background radiation and half-life simulation
Aim: Measure background radiation and simulate radioactive decay with dice to model half-life.
Key variables: Background: count rate with no source. Simulation: number of 'undecayed' dice vs throw number.
Method: Background: 1. GM tube + counter; no source present; record count every 10 s for 5 min. 2. Calculate mean background count rate and standard deviation. Dice simulation: 3. Start with 200 dice; throw all; remove any showing a '6' (decayed). 4. Count remaining dice; record as N after 1 throw. Repeat until N < 5. 5. Pool class data for smoother curve.
Measurements: Background: count rate over time. Dice: N remaining after each throw.
Analysis: Background: mean ± σ (σ ≈ √N for Poisson). Dice: N = N₀ × (5/6)^n. Plot ln N vs n; gradient = ln(5/6) = −0.182. Experimental half-life ≈ n½ where N = N₀/2; theoretical = ln2/ln(6/5) ≈ 3.8 throws.
Safety: GM tube: don't touch the tube window (fragile mica). No radioactive source needed for this practical.
Data skills: Poisson statistics (σ = √N); log-linear plot; experimental vs theoretical half-life; law of large numbers (class pooling).
Common errors / improvements: Background count is NOT zero — students often forget to subtract it when using real sources later. Standard deviation of background count ≈ √(mean count) — verify this and discuss Poisson distribution. Dice simulation: 6 sides means probability of decay = 1/6 per throw — any other number of sides changes the half-life; use standard dice. Small sample of dice → large statistical scatter; pooling class data is the key lesson about counting statistics.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. For simulation: bags of ~100 dice (shaking out 6s as 'decayed' nuclei), large containers. For Geiger counter: see AL-13. Pre-count dice if using physical simulation.

Title: Absorption of alpha, beta and gamma radiation
Aim: Investigate the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation using absorbers of different materials and thicknesses.
Key variables: IV: absorber material and thickness. DV: corrected count rate.
Method: 1. Measure background count rate (no source). 2. Alpha source (e.g. Am-241): measure count rate at ≤5 cm with no absorber; insert paper, then card — alpha stops in a few cm of air or one sheet of paper. 3. Beta source (e.g. Sr-90): measure count rate through increasing thicknesses of aluminium sheet (0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 mm); plot corrected count vs thickness. 4. Gamma source (e.g. Co-60 or Cs-137): measure through increasing lead thicknesses (1, 2, 5, 10, 20 mm); plot ln(corrected count) vs thickness.
Measurements: Absorber thickness x, corrected count rate C.
Analysis: Alpha: stopped by paper/few cm air. Beta: C = C₀ e^(−μx) for aluminium; plot ln C vs x; gradient = −μ (attenuation coefficient). Gamma: same exponential law in lead; compare μ values.
Safety: All three source types require strict school radioactive source regulations. Teacher handles sources. Tongs. Log usage. Lock away after.
Data skills: Background subtraction; exponential attenuation (ln C vs x); attenuation coefficient; comparing penetrating power qualitatively and quantitatively.
Common errors / improvements: Alpha source: moisture or dust on the source surface absorbs alpha particles before they enter the detector — use only freshly-cleaned sources. Beta source: bremsstrahlung X-rays are produced when beta particles decelerate in aluminium — these are more penetrating and create a 'tail' on the curve. Use a linear extrapolation to identify the true beta range. Gamma source: the inverse-square law and the absorption are both reducing the count; keep source-to-detector distance fixed and only vary absorber thickness. Background must be subtracted before taking logarithms — ln(negative number) is undefined.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. RADIATION SOURCES — consult CLEAPSS. Alpha source (e.g. Am-241 in sealed holder), beta source (Sr-90), gamma source (Co-57 or Cs-137). Geiger-Müller tube + ratemeter, absorber sheets (paper, aluminium, lead). Sign sources in/out. Record background before lesson. All handling with tongs — never touch sources.

Title: Radioactive decay counting (short half-life source)
Aim: Measure the half-life of a short-lived radioactive source (e.g. protactinium-234 or radon-220) directly.
Key variables: IV: time t. DV: count rate C (corrected for background).
Method: Protactinium generator method: 1. Shake the Pa generator bottle; allow Pa-234 (t½ ≈ 1.2 min) to separate into the organic layer. 2. Immediately place GM tube adjacent to the organic layer; record count every 10 s for 10 min. 3. Subtract background; plot ln(C − C_background) vs t; gradient = −λ; t½ = ln2/λ.
Measurements: Count rate C at each time t (every 10 s).
Analysis: C(t) = C₀ e^(−λt). Plot ln C (corrected) vs t; gradient = −λ; t½ = ln2/λ. Compare with known t½.
Safety: Pa generator: sealed bottle — do not open. Organic solvent (iso-octane) — flammable, ventilate room. Teacher supervision throughout.
Data skills: Log-linear decay plot; gradient → λ; half-life from λ; Poisson uncertainty on individual counts.
Common errors / improvements: Pa generator must be shaken vigorously for at least 1 min for full separation — insufficient shaking gives a low initial count. Start timing immediately after shaking — delay means you miss the steepest part of the decay curve. Counts per 10 s are small at late times → large Poisson uncertainty → scatter dominates the tail; restrict fit to first 5 min. Students often plot C not ln C and try to read t½ by eye — the log plot is far more reliable.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Protactinium generator (Pa-234, prepared from uranyl nitrate solution) — CLEAPSS HG147. Prepare generator the day before and store according to regulations. Geiger counter + ratemeter + stopwatch. Ensure regulatory compliance for storage, use, and disposal.

Title: Photoelectric effect (demonstration)
Aim: Demonstrate the photoelectric effect using a gold-leaf electroscope and UV lamp; show frequency threshold.
Key variables: UV light causes a negatively-charged electroscope to discharge; visible light does not.
Method: 1. Charge a gold-leaf electroscope negatively (leaves diverge). 2. Shine UV lamp on the zinc plate — leaves collapse (electrons emitted). 3. Repeat with visible light (same intensity) — leaves remain diverged (no emission). 4. Place a glass sheet between UV lamp and plate — UV is absorbed by glass; no discharge. 5. Try positively-charged electroscope — UV has no effect (no electrons to remove).
Measurements: Qualitative: leaf divergence vs radiation type and charge sign.
Analysis: Threshold frequency f₀: hf₀ = φ (work function). Only UV (f > f₀) causes emission. Explains wave theory failure: intensity of visible light irrelevant — frequency determines emission.
Safety: UV lamp: avoid direct exposure to skin or eyes — UV-protective goggles. Zinc plate must be clean.
Data skills: Qualitative threshold frequency argument; wave theory vs photon theory comparison; work function concept.
Common errors / improvements: Zinc plate must be freshly cleaned with sandpaper immediately before use — an oxide layer prevents electron emission entirely. The effect fails if the electroscope is not well-insulated at the base — moisture on the insulating rod leaks the charge. UV lamp takes 1–2 min to warm up to full intensity — allow warm-up before the demonstration. Students must predict what will happen with glass sheet before inserting it — the surprise is the teaching point.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. DEMO ONLY. Zinc plate + electroscope, UV lamp, earthing strap. Polish zinc plate immediately before lesson with emery paper. UV lamp: ensure UV-blocking goggles available. Check electroscope leaf is not sticky.

Title: Measuring Planck's constant (LEDs)
Aim: Estimate Planck's constant h from the threshold voltage of LEDs of different colours.
Key variables: IV: LED colour (frequency f). DV: threshold voltage V_th.
Method: 1. Connect LED in series with a variable resistor and a milliammeter; voltmeter across LED. 2. Slowly increase voltage; record V_th as the voltage at which the LED just begins to emit light (dim glow visible). 3. Repeat for LEDs of different colours (red ≈ 625 nm, orange, yellow, green ≈ 530 nm, blue ≈ 470 nm). 4. Look up (or measure with spectrometer) the peak wavelength λ of each LED; f = c/λ.
Measurements: Threshold voltage V_th, frequency f for each LED colour.
Analysis: eV_th = hf (energy of photon ≈ energy given to electron). Plot V_th vs f; gradient = h/e → h = gradient × e. Compare with accepted value (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
Safety: Low voltage only. LEDs are fragile — don't exceed rated current.
Data skills: Linear plot (V_th vs f); gradient → h/e; multiplying by e → h; % difference from accepted.
Common errors / improvements: Threshold voltage is not sharply defined — the LED emits over a range. Standardise the definition (e.g. 1 mA current threshold) and apply consistently to all colours. LED peak emission wavelength differs from its colour appearance — use a spectrometer or data sheet value for λ. Series resistor limits current and allows fine voltage control — without it, LED current jumps suddenly and the threshold is hard to find. The method gives h to ~20% accuracy at best due to the threshold ambiguity — discuss as a systematic limitation, not a random one.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: selection of coloured LEDs (known peak wavelengths), variable PSU (0–3 V), voltmeter, current-limiting resistors, photodiode (optional). Measure and label LED peak wavelengths (from datasheets). Ensure LEDs are not burned out from previous classes.

Title: Electron diffraction (demonstration)
Aim: Observe the diffraction of electrons through a graphite target; verify de Broglie wavelength.
Key variables: Electron diffraction tube produces rings on a fluorescent screen.
Method: 1. Set up electron diffraction tube (Teltron or similar) with EHT supply (3–5 kV). 2. Observe two diffraction rings on the phosphor screen. 3. Measure ring diameters D₁ and D₂ at several accelerating voltages V_a. 4. Calculate λ = h/p = h/√(2meV_a) for each V_a.
Measurements: Ring diameter D, accelerating voltage V_a.
Analysis: λ = h/√(2meV_a). From Bragg's law: 2d sin θ = λ; d (graphite lattice spacing) ≈ 0.123 nm and 0.213 nm. Plot D vs 1/√V_a; expect straight line through origin.
Safety: EHT supply up to 5 kV — teacher operates. Do not touch the tube terminals. X-rays produced at anode — keep behind lead glass screen of tube.
Data skills: de Broglie wavelength; Bragg diffraction; linear plot D vs 1/√V_a; wave-particle duality evidence.
Common errors / improvements: EHT supply warm-up: rings may be faint until the tube reaches steady state (~1 min). Ring measurement: diameter not radius — easy to measure the wrong quantity. Measure full diameter across the ring. Two rings correspond to two different lattice spacings in polycrystalline graphite — identify both. Higher voltage → smaller λ → smaller rings (rings shrink as V increases) — counter-intuitive to students expecting 'more energy = bigger effect'.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: DEMO ONLY — specialist equipment. Electron diffraction tube, EHT supply (≥5 kV). EHT SAFETY: ensure all connections are insulated. Do not touch terminals. Check tube is not cracked (implosion risk). Only teacher operates EHT supply.

Title: Rutherford scattering analogue
Aim: Use a rolling-ball analogue to model Rutherford scattering; discuss nuclear size and charge.
Key variables: Steel balls rolling on a curved surface (representing the Coulomb potential) are deflected.
Method: 1. Place a 'hill-shaped' curved surface (representing the nuclear Coulomb potential) on a flat board. 2. Roll steel balls at different impact parameters (distances from centre) and observe deflection angles. 3. Count the number of balls deflected at large angles (>90°) vs small angles. 4. Compare expected scattering patterns for a Thomson 'plum-pudding' model (no deflections) vs nuclear model (large deflections).
Measurements: Impact parameter b, deflection angle θ.
Analysis: Rutherford scattering: large-angle scattering only from a tiny, dense nucleus. Most alpha particles pass through undeflected → atom mostly empty space.
Safety: Steel balls can roll off the bench — use a raised edge or tray. Balls are small choking hazard.
Data skills: Qualitative probability argument; nuclear model vs Thomson model; inverse-square Coulomb force analogy.
Common errors / improvements: The analogy breaks down because the curved surface is a gravitational (r⁻¹) potential, not a Coulomb (r⁻¹) force — but both give the same r⁻² scattering angle relationship. Students must understand that the alpha particle never touches the nucleus in elastic scattering. The probability of large-angle scattering is very low — rolling many balls shows this statistically.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: rolling-ball Rutherford scattering analogue (plastic cone + ball bearings) or mounted 'hill' analogue. Check ball bearings are not chipped. Tape 'target' position securely.

Title: Cloud chamber observation
Aim: Observe tracks of alpha and beta particles in a diffusion cloud chamber; identify particle type from track characteristics.
Key variables: Qualitative observation of ionisation tracks.
Method: 1. Set up diffusion cloud chamber (dry ice or Peltier cooled) with a sealed alpha source inside. 2. Allow isopropyl alcohol vapour to supersaturate near the cold base (~−30 °C). 3. Observe thick, straight, short tracks (alpha) and thin, tortuous, longer tracks (beta/electrons). 4. Apply a magnetic field across the chamber; observe curvature direction to identify charge sign.
Measurements: Qualitative: track length, width, straightness.
Analysis: Alpha: thick, straight, ~3–5 cm — high ionisation density, low penetration. Beta: thin, wandering, longer — lower ionisation density. Magnetic field: α curves one way, β the other (opposite charge).
Safety: Dry ice: −78 °C — insulated gloves essential. IPA vapour — flammable, ventilate room. Sealed source only.
Data skills: Qualitative ionisation density argument; track curvature in B field; charge-to-mass ratio differences.
Common errors / improvements: Cloud chamber must reach stable operating temperature — allow 10–15 min for thermal equilibrium. Too much IPA or too hot → supersaturation is unstable and tracks appear then vanish immediately. Light the chamber from the side (a torch at an angle) — tracks are nearly invisible from above. Background cosmic-ray muon tracks (long, thin, straight) are occasionally visible — a welcome addition to discussion.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. DEMO ONLY. Diffusion cloud chamber + dry ice (solid CO₂) + isopropanol + radioactive source. COSHH: dry ice — cryogenic burns; gloves essential. Isopropanol — flammable; no flames. Set up 20 min before lesson: chamber needs time to reach equilibrium. Dim room lights for visibility. Source must comply with regulations.

Title: Upthrust and Archimedes' principle
Aim: Verify Archimedes' principle: upthrust equals weight of fluid displaced.
Key variables: IV: volume of object submerged. DV: upthrust (reduction in apparent weight).
Method: 1. Weigh a metal object in air on a Newton meter: W_air. 2. Submerge in water; record apparent weight W_water. Upthrust U = W_air − W_water. 3. Collect displaced water in a pre-weighed beaker (overflow can / eureka can); weigh it. 4. Verify U = weight of displaced water. 5. Repeat with different objects (different materials, same volume; or same material, different volumes submerged).
Measurements: W_air, W_water, mass of displaced water m_d.
Analysis: U = W_air − W_water = m_d × g. Verify numerically. Extension: find density of object ρ = W_air / (W_air − W_water) × ρ_water.
Safety: Glassware on stable surface. Wipe spills immediately.
