Common errors / improvements: Not adding equal volumes of yoghurt/bacteria to each tube — not a fair test. pH indicator colour difficult to read — pH probe more reliable. Temperature of water bath not maintained — check and adjust. Not mixing tube contents — bacteria settle. Dairy allergy — check before students handle milk.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Full-fat milk: 30 cm³ per group in small beakers. Live natural yoghurt (contains Lactobacillus): 10 cm³ per group in dropper bottles. Water baths: set to 5, 15, 25, 35, 45 °C — allow 20 min to equilibrate. pH probes: calibrate at pH 4 and 7. Alternatively: universal indicator + colour chart. Disinfectant spray on benches before and after.

Title: Plant responses — phototropism
Aim: Investigate the effect of unilateral light on the direction of growth in germinating seedlings (phototropism).
Key variables: IV: direction of light source. DV: angle of curvature of seedling shoot (degrees). Control: temperature, water, seed type, growth time.
Method: 1. Germinate cress or radish seeds in damp cotton wool in a box lined with black card. 2. Cut a small hole on one side of the box to provide unilateral light. 3. Grow for 5–7 days. 4. Photograph seedlings; measure angle of curvature from vertical using a protractor overlay. 5. Compare with a control box lit from all sides (no curvature expected).
Measurements: Angle of curvature of each seedling (degrees), percentage of seedlings showing positive phototropism.
Analysis: Mean angle of curvature; describe as positive phototropism (shoots bend toward light). Explain: unilateral light causes unequal auxin distribution; more auxin on shaded side causes faster cell elongation. Link to IAA (indole acetic acid).
Safety: Standard low-hazard practical. Ensure seeds are not mouldy. Water regularly but don't waterlog.
Data skills: Mean and variability; biological drawing; qualitative and quantitative measurement.
Common errors / improvements: Box not light-tight enough — light enters from multiple directions. Seeds too crowded — seedlings compete and distort each other. Not growing long enough — curvature too slight to measure. Only qualitative description — measure angle for quantitative data. Forgetting control experiment with even lighting.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 5 min + 7 days advance setup. Sow cress seeds in boxes 7 days before required lesson. Set up light-directional boxes at same time. Water regularly (daily). Bring to lesson on day. Advance notice to teacher: plan 2 weeks ahead for this experiment.

Title: Making a salt by reacting acid with alkali (titration method)
Aim: Prepare a pure, dry sample of sodium chloride by titrating sodium hydroxide against hydrochloric acid, then evaporating to crystallise.
Key variables: IV: volume of acid. DV: pH at endpoint. Control: concentration of reactants, volume of alkali.
Method: 1. Titrate 25 cm³ NaOH against HCl using phenolphthalein to find exact neutralisation volume. 2. Repeat the titration without indicator using the exact titre volume. 3. Pour the neutral solution into an evaporating basin. 4. Heat gently on a water bath to reduce volume to ~half. 5. Allow to cool and crystallise; filter and dry.
Measurements: Titre volume (cm³), crystal yield (g).
Analysis: Write equation: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Ionic equation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Discuss why indicator cannot be used in the preparative run.
Safety: Corrosive alkali — eye protection. Hot solutions — water bath only.
Data skills: Titration technique; salt preparation; ionic equations.
Common errors / improvements: Using indicator in preparative run — contaminates final salt. Heating too strongly — salt spits. Not using concordant titres — impure product.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min — see CHEM-02 for solution preparation. Additional: prepare evaporating basins and water bath as CHEM-01. Ensure students do preparative run without indicator. Note to teacher: confirm correct titre is used before students proceed to large-scale preparation.

Title: pH of common substances and neutralisation curves
Aim: Measure the pH of a range of household substances and plot a pH curve for the addition of alkali to acid.
Key variables: IV: substance tested / volume of alkali added. DV: pH. Control: volume of acid, concentration.
Method: 1. Test pH of lemon juice, vinegar, water, milk, baking soda solution, bleach using universal indicator or pH probe. 2. Neutralisation curve: add NaOH (1 mol/dm³) from burette to 25 cm³ HCl (1 mol/dm³) in 1 cm³ steps; record pH after each addition. 3. Add 0.1 cm³ drops near the equivalence point for detail. 4. Plot pH vs volume of NaOH added.
Measurements: pH at each volume of alkali added; pH of each household substance.
Analysis: Describe S-shaped neutralisation curve. Identify equivalence point. Explain buffer region. Compare weak vs strong acid/base curves if time allows.
Safety: Bleach — corrosive; do not mix with acids (chlorine gas). NaOH — corrosive. Eye protection throughout.
Data skills: S-curve; equivalence point; reading gradients; interpolation.
Common errors / improvements: Not stirring between each addition. Too large steps near equivalence — miss the sharp rise. pH probe not calibrated — always calibrate with buffer solutions first.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Household substance samples: lemon juice, white vinegar, milk, baking soda solution (1 tsp/100 cm³), dilute bleach (5% commercial bleach, diluted 1:10). Dispense in small dropper bottles (3 cm³ each). Make up NaOH and HCl as CHEM-02. Calibrate pH probes against pH 4 and pH 7 buffers.

Title: Reactivity of metals with acids and water
Aim: Investigate the reactivity of different metals with dilute acids and with water to establish a reactivity series.
Key variables: IV: metal type. DV: rate of bubble production / temperature change / whether reaction occurs. Control: acid concentration, surface area.
Method: 1. Add small pieces of Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu to separate test tubes of 2 mol/dm³ HCl. 2. Observe rate of effervescence; test gas with a lit splint (squeaky pop = H₂). 3. Add Mg and Ca (small pieces) to cold water — observe reaction; test solution with universal indicator (alkaline = metal hydroxide). 4. Rank metals by reactivity.
Measurements: Observations for each metal: bubble rate, temperature change, whether reaction occurs.
Analysis: Order metals: Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu. Write equations: e.g. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Explain in terms of electron loss. Relate to everyday uses (e.g. why copper used in pipes).
Safety: H₂ is flammable — keep lit splint away from reaction vessel. Mg burns — do not allow to ignite. Ca and Na violent with water — use small pieces, safety screen. Eye protection.
Data skills: Qualitative ordering; writing equations; pattern recognition.
Common errors / improvements: Using same-sized pieces — surface area effect. Adding too much metal — reaction too vigorous. Not testing gas — missing evidence for H₂.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Cut metals: Mg ribbon 1 cm pieces, Zn granules, Fe nails, Cu wire. Make up HCl (2 mol/dm³) — 50 cm³ per group. For water reactions (teacher-managed): Ca lumps under oil in small jar, trough of water + UDI on bench. Safety screen available for Ca reaction. Prepare wooden splints for H₂ test.

Title: Preparation of carbon dioxide and testing for gases
Aim: Prepare carbon dioxide by reacting marble chips with hydrochloric acid, and test for CO₂, H₂, O₂, and NH₃.
Key variables: IV: gas tested. DV: result of test. Control: fresh reagents for each test.
Method: 1. CO₂: react marble chips + HCl; bubble gas through limewater — turns milky. 2. H₂: react Zn + HCl; test with lit splint — squeaky pop. 3. O₂: decompose H₂O₂ with MnO₂ catalyst; test with glowing splint — relights. 4. NH₃: warm ammonium chloride + NaOH; test with damp red litmus paper — turns blue; test with damp universal indicator — turns purple/blue.
Measurements: Colour change of each test reagent; result (positive/negative).
Analysis: Tabulate gas name, test reagent, positive result. Link each test to chemical properties of the gas.
Safety: H₂ flammable. NH₃ — toxic, pungent; use small amounts in fume cupboard. H₂O₂ — oxidising; eye protection. HCl — fuming; ventilated area.
Data skills: Qualitative positive/negative tests; systematic recording.
Common errors / improvements: Letting gas collect before testing — some gases heavier than air (CO₂) sink out. Confusing squeaky pop (H₂) with relighting splint (O₂). Limewater going milky from breath contamination — ensure clean delivery tube.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min. Teacher demo setup. Gas jars, delivery tubes, trough of water, limewater, damp litmus paper. Set up 4 separate gas-preparation rigs. NH₃: set up last, in fume cupboard. All apparatus tested before class. Check all glassware is not chipped or cracked.

Title: Atomic emission spectra — flame photometry demo
Aim: Demonstrate that different elements produce characteristic emission spectra when heated, linking to electron energy levels.
Key variables: IV: element tested. DV: colour of flame / spectral lines observed. Control: clean wire, same flame.
Method: 1. Prepare solutions of LiCl, NaCl, KCl, CaCl₂, CuCl₂, SrCl₂ in small beakers. 2. Clean nichrome wire in HCl; dip in first solution; hold in blue Bunsen flame. 3. Observe flame colour; view through diffraction grating to see spectral lines. 4. Record colour and spectral line pattern for each element. 5. Compare to emission line diagrams in textbook.
Measurements: Flame colour for each element, spectral lines observed through diffraction grating.
Analysis: Each element has unique electron energy levels; photons emitted when electrons drop to lower level. E = hf links photon energy to frequency of light. Explain why Na dominates (yellow/orange) even in trace amounts.
Safety: Bunsen — burns. HCl fumes — ventilated area. Hot wire — allow to cool before touching.
Data skills: Qualitative observation; linking observation to atomic model.
Common errors / improvements: Na contamination — cleans wire inadequately. Only observing colour not spectral lines — less evidence for discrete levels. Students too far away to see spectral lines clearly — arrange close observation or use diffraction film handed out.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Clean wire loops × 6 (one per element) — see CHEM-08. Salt solutions as CHEM-08. Diffraction gratings: issue one per student or pair. Check sodium lamp is working — switch on 10 min before lesson (warm-up needed). Darken room for spectral line observation.

Title: Properties of Group 1 metals — reactions with water
Aim: Demonstrate the reactions of lithium, sodium, and potassium with water to show trends in reactivity down Group 1.
Key variables: IV: Group 1 metal used (Li, Na, K). DV: vigour of reaction, temperature change, pH of solution. Control: volume of water, size of metal piece.
Method: 1. Half-fill a large glass trough with cold water. Add universal indicator. 2. Cut a small piece of lithium (~5 mm); drop into water; observe. 3. Repeat with sodium (behind safety screen). 4. Repeat with potassium (behind safety screen; potassium ignites spontaneously). 5. Test pH of solution after each — alkaline (metal hydroxide formed).
Measurements: Vigour of effervescence, whether metal floats/melts/ignites, pH of product solution.
Analysis: Down the group: reaction becomes more vigorous. Equations: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Explain in terms of ionisation energy decreasing down group.
Safety: SAFETY CRITICAL: K reacts violently — use safety screen; have sand ready; use tongs not hands. Na — never touch with damp hands. Li — least reactive but still vigorous. Teacher demonstration only for K. Eye protection, lab coat.
Data skills: Qualitative trend; periodic table patterns; writing equations.
Common errors / improvements: Using too large a piece of K — dangerous explosion. No safety screen for Na or K. Not drying K before use — reacts more vigorously. Forgetting to test pH after reaction.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. TEACHER DEMO ONLY. Alkali metals: obtain from CLEAPSS-approved storage; remove small pieces with dry forceps only. Li: ~5 mm cube; Na: ~4 mm cube; K: ~3 mm cube. Trough: fill large glass tank with cold water + universal indicator. Safety screen: position between students and trough. K must be the smallest piece; have sand bucket and dry cloth ready. Do not cut K under water — cut on dry tile, immediately transfer to trough.

Title: Properties of Group 7 halogens — displacement reactions
Aim: Investigate the displacement reactions of halogens with halide solutions to determine the reactivity trend in Group 7.
Key variables: IV: halogen solution used (Cl₂, Br₂, I₂). DV: colour change in halide solution / cyclohexane layer. Control: concentration, volume.
Method: 1. Add a few drops of chlorine water to separate test tubes of KBr(aq) and KI(aq). 2. Add a few drops of bromine water to KCl(aq) and KI(aq). 3. Add a few drops of iodine solution to KCl(aq) and KBr(aq). 4. Add 1 cm³ cyclohexane to each tube; shake gently; observe organic layer colour.
Measurements: Colour of aqueous layer, colour of cyclohexane (organic) layer for each combination.
Analysis: Organic layer colours: Cl₂ = pale yellow-green; Br₂ = orange; I₂ = purple/violet. More reactive halogen displaces less reactive halide. Reactivity order: Cl > Br > I. Write ionic equations: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.
Safety: Halogen solutions — toxic and oxidising. Cyclohexane — flammable, no flames. Chlorine water — irritant vapour, ventilated area. Bromine — highly toxic, stains skin. Eye protection and gloves.
Data skills: Colour observation; organic layer separation; ionic equations; reactivity trend.
Common errors / improvements: Confusing aqueous and organic layer colours. Cyclohexane forms emulsion if shaken too hard. Iodine solution too concentrated — dark colour hard to assess. Not using clean tubes for each combination.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Prepare halogen solutions in fume cupboard: chlorine water (dilute, freshly prepared from Cl₂ cylinder or diluted bleach + acid); bromine water (saturated); iodine solution (0.1 mol/dm³ in KI). Halide solutions (0.1 mol/dm³): KCl, KBr, KI. Cyclohexane: dispense in small dropper bottles — flammable, keep away from flames. Ensure fume cupboard is working for bromine work.

Title: Properties of Period 3 oxides — acid/base character
Aim: Investigate the acid-base character of oxides across Period 3 and relate to the metallic/non-metallic character of the elements.
Key variables: IV: oxide tested (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₂O₅, SO₂). DV: pH of solution formed with water; reaction with HCl or NaOH. Control: volume of water, concentration.
Method: 1. Dissolve or suspend each solid oxide in water; test pH. 2. Na₂O and MgO: alkaline (metal oxides → basic). 3. SO₂: acidic solution (acid rain model). 4. Al₂O₃: amphoteric — test with both HCl and NaOH; dissolves in both. 5. SiO₂: insoluble, test directly with NaOH (reacts).
Measurements: pH of each oxide dissolved in water; whether it reacts with acid, alkali, or both.
Analysis: Trend: metal oxides basic; non-metal oxides acidic; Al₂O₃ amphoteric (in the middle). Link to position in periodic table. Connect SO₂ to acid rain.
Safety: SO₂ — toxic gas; fume cupboard or use dilute sulfurous acid (H₂SO₃) as substitute. NaOH — corrosive. P₂O₅ — reacts vigorously with water — teacher demo only. Eye protection.
Data skills: pH measurement; pattern across period; acid-base definitions.
Common errors / improvements: Using insoluble oxides without explaining why pH test is less valid. Not linking to metallic character trend. Confusion about amphoteric — students often think Al₂O₃ is neutral rather than reactive with both.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Obtain Period 3 oxides: MgO (common), Al₂O₃, SiO₂ (sand), Na₂O (very reactive — teacher handles only, stored in oil or gas). Safer alternative to SO₂: prepare H₂SO₃ by dissolving SO₂ in water, or use dilute H₂SO₄ as demonstration. Make up NaOH (2 mol/dm³) and HCl (2 mol/dm³). pH probes: calibrate before class.

Title: Properties of ionic and covalent compounds
Aim: Compare the physical properties (melting point, electrical conductivity, solubility) of ionic and covalent compounds and relate to bonding.
Key variables: IV: substance type (ionic: NaCl, CuSO₄; covalent: glucose, wax, sulfur; giant covalent: sand). DV: melting point, conductivity (solid/solution), solubility in water and hexane.
Method: 1. Test electrical conductivity of each substance as solid using a circuit with bulb. 2. Dissolve in water; test conductivity of solution. 3. Try dissolving in hexane (non-polar solvent). 4. Approximate melting point test: heat small sample on metal spatula over Bunsen — note ease of melting.
Measurements: Conductivity (yes/no) as solid and in solution, solubility in water and hexane, relative melting point.
Analysis: Ionic compounds: high melting point, conduct when dissolved or molten, dissolve in water. Simple covalent: low melting point, do not conduct, may dissolve in non-polar solvents. Giant covalent: very high melting point, do not conduct (except graphite).
Safety: Hexane — flammable, no flames. Heated substances — burns. Copper sulfate — harmful. Eye protection.
Data skills: Systematic table completion; linking properties to structure.
Common errors / improvements: Confusing conductivity of solid NaCl (no) with dissolved NaCl (yes). Students think all covalent compounds don't dissolve in water — glucose and ethanol do. Wax spatula melting — use metal spatula only.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Per group: labelled samples of NaCl, CuSO₄, glucose, wax, sulfur, sand, graphite rod. Conductivity circuit: prepare with crocodile clip probes and LED or bulb. Test each before class. Hexane: dispense in small sealed vials — flammable, no flames. Metal spatulas only for melting test — not plastic.

Title: Determining the formula of a metal oxide by oxidation
Aim: Determine the empirical formula of copper oxide by reducing it with hydrogen or by direct oxidation of copper.
Key variables: IV: mass of copper used. DV: mass of oxygen gained (oxidation) or mass of oxygen removed (reduction). Control: complete oxidation, same heating time.
Method: 1. Weigh a clean copper foil strip; place in crucible. 2. Heat strongly in Bunsen flame for 5 min; allow to cool; weigh (should gain mass = oxygen). 3. Calculate mass of oxygen added; find mole ratio Cu:O. 4. Alternative (reduction): weigh CuO; pass hydrogen gas over heated CuO in combustion tube; weigh residual Cu. Calculate mass of O removed.
Measurements: Mass of Cu before and after (g), mass of CuO (g), mass of O gained or lost (g).
Analysis: Moles of Cu = mass/64; moles of O = mass/16. Ratio gives empirical formula CuO. Compare to actual formula. % error calculation.
Safety: H₂ reduction method: H₂ is extremely flammable — ensure no air in apparatus before heating; collect excess H₂ safely; never heat copper until H₂ flowing. Oxidation method: hot crucible — heat-proof mat. Eye protection.
Data skills: Mole calculations; empirical formula; % error.
Common errors / improvements: Incomplete oxidation → ratio not exactly 1:1. Allowing H₂ to escape without burning off at exit — fire hazard. Not cooling completely before weighing — reading too low (hot balance). Crucible lid ajar — incomplete oxidation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Per group: 2 g copper foil or turnings, crucible, clay triangle, tripod, Bunsen. Desiccators: ensure silica gel is active (blue, not pink — replace if pink). Calibrate balances (0.001 g) — allow 15 min warm-up. Check crucibles are clean and dry.

Title: Gravimetric analysis — water of crystallisation
Aim: Determine the formula of hydrated copper sulfate (CuSO₄·xH₂O) by heating to constant mass.
Key variables: IV: mass of hydrated salt. DV: mass after heating (anhydrous salt). Control: same crucible, complete dehydration.
Method: 1. Weigh a clean, dry crucible; add ~5 g hydrated copper sulfate; weigh again. 2. Heat gently over Bunsen for 3 min; allow to cool in desiccator; weigh. 3. Reheat for 2 min; cool; reweigh — repeat until constant mass. 4. Calculate mass of water lost and mass of anhydrous CuSO₄ remaining.
Measurements: Mass of crucible, hydrated salt, anhydrous salt at each heating (g).
Analysis: Moles of CuSO₄ = mass/160; moles of H₂O = mass/18. x = moles H₂O / moles CuSO₄ = 5. Expected formula CuSO₄·5H₂O. Discuss significance of heating to constant mass.
Safety: Hot crucible — burns. Blue → white colour change is normal. Avoid breathing copper dust. Eye protection.
Data skills: Constant mass concept; mole ratios; formula determination.
Common errors / improvements: Not heating to constant mass — water not fully removed. Absorbing moisture from air when cooling — use desiccator. Spitting of crystals at high temperature — heat gently at first. Rounding ratio too early — use unrounded moles in calculation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Per group: 6 g hydrated CuSO₄ in labelled weighing boat, crucible. Setup as CHEM-21. Warn: students must heat gently at first to prevent spitting.

Title: Electrolysis — Faraday's law (mass deposited)
Aim: Investigate the relationship between the mass of copper deposited at the cathode and the charge passed during electrolysis of copper sulfate.
Key variables: IV: time of electrolysis / current. DV: mass of copper deposited (g). Control: current, electrode area, concentration.
Method: 1. Weigh clean copper cathode; set up electrolysis of CuSO₄ (0.5 mol/dm³) with copper anode and cathode. 2. Pass a steady current of 0.5 A for 10, 20, 30, 40 min. 3. Remove cathode; rinse with distilled water; dry; weigh. 4. Calculate charge Q = I × t; plot mass deposited vs charge.
Measurements: Current I (A), time t (s), charge Q = It (C), mass of Cu deposited (g).
Analysis: Linear graph: mass ∝ charge. Gradient = mass per coulomb = M/(nF) = 64/(2×96500) = 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ g/C. Faraday's law. Electroplating application.
Safety: Electrical equipment near liquids — ensure no short circuits. Copper sulfate — harmful. Eye protection and gloves.
Data skills: Linear graph; gradient interpretation; Faraday constant.
Common errors / improvements: Current not steady — use a regulated supply and monitor with ammeter. Electrode not fully dry before weighing — water adds mass. Anode dissolving unevenly — use same anode throughout. Poor contact at electrodes — clean with sandpaper before use.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Make up CuSO₄ (0.5 mol/dm³): 62.5 g per 500 cm³ — see CHEM-03. Per group: 2 copper electrodes — clean with fine sandpaper; record initial mass; label. Regulated DC supply: check ammeter in circuit is calibrated. Allow balances to warm up for 15 min.

Title: Cracking of hydrocarbons
Aim: Demonstrate thermal cracking of a long-chain liquid hydrocarbon (liquid paraffin) over a hot catalyst to produce shorter alkanes and alkenes.
Key variables: IV: temperature. DV: gas produced, test for alkene. Control: flow rate, catalyst amount.
Method: 1. Set up apparatus: hard glass test tube with liquid paraffin-soaked mineral wool at one end; broken pottery/alumina catalyst at hot zone; gas collection by displacement of water. 2. Heat catalyst zone strongly; collect gas when production steady. 3. Test collected gas with bromine water — decolourises = alkene present. 4. Test flammability with lit splint (away from apparatus).
Measurements: Whether bromine water decolourises, whether gas is flammable.
Analysis: Cracking breaks C–C bonds: thermal energy + catalyst. Products: shorter alkane + alkene. e.g. C₁₅H₃₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₇H₁₄. Industrial importance: refining crude oil fractions.
Safety: CRITICAL: Never allow tube to cool with water suck-back — remove delivery tube before removing flame. Flammable vapours — ensure no naked flames near collection. Bromine water — toxic, wear gloves. Eye protection. Teacher demonstration only or with close supervision.
Data skills: Gas tests; understanding industrial cracking; writing equations.
Common errors / improvements: Suck-back when tube cools — always remove delivery tube first. Collecting gas too early — contains mostly air. Not testing with bromine water — missing evidence for alkene.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min. TEACHER DEMO ONLY. Soak mineral wool with liquid paraffin; place in hard glass tube (NOT soft glass — will crack). Set up gas collection by water displacement. Test apparatus for leaks before class. Bromine water: in a separate small test tube for alkene test. CRITICAL: brief the teacher on suck-back prevention.

Title: Testing for alkenes — bromine water addition
Aim: Test a range of hydrocarbons with bromine water to distinguish alkanes from alkenes.
Key variables: IV: hydrocarbon type (hexane, hexene, cyclohexane, cyclohexene). DV: decolourisation of bromine water. Control: volume of bromine water, same shaking technique.
Method: 1. Add 1 cm³ of each hydrocarbon to separate test tubes. 2. Add 5 drops of bromine water to each; stopper and shake gently. 3. Observe whether bromine water decolourises (orange → colourless = alkene) or remains orange (alkane). 4. Repeat with cyclohexane vs cyclohexene.
Measurements: Colour of bromine water before and after with each hydrocarbon.
Analysis: Alkenes decolourise bromine water by addition across C=C double bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. Alkanes do not react (no double bond). Distinguish saturated from unsaturated.
Safety: Bromine water — toxic, oxidising. Hydrocarbons — flammable, no flames. Fume cupboard or well-ventilated area. Gloves and eye protection.
Data skills: Positive/negative test; understanding electrophilic addition mechanism.
Common errors / improvements: Bromine water bleaches in UV light — keep tubes away from direct sunlight. Using too much bromine water — hard to see decolourisation. Shaking too hard — emulsion forms.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Dispense hydrocarbons in small vials (1 cm³) with stoppers: hexane, hex-1-ene, cyclohexane, cyclohexene. Bromine water: dilute orange solution in dropper bottles. All flammable — ensure no flames in room. Work in well-ventilated area or fume cupboard.

Title: Fermentation and distillation of ethanol
Aim: Produce ethanol by fermentation of glucose using yeast, then purify by distillation.
Key variables: IV: temperature of fermentation. DV: rate of CO₂ production (bubbles/min), % ethanol by distillation. Control: glucose concentration, yeast amount.
Method: 1. Dissolve 50 g glucose in 500 cm³ warm water (~35 °C) in a conical flask. 2. Add 5 g dried yeast; seal with a bung and delivery tube leading to limewater. 3. Incubate at 30–35 °C; count bubbles per minute daily for 5 days. 4. After 5 days, filter fermentation mixture; distil (collect fraction 78–82 °C for ethanol). 5. Test distillate with anhydrous CuSO₄ (turns blue = water present); burn on watch glass.
Measurements: Bubble count per minute each day, temperature, ethanol fraction volume, % purity (by density or combustion).
Analysis: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Rate peaks at optimum temperature; yeast enzymes denature above ~45 °C. Fractional distillation needed for higher purity. Discuss industrial fermentation and biofuels.
Safety: Ethanol vapour — flammable, no naked flames near still; fume cupboard for distillation. Yeast — low hazard. CO₂ — ensure no blocked delivery tube (pressure build-up).
Data skills: Rate over time graph; distillation; purity testing.
Common errors / improvements: Fermentation too cold or too hot — slow rate or yeast death. Delivery tube blocks if glucose crystallises — check regularly. Not filtering before distilling — yeast blocks still. Collecting wrong fraction — boiling point of ethanol-water mixture varies with composition.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min + 5-day fermentation period. Day 1: dissolve glucose, prepare yeast solution, set up conical flasks in incubator at 30–35 °C. Lesson: distillation apparatus assembled and tested — run water through condenser before class. Have fresh glucose/yeast setup to show current fermentation if distilling a pre-made batch. Anhydrous CuSO₄ in small vials. Warn: ethanol vapour — fume cupboard for distillation.

Title: Polymerisation — making nylon (interfacial polymerisation)
Aim: Demonstrate addition and condensation polymerisation by making nylon-6,6 at the interface of two immiscible solutions.
Key variables: IV: reactant concentrations. DV: rate of nylon thread formation.
Method: 1. Pour 5 cm³ of diaminohexane solution (5% in NaOH solution) into a beaker. 2. Very slowly pour 5 cm³ of decanedioyl dichloride solution (5% in cyclohexane) on top — do not mix. 3. Use a glass rod to pick up the film at the interface and pull slowly — a continuous thread of nylon forms. 4. Wind thread onto a glass rod; wash with water.
Measurements: Whether thread forms, estimated rate, physical properties of product.
Analysis: Nylon-6,6: condensation polymer. Monomers: diamine + dicarboxylic acid (or acid chloride). Amide linkages form, HCl released. Compare to addition polymerisation of alkenes (no small molecule lost). Industrial applications of nylon.
Safety: Dicarboxylic acid chloride — corrosive, fumes in air. Cyclohexane — flammable. Use in fume cupboard. Teacher demonstration. Gloves, eye protection, lab coat.
Data skills: Condensation vs addition polymerisation; linking structure to properties.
Common errors / improvements: Mixing the two layers — reaction too diffuse; must maintain interface. Pulling too fast — thread breaks. Not washing thread — HCl residue is corrosive.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. TEACHER DEMO or closely supervised. Prepare solutions in fume cupboard: diaminohexane in NaOH (5%), dianedioyl dichloride in cyclohexane (5%). Keep solutions cold until used. Have distilled water ready for washing thread. Gloves, eye protection, lab coat mandatory.

Title: Thermite reaction — reduction of iron oxide
Aim: Demonstrate the thermite reaction to show reduction of iron(III) oxide by aluminium, illustrating relative reactivity.
Key variables: IV: ratio of reactants. DV: temperature reached, iron produced.
Method: 1. Mix 8 g iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) with 3 g aluminium powder in a clay flower pot over a sand tray. 2. Insert a magnesium ribbon fuse (~10 cm). 3. Clear a 3-metre radius; ignite magnesium fuse with Bunsen; stand back. 4. Observe molten iron produced and white Al₂O₃ slag.
Measurements: Temperature estimate (very high, >2000 °C); observation of molten iron; colour of slag.
Analysis: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. Al is more reactive than Fe — displaces it. Highly exothermic. Industrial application: welding rail tracks (Thermit welding).
Safety: EXTREMELY HAZARDOUS — teacher demonstration only. Clear 3 m radius. Eye protection (UV from molten metal). Heat-resistant bench mat. Bucket of dry sand ready. NEVER use water — molten metal + water = steam explosion. Do not lean over reaction at any point.
Data skills: Displacement reactions; reactivity series; highly exothermic reactions.
Common errors / improvements: Adding water — catastrophic. Insufficient clearance — spatter risk. Using more than recommended quantities — dangerously exothermic.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min. TEACHER DEMO ONLY. Mix Fe₂O₃ and Al powder in clay pot at least 30 min before lesson — allow to settle. Position sand tray; check 3 m clearance. Brief students on safety position (behind blast screen, ≥ 3 m). Have sand bucket and face shield ready. NEVER prepare on same day as other oxidiser experiments.

Title: Rusting of iron — conditions required
Aim: Investigate the conditions necessary for rusting of iron and test methods of corrosion prevention.
Key variables: IV: conditions (water only, air only, water + air, boiled water + oil layer, salt water). DV: whether rust forms after 1 week. Control: same iron nails, same tube size.
Method: 1. Set up 5 boiling tubes: (a) nail + dry air (silica gel, sealed); (b) nail + boiled water (no O₂) under oil; (c) nail + tap water + air; (d) nail + salt water + air; (e) nail + water + air + galvanised zinc strip. 2. Leave for 1 week; observe.
Measurements: Presence/absence of rust in each tube after 1 week; comparative extent of rusting.
Analysis: Both water and oxygen required for rusting. Salt water accelerates corrosion. Zinc prevents rusting (sacrificial anode). Discuss other prevention methods: painting, galvanising, alloying (stainless steel), electroplating, greasing.
Safety: Long-term experiment — set up and leave. Iron nails — not hazardous. Salt water — not hazardous. Silica gel — desiccant, wash hands if touched.
Data skills: Long-term observation; controlled variables; evaluating corrosion prevention.
Common errors / improvements: Not fully sealing tube (a) — moisture enters. Not boiling water fully (b) — dissolved O₂ remains. Not making fair comparison — different sized nails or different amounts of water.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Set up 5 tubes per group in advance. Boil water for tube b and allow to cool under oil seal before class. Seal tube a with silica gel and rubber bung — check it's airtight. Salt water: dissolve 25 g NaCl in 500 cm³ water. Label all tubes clearly 1–5 with conditions. Store in safe place for 1 week — inform other staff not to disturb.

Title: Electroplating
Aim: Electroplate a metal object with copper and investigate factors affecting the quality of the deposit.
Key variables: IV: current, time, concentration of electrolyte. DV: mass of copper deposited, appearance of deposit.
Method: 1. Clean and weigh the cathode (e.g. zinc or steel object). 2. Set up electrolysis cell: copper anode, object as cathode, copper sulfate electrolyte. 3. Apply 3–6 V for 10 min; observe copper depositing on cathode. 4. Remove cathode; rinse; dry carefully; reweigh. 5. Compare appearance at different currents.
Measurements: Mass of cathode before and after, appearance of coating, mass of anode (should decrease by equal amount).
Analysis: Copper dissolves at anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. Deposits at cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Solution concentration stays constant. Discuss industrial electroplating applications (chrome bumpers, gold-plated jewellery).
Safety: Electrical equipment near liquids. Copper sulfate — harmful. Eye protection and gloves.
Data skills: Mole calculations; Faraday's law application; industrial application.
Common errors / improvements: Object not cleaned — poor adhesion. High current → rough, lumpy deposit. Anode not copper — solution becomes depleted. Not weighing dry cathode — water adds mass.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Pre-sand cathode objects and weigh — record mass on label. Make up CuSO₄ (0.5 mol/dm³) as CHEM-03. Assemble electrolysis cells; check connections. Regulated PSU: check ammeter accuracy.

Title: Rates of reaction — effect of a catalyst
Aim: Investigate the effect of a catalyst on the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
Key variables: IV: catalyst type (none, MnO₂, liver/potato as enzyme catalase, Fe³⁺ ions). DV: volume of O₂ per minute. Control: H₂O₂ concentration, volume, temperature.
Method: 1. Measure 20 cm³ of H₂O₂ (20 vol = 6%) into a conical flask connected to a gas syringe. 2. Add a spatula of MnO₂ powder; record O₂ volume every 30 s for 5 min. 3. Repeat with no catalyst, with FeCl₃ solution (5 cm³), and with small piece of raw liver or potato. 4. Plot volume vs time for each; compare initial gradients.
Measurements: Volume of O₂ (cm³) at each 30 s interval for each catalyst.
Analysis: Catalyst increases rate without being used up. Rate = initial gradient. Catalase in liver/potato = biological catalyst. MnO₂ = heterogeneous catalyst. Explain in terms of activation energy (lower Ea pathway).
Safety: H₂O₂ above 6% — irritant/corrosive; wear gloves and eye protection. Vigorous reaction with liver at high [H₂O₂] — use 6% max.
Data skills: Rate from gradient; comparing rates; catalyst concept.
Common errors / improvements: Catalyst amount varying between runs — not a fair test. Gas syringe sticking — lubricate plunger. Liver too large — reaction too fast to measure. Not keeping temperature constant.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. H₂O₂ (6%): dispense 100 cm³ per group — store in dark bottle in fridge. MnO₂: spatula amounts in labelled tubes. FeCl₃ (0.1 mol/dm³): 10 cm³ per group. Fresh raw liver/potato pieces: cut just before lesson. Gas syringes: lubricate plungers. Check all bung/delivery tube assemblies are airtight.

Title: Reversible reactions and equilibrium — cobalt chloride
Aim: Demonstrate a reversible reaction and Le Chatelier's principle using the cobalt chloride equilibrium.
Key variables: IV: temperature change, addition of water or hydrochloric acid. DV: colour of solution (pink/blue).
Method: 1. Dissolve CoCl₂ in water — pink solution (Co(H₂O)₆²⁺). 2. Add concentrated HCl slowly — solution turns blue (CoCl₄²⁻). 3. Add water — returns to pink. 4. Heat blue solution — stays/goes blue. Cool — returns pink. 5. Relate to equilibrium: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O
Measurements: Colour of solution at each stage.
Analysis: Le Chatelier's principle: equilibrium shifts to oppose change. Adding Cl⁻ shifts right (blue); adding water shifts left (pink); heating shifts to endothermic direction. Apply to Haber process and Contact process.
Safety: Cobalt compounds — toxic/carcinogenic; minimise use; gloves; wash hands. Concentrated HCl — fuming, fume cupboard. Eye protection.
Data skills: Qualitative observation; Le Chatelier's principle; reversible reactions.
Common errors / improvements: Using too dilute HCl — insufficient Cl⁻ to shift equilibrium visibly. Not recording intermediate colours — change is gradual. Confusing reversible reaction with equilibrium — they are not the same.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. TEACHER DEMO or supervised. CoCl₂ solution (0.5 mol/dm³): dissolve 11.9 g CoCl₂·6H₂O per 100 cm³ — pink. Conc. HCl: dispense in small dropper bottles in fume cupboard — 5 cm³ per demo. Hot and cold water baths ready. COSHH: cobalt compounds are toxic and possible carcinogens — minimise quantities, gloves essential.

Title: Composition of air — rusting or burning
Aim: Determine the percentage of oxygen in air by allowing iron to rust in a closed volume of air and measuring the reduction in volume.
Key variables: IV: time elapsed (days). DV: volume of air remaining (cm³). Control: sealed apparatus, temperature.
Method: 1. Fill a graduated tube with damp steel wool. 2. Invert in a water trough; mark initial water level. 3. Leave 3–5 days; observe water rising as O₂ is consumed by rusting. 4. Measure new water level; calculate volume of O₂ consumed. 5. Calculate % O₂ = (volume consumed / original volume) × 100.
Measurements: Initial volume of air, final volume of air (after O₂ consumed), volume of O₂ consumed.
Analysis: O₂ is approximately 21% of air. Iron reacts with O₂ and H₂O. Discuss remaining 79% (mostly N₂). Compare to burning magnesium method (produces oxide so volume decreases).
Safety: Steel wool — not a significant hazard. Ensure apparatus sealed tightly. Patience required — long experiment.
Data skills: % calculation; controlled experiment; understanding atmospheric composition.
Common errors / improvements: Apparatus not sealed — air enters. Steel wool too dry — rusting requires water. Not waiting long enough. Forgetting to account for water vapour in calculation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Dampen steel wool with water but do not saturate — wring out. Set up graduated tubes inverted over water trough; pack with steel wool. Mark initial water level with marker pen. Leave set up in lab for duration of experiment (3–5 days). Note on setup: 'Do not disturb — ongoing experiment.'

Title: Acid rain effects — reaction of SO₂ and NO₂ with water
Aim: Demonstrate the formation of acidic rain by dissolving SO₂ in water and measuring pH; relate to environmental effects.
Key variables: IV: gas dissolved in water (SO₂, CO₂, clean air). DV: pH of resulting solution. Control: volume of water, time of bubbling.
Method: 1. Bubble SO₂ into universal indicator solution — colour changes from green to red/orange. 2. Repeat with CO₂ — smaller pH drop. 3. Compare to clean air (no colour change). 4. Test effect on marble chips (CaCO₃) — acid rain dissolves limestone.
Measurements: pH of each solution, colour of indicator, rate of marble dissolution.
Analysis: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (sulfurous acid); CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid). Acid rain pH ~4–5. Environmental effects: weathering of limestone buildings, acidification of lakes. Sources: burning fossil fuels.
Safety: SO₂ — toxic, irritant; small amounts only in fume cupboard or behind glass screen. Eye protection.
Data skills: pH comparison; environmental chemistry; equations for acid rain formation.
Common errors / improvements: Using too much SO₂ — overwhelming gas. Confusing carbonic acid (weak, natural CO₂) with sulfurous/sulfuric acid (acid rain). Not relating to real world sources.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. TEACHER DEMO. Safer approach: use H₂SO₃ solution (dilute SO₂ in water, purchased) rather than generating SO₂ gas. Have CO₂ generation apparatus (marble + HCl) and clean air as comparisons. Universal indicator solution in small flasks. Fume cupboard for any SO₂ gas work.

Title: Rock formation and the rock cycle — crystallisation rate
Aim: Investigate how the rate of cooling of a melt affects crystal size, modelling igneous rock formation.
Key variables: IV: cooling rate (fast in ice water, slow in sand, very slow in air). DV: crystal size (mm). Control: concentration of salite/salol, same volume.
Method: 1. Melt a small amount of salol (phenyl salicylate) on a warm microscope slide. 2. Allow to cool rapidly (touch a cold metal block); observe crystal size under microscope. 3. Repeat, cooling slowly (leave on warm tile). 4. Compare crystal sizes.
Measurements: Crystal size (mm) for each cooling rate.
Analysis: Fast cooling → small crystals (e.g. basalt, extrusive igneous). Slow cooling → large crystals (e.g. granite, intrusive igneous). Link to igneous rock formation in the rock cycle.
Safety: Salol — low melting point, low hazard. Hot slide — burns. Eye protection.
Data skills: Qualitative observation; microscopy; geological application.
Common errors / improvements: Slide too hot — salol doesn't solidify. Not observing under microscope — crystal size difference hard to see with naked eye. Cooling too slowly even on 'fast' run.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Salol: dispense ~0.5 g per slide on small weighing papers. Prepare hot plate or Bunsen + water bath at 45 °C. Cold aluminium block: store in freezer or on ice for 1 h before lesson. Ensure microscopes are working — set to ×40 objective. Clean slides: one per slide preparation.

Title: Plasmolysis and turgor in plant cells
Aim: Observe plasmolysis and turgor in plant cells using red onion epidermis and hypertonic/hypotonic solutions.
Key variables: IV: solution concentration (distilled water vs concentrated salt/sugar solution). DV: % cells showing plasmolysis, cell appearance under microscope. Control: same onion, same objective lens.
Method: 1. Peel red onion epidermis; mount in distilled water — observe turgid cells (purple vacuole fills cell). 2. Replace water with concentrated NaCl solution by capillary action (pipette on one side, absorb with paper on other). 3. Observe plasmolysis: vacuole shrinks, cytoplasm pulls away from cell wall (protoplast shrinks). 4. Replace with distilled water — observe deplasmolysis (recovery).
Measurements: % cells plasmolysed, extent of plasmolysis, recovery observations.
Analysis: Plasmolysis = cell membrane pulls away from wall in hypertonic solution (water leaves by osmosis). Turgid = hypotonic solution; water enters vacuole. Cell wall prevents lysis (unlike animal cells). Plot % plasmolysis vs concentration to find incipient plasmolysis point.
Safety: Low hazard. Iodine and salt solutions — low risk. Eye protection when using solutions.
Data skills: Microscopy technique; % calculations; osmosis mechanism.
Common errors / improvements: Moving slide while changing solution — cell lost. Not waiting long enough after adding salt solution. Confusing plasmolysis with cell death — cells recover when water returned.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Red onion: provide inner fleshy layers (as BIO-01). NaCl solution (10%): dissolve 10 g NaCl in 100 cm³ water. Iodine in dropper bottles (optional — to stain nuclei). Microscopes: set up as BIO-01. Filter paper strips: cut into 1 cm × 8 cm strips for drawing solution under coverslip.

Title: Cell division — observing mitosis in root tip squash
Aim: Prepare a temporary stained squash of onion or garlic root tip and observe stages of mitosis under a microscope.
Key variables: IV: stage of cell cycle. DV: relative frequency of cells in each stage. Control: same root tip region, same stain.
Method: 1. Cut 1 cm of root tip from germinated onion/garlic; place in 1 mol/dm³ HCl at 60 °C for 5 min (maceration). 2. Transfer to slide; add 1–2 drops of orcein ethanoic stain (or toluidine blue); leave 1 min. 3. Lower coverslip; fold filter paper over slide; press firmly but gently (squash). 4. View under ×400; identify cells in interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. 5. Count at least 50 cells; record number in each stage.
Measurements: Number of cells in each stage, % of total in each stage, mitotic index = (cells in mitosis / total cells) × 100.
Analysis: Mitotic index indicates rate of cell division. Most cells in interphase (longest stage). Interpret cell cycle duration from relative frequency. Link to cancer (uncontrolled mitosis).
Safety: HCl — corrosive; orcein stain — stains skin, ethanoic acid component. Eye protection, gloves.
Data skills: % frequency; mitotic index; microscopy; biological drawing.
Common errors / improvements: HCl not warmed enough — poor maceration. Squash too vigorous — cells damaged. Stain too concentrated — can't distinguish chromosomes. Not focusing at ×100 first before ×400.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min + 2 days advance. Germinate onion or garlic bulbs 2 days before: place on water-filled jar so roots grow down. Lesson prep: HCl (1 mol/dm³) in small dropper bottles. Water bath at 60 °C: set 15 min before. Orcein stain: dispense in dropper bottles — stains everything (protect bench with absorbent paper). Microscopes: as BIO-01. Scalpels and cutting tiles per group.

Title: Diffusion across a visking tube membrane
Aim: Model diffusion and osmosis across a partially permeable membrane using visking tubing containing glucose and starch solution.
Key variables: IV: time elapsed, molecule size (glucose vs starch). DV: presence of glucose/starch inside/outside tubing over time. Control: same tubing length, same volume.
Method: 1. Fill visking tubing (pre-soaked) with starch + glucose solution; tie ends. 2. Place in a beaker of distilled water + iodine solution. 3. After 30 min, test water in beaker for glucose using Benedict's test and for starch using iodine. 4. Test remaining contents of tubing.
Measurements: Colour change of iodine solution (starch present?), colour change of Benedict's test of beaker water (glucose present?).
Analysis: Glucose (small molecule) diffuses out through partially permeable membrane — detected by Benedict's test in beaker. Starch (large molecule) does not pass through — iodine inside tubing turns blue-black, outside stays orange. Model of intestinal absorption and kidney filtration.
Safety: Benedict's test — hot water bath required. Iodine — stains. Standard lab precautions.
Data skills: Positive/negative tests; model limitations; membrane permeability concept.
Common errors / improvements: Visking tubing not pre-soaked — leaks. Knots not tight enough — contents leak into beaker. Benedict's test not heated long enough. Using universal indicator instead of iodine — won't give starch test.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Visking tubing: cut into 20 cm lengths; soak in distilled water for 30 min to soften. Tie one end of each piece with string or elastic band. Starch solution (2%): 20 cm³ per group. Glucose solution (2%): 20 cm³ per group — mix both together for filling tubing. Iodine solution: add to beaker water (5 drops per 200 cm³). Benedict's reagent: 10 cm³ in labelled tube. Water bath at 80 °C for Benedict's test.

Title: Investigation of transpiration — potometer
Aim: Measure the rate of water uptake (as a proxy for transpiration) in a leafy shoot using a bubble potometer under different conditions.
Key variables: IV: environmental condition (humidity, temperature, air movement, light intensity). DV: distance moved by air bubble per minute (mm/min). Control: same shoot, same potometer, equilibration time.
Method: 1. Cut shoot stem underwater to avoid air locks; insert into potometer underwater. 2. Allow bubble to form at capillary tube opening; record position at t=0, t=1 min, t=2 min. 3. Reset bubble by opening reservoir tap. 4. Test: normal conditions, then fan (increases transpiration), then plastic bag over leaves (decreases), then bright light.
Measurements: Distance bubble moves per minute (mm/min) for each condition.
Analysis: Rate of bubble movement ∝ rate of water uptake ≈ transpiration rate. High temperature, low humidity, high wind speed, high light intensity all increase transpiration. Explain via stomata opening and water potential gradients.
Safety: Glassware — handle carefully. Sharp scalpel for cutting stem. Shoot may drip water — protect bench.
Data skills: Rate calculation; controlled experiment; relating to stomata mechanism.
Common errors / improvements: Air locks in potometer stem — all setup must be done underwater. Shoot wilting — set up quickly. Bubble moves irregularly — check for leaks. Not allowing equilibration time between conditions.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min. Leafy shoots: cut from plants (privet, cherry laurel) the morning of the experiment — place stems in water immediately. Cut stem end again at 45° underwater just before assembling potometer. Potometers: assemble underwater, ensuring no air bubbles in capillary. Vaseline: available for sealing joints. Fan: set up at one end of bench. Plastic bags: one per group for humidity condition.

Title: Effect of caffeine on heart rate — Daphnia
Aim: Investigate the effect of caffeine concentration on the heart rate of Daphnia (water flea), a model organism with a visible heartbeat.
Key variables: IV: caffeine concentration (0, 0.1%, 0.5%, 1%). DV: Daphnia heart rate (beats/min). Control: same Daphnia, temperature, same microscope setting.
Method: 1. Place a Daphnia on a cavity slide in a drop of pond water; observe under ×40. 2. Count heartbeats for 15 s × 4 = beats/min (or use tally counter). 3. Transfer to a drop of caffeine solution (wait 2 min); recount heart rate. 4. Repeat for each concentration using a fresh Daphnia each time.
Measurements: Heart rate (beats/min) at each caffeine concentration.
Analysis: Caffeine is a stimulant — increases heart rate. Plot heart rate vs concentration. Discuss ethical issues with using living organisms and how Daphnia minimise this (invertebrate). Compare to effect on human heart. Discuss drug regulation.
Safety: Daphnia — living organisms; treat humanely; return to pond water after; do not over-expose to solutions. Limit time out of pond water. Caffeine solutions — low concentration, low hazard.
Data skills: Counting technique; mean; ethical issues; drug action.
Common errors / improvements: Daphnia overheating under microscope lamp — use LED microscope or reduce exposure time. Heart rate too fast to count accurately — tally counter helps. Caffeine concentration too low — no visible effect. Same Daphnia for all concentrations — order effect; use fresh individuals.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Daphnia: obtain from aquarium shop or science supplier 1–2 days before. Keep in aerated pond/aquarium water at room temperature. Caffeine solutions: 0.1%, 0.5%, 1% — dissolve in pond water (not distilled water). Cavity slides: clean and dry. Pipettes: wide-bore to avoid damaging Daphnia. Tally counters: one per pair.

Title: Effect of antiseptics and disinfectants on bacterial growth
Aim: Compare the effectiveness of different antiseptics and disinfectants against bacteria using disc diffusion assay.
Key variables: IV: type/brand of antiseptic or disinfectant. DV: diameter of inhibition zone (mm). Control: same bacterial strain, same incubation conditions.
Method: 1. Follow aseptic technique as in BIO-09. 2. Inoculate plate with bacterial lawn. 3. Soak paper discs in different antiseptic solutions (TCP, Dettol, hand sanitiser, distilled water control). 4. Place on agar with sterile forceps; incubate at 25 °C for 24 h. 5. Measure inhibition zones without opening plates.
Measurements: Diameter of inhibition zone (mm) for each antiseptic.
Analysis: Larger zone = more effective at that concentration. Calculate area = π(d/2)². Discuss: antiseptics for skin (too dilute to sterilise); disinfectants for surfaces (too concentrated for skin). Practical significance for infection control.
Safety: CRITICAL: Same biosafety rules as BIO-09. Never exceed 25 °C. Never open plates after incubation. Autoclave all materials. Wash hands thoroughly.
Data skills: Zone measurement; comparing effectiveness; disinfectant vs antiseptic distinction.
Common errors / improvements: Same errors as BIO-09 plus: not using a negative control (distilled water disc). Not accounting for disc sizes varying between antiseptics. Measuring inhibition including disc — should measure from disc edge.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 60 min the day before + 15 min lesson day — see BIO-09 for aseptic technique setup. Antiseptic solutions: TCP (undiluted and 1:10 dilution), Dettol (undiluted), hand sanitiser (undiluted), distilled water (negative control). Pre-soak paper discs the day before in each solution. Label clearly. Incubator: 25 °C. Autoclave plates before disposal.

Title: Modelling spread of infection
Aim: Model the spread of an infectious disease through a population using a dilution/indicator simulation.
Key variables: IV: number of contacts (rounds of mixing). DV: number 'infected' (indicated by NaOH turning phenolphthalein pink). Control: volume transferred each round.
Method: 1. Give each student a test tube of water; one student has NaOH (unknowingly 'infected'). 2. Each round: students pour half their solution into a partner's tube, mix, half back. 3. After 3 rounds, add phenolphthalein to all tubes — pink = infected. 4. Trace back contacts to identify index case. 5. Repeat with 'vaccination' (water only, NaOH neutralised) for some students.
Measurements: Number infected after each round, contact tracing diagram.
Analysis: Exponential spread: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → ... Draw epidemic curve. Effect of isolation and vaccination on transmission. R₀ concept (reproduction number). Discuss herd immunity threshold.
Safety: NaOH dilute (0.1 mol/dm³ is sufficient) — low risk, but wash hands. Phenolphthalein — stains.
Data skills: Exponential growth; epidemic modelling; contact tracing.
Common errors / improvements: Not mixing thoroughly — some exposures not detected. Too few rounds — not enough spread to be interesting. Not recording contacts — can't trace back. Not including a vaccination group — misses the key teaching point.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Test tubes: one per student, pre-filled with 5 cm³ distilled water. One tube: replace water with 0.1 mol/dm³ NaOH (5 cm³) — mark as 'infected' on reverse of tube. Phenolphthalein: in dropper bottle. Contact tracing sheets: print 1 per group. Pipettes: 1 per student.

Title: Sampling techniques — quadrats and transects
Aim: Use quadrats and belt transects to estimate population size and distribution of plant species in a habitat.
Key variables: IV: position along transect (m from one end). DV: % cover of each species, species frequency. Control: same quadrat size, same observer.
Method: 1. Random quadrats: use random number table to generate coordinates; place 0.5 m² quadrat at each; count individual plants or estimate % cover. Do minimum 10 quadrats. 2. Belt transect: lay tape from one habitat boundary to another (e.g. shaded to open); place quadrats every 1 m. 3. Record species in each quadrat; calculate frequency (% of quadrats containing that species). 4. Calculate mean % cover and estimated total population.
Measurements: Species in each quadrat, % cover or count, position along transect.
Analysis: Population estimate = mean density × total area. Frequency index. Discuss zonation along abiotic gradient (light, moisture). Explain why random sampling avoids bias. Limitations: quadrat size, sample size, identification errors.
Safety: Outdoor activity — appropriate clothing and footwear. Be aware of nettles, uneven ground. Respect the habitat — do not trample plants unnecessarily.
Data skills: Mean and variation; population estimation formula; sampling bias discussion.
Common errors / improvements: Non-random sampling — students pick 'nice' spots. Too few quadrats for reliable mean. Not identifying species correctly — use field guides. Forgetting to randomise quadrat placement at start of transect.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min. Quadrat frames: make from garden wire (~0.5 m × 0.5 m) or purchase. Tape measures: check length, clip to working order. ID guides: print or purchase for local common plant species. Recording sheets: design and print before class. Check suitable outdoor area (school field, grassy boundary) — inform groundskeeper not to mow the week before.

Title: Estimating population size — mark-release-recapture
Aim: Use the mark-release-recapture technique (Lincoln index) to estimate the population of woodlice or isopods in a habitat.
Key variables: IV: habitat area. DV: estimated population size. Control: same trapping method, same time intervals.
Method: 1. Collect invertebrates from leaf litter (pitfall traps or by searching); count and mark with Tipp-Ex dot. 2. Release marked individuals back into habitat; wait 24 h. 3. Collect a second sample; count total caught and number marked. 4. Apply Lincoln index: N = (n₁ × n₂) / m.
Measurements: n₁ = first sample size, n₂ = second sample size, m = marked individuals in second sample, N = estimated population.
Analysis: Lincoln index formula. Assumptions: marking doesn't affect survival, marks don't rub off, no immigration/emigration, population closed, random mixing. Discuss how each assumption might be violated.
Safety: Handle invertebrates gently; return all animals to habitat. Outdoor — appropriate clothing. Mark should not harm the organism.
Data skills: Lincoln index formula; assumptions of method; sources of error.
Common errors / improvements: Marking too conspicuously — predation increases. Not waiting long enough for mixing. Too small a second sample — m becomes very small and N is unreliable. Not accounting for marks rubbing off.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 30 min + 24 h between samples. Pitfall traps: dig and set the day before (small cups sunk to ground level under leaf litter). Collect first sample from traps. Mark with white paint pen: let dry before release. Second sample collected next day. Pooters or small paintbrushes for gentle handling.

Title: Food web construction and energy flow
Aim: Construct food chains and webs from habitat sampling data and calculate efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels.
Key variables: IV: trophic level. DV: biomass or energy content at each level. Control: same sampling area.
Method: 1. From quadrat/pitfall trap data, identify producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers. 2. Construct food web; identify trophic levels. 3. Use provided biomass data (g/m²) for each trophic level. 4. Calculate energy transfer efficiency = (biomass at level n+1 / biomass at level n) × 100%. 5. Draw a pyramid of biomass and a pyramid of numbers.
Measurements: Biomass at each trophic level (g/m²), energy transfer efficiency (%).
Analysis: Approximately 10% efficiency per trophic level (90% lost as heat/waste/movement). This limits food chain length. Pyramids: biomass always shows true pyramid; numbers can be inverted (e.g. tree with many insects). Apply to food security arguments.
Safety: Low hazard — data-based activity. Outdoor component: appropriate clothing for sampling.
Data skills: % efficiency calculation; pyramid construction; interpreting inverted pyramids.
Common errors / improvements: Confusing food web arrows — should point from eaten to eater (energy flow direction). Using numbers instead of biomass — pyramid can be inverted unexpectedly. Not explaining why 90% is lost.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Print data worksheets with trophic level biomass figures. Graph paper: 2 sheets per student. Calculators: check batteries. No live specimens needed.

Title: Modelling genetic crosses — probability and inheritance
Aim: Use a simulation (coin toss or coloured counters) to model monohybrid and dihybrid crosses and compare results to predicted ratios.
Key variables: IV: number of 'offspring' generated. DV: ratio of phenotypes observed. Control: same sample size.
Method: 1. Monohybrid: each student has two coins (H = dominant, T = recessive). Two 'parents' (Aa × Aa) each flip a coin. Record offspring genotype. Repeat 50 times. 2. Tally phenotypes; calculate observed ratio; compare to expected 3:1. 3. Dihybrid: use 4 coins (two pairs) for AaBb × AaBb. Record 50 offspring. 4. Chi-squared test: χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E to test goodness of fit.
Measurements: Number of each phenotype, observed ratio, expected ratio, χ² value.
Analysis: 3:1 (monohybrid) and 9:3:3:1 (dihybrid) ratios. Law of segregation and law of independent assortment. χ² test determines if deviation from expected is due to chance (p > 0.05 = not significant). Discuss why real results deviate.
Safety: No significant hazard. Coins and counters only.
Data skills: Probability; chi-squared test; ratio comparison; genetic notation.
Common errors / improvements: Too few trials — ratio very different from 3:1 due to chance. Not distinguishing genotype from phenotype in tally. Forgetting that chi-squared requires expected numbers ≥ 5 in each class.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Coins: 2 per student. Tally chart templates: print 1 per student. Chi-squared critical values table: print 1 per pair. Calculators: 1 per student.

Title: Variation — continuous and discontinuous, and normal distribution
Aim: Investigate variation in a biological characteristic within a class population and determine whether it is continuous or discontinuous.
Key variables: IV: individual measured. DV: measurement (height, hand span, tongue rolling, ear lobe attachment). Control: same measuring technique.
Method: 1. Measure height (continuous) and hand span of every student in the class. 2. Assess tongue rolling and earlobe attachment (discontinuous). 3. Plot frequency histogram for continuous data; bar chart for discontinuous. 4. Check if height data approximates a normal distribution; find mean and SD.
Measurements: Height (cm), hand span (cm), count of each tongue roll/earlobe phenotype.
Analysis: Continuous variation = environmental + genetic influence → normal distribution. Discontinuous = mainly genetic → distinct categories. Calculate mean, median, mode, range, standard deviation. Explain how natural selection acts differently on continuous vs discontinuous traits.
Safety: Students may be sensitive about height data — allow anonymous recording (post-it notes on board). Respect privacy. Handle data responsibly.
Data skills: Frequency histogram vs bar chart; normal distribution; mean and standard deviation.
Common errors / improvements: Using a bar chart for continuous data instead of histogram. Not using enough individuals — < 20 gives poor normal distribution. Not discussing sources of both types of variation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Height tape: fix to wall at suitable location — check calibration against known object. Rulers: 1 per student for hand span. Post-it notes: class set (for anonymous data). Graph paper: 1–2 sheets per student. Calculators: 1 per student.

Title: Skin temperature regulation — thermoregulation investigation
Aim: Investigate the role of skin in temperature regulation by measuring skin temperature change during exercise and in different conditions.
Key variables: IV: condition (rest, exercise, cool air, warm air). DV: skin temperature at fingertip and forehead (°C). Control: same individual, same thermometer position.
Method: 1. Measure resting skin temperature at fingertip and forehead using a thermistor probe or infrared thermometer. 2. Exercise for 3 min (jumping jacks); measure immediately and at 1, 2, 3, 5 min after. 3. Hold hand in cold water (5 °C) for 30 s; measure fingertip temperature every 30 s for 5 min. 4. Compare rate of recovery between fingers and forehead.
Measurements: Skin temperature (°C) at each time point for each condition.
Analysis: Vasodilation increases blood flow to skin → heat loss → skin warms. Vasoconstriction in cold → skin cools to conserve core temperature. Explain negative feedback loop: core temperature receptor → hypothalamus → effectors (sweat glands, blood vessels, hair erector muscles).
Safety: Cold water exposure — not for students with Raynaud's disease; brief exposure only. Exercise — same precautions as BIO-08.
Data skills: Recovery curves; negative feedback concept; relating to homeostasis.
Common errors / improvements: Thermometer not placed consistently — varies between readings. Cold water too cold — unpleasant and potentially harmful. Not accounting for ambient temperature differences between trials.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 15 min. Infrared thermometers: check batteries; calibrate against a known temperature. Bowl of cold water: 5 °C (add ice). Stopwatches: check batteries. Medical note: remind teacher to check for Raynaud's disease — exclude affected students from cold water part.

Title: Investigating the effect of glucose on insulin response — model investigation
Aim: Analyse blood glucose data from a glucose tolerance test and interpret the regulatory role of insulin.
Key variables: IV: time after glucose drink (min). DV: blood glucose concentration (mmol/L). Control: same individual, standardised glucose dose.
Method: 1. Analyse provided data sets showing blood glucose over 2 h after consuming glucose for: a healthy person, a person with Type 1 diabetes, a person with Type 2 diabetes. 2. Plot all three on same axes. 3. Identify key features: peak, rate of return to normal, level at 2 h. 4. Explain in terms of insulin production and sensitivity.
Measurements: Blood glucose (mmol/L) at 0, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120 min.
Analysis: Normal: blood glucose rises then returns to ~5 mmol/L by 120 min (insulin secreted by pancreas β cells). Type 1: insulin not produced — blood glucose stays high. Type 2: insulin produced but cells insensitive — slower return. Negative feedback. Treatment implications: insulin injection (Type 1) vs diet/exercise/metformin (Type 2).
Safety: Data-based activity — no significant hazard. Do not use actual finger-prick testing on students.
Data skills: Graph skills; interpreting health data; negative feedback mechanism.
Common errors / improvements: Confusing Type 1 and Type 2 mechanisms. Drawing smooth curves through data points instead of best-fit line. Not labelling axes with units. Claiming that the glucose level never returns to normal in Type 2 — it does, just more slowly.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Print blood glucose data tables and graph paper worksheets (1 per student). No apparatus required. Calculators: 1 per student.

Title: Reaction time — ruler drop test
Aim: Measure reaction time using a ruler drop test and investigate factors that affect it (e.g. practice, distraction, dominant vs non-dominant hand).
Key variables: IV: condition (dominant hand, non-dominant, distracted, practiced). DV: reaction time (ms). Control: same drop height, same dropper.
Method: 1. Partner holds ruler vertically with 0 cm at the bottom; subject places hand at 0 cm, ready to catch. 2. Partner drops without warning; subject catches; record distance fallen (cm). 3. Calculate reaction time: t = √(2d/g) where d in metres and g = 9.81 m/s². 4. Repeat 5 times; calculate mean, excluding anomalies. 5. Investigate variables: dominant vs non-dominant hand; after 10 practice drops; while counting backwards.
Measurements: Distance ruler falls (cm), calculated reaction time (ms), mean for each condition.
Analysis: Typical human reaction time ≈ 200 ms. Reflex arc much faster. Effect of practice = strengthening neural pathways. Distraction = competing stimuli slow response. Link to stopping distance in road safety. Discuss limitations of ruler as a measure.
Safety: Do not compete to catch more objects simultaneously — risk of hitting partner. Standard care around falling objects.
Data skills: Formula application (t = √(2d/g)); mean calculation; anomaly rejection.
Common errors / improvements: Not repeating enough to get reliable mean. Anticipating the drop — some students watch the fingers, not the ruler. Not converting cm to metres in formula. Failing to identify and reject outliers from mean calculation.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 5 min. Metre rulers: 1 per pair. Mark 30 cm drop-height with tape on ruler. Recording tables: print 1 per student. Calculators: 1 per student.

Title: Natural selection simulation — peppered moth
Aim: Simulate natural selection using cut-out 'moths' on light and dark backgrounds to model the peppered moth case study.
Key variables: IV: background colour (light bark / dark soot-covered bark). DV: % pale vs dark moths 'predated'. Control: same number of moths, same time to collect, same distance from background.
Method: 1. Cut out equal numbers of pale and dark paper circles (30 of each). 2. Scatter on a pale background; partner picks up as many as they can in 10 s (eyes closed between scattering and picking). 3. Count remaining; calculate % of each type surviving. 4. Repeat on dark background (e.g. black card). 5. Run 5 'generations': survivors breed — duplicate survivors; add back to original total.
Measurements: Number of pale and dark 'moths' remaining after each generation on each background.
Analysis: Pale moths have higher survival on pale background (camouflage); dark on dark. Over generations, proportion of better-camouflaged type increases. Link to real peppered moth data (Biston betularia) and Industrial Revolution. Natural selection: variation → differential survival → inherited advantage passed on.
Safety: Scissors and paper — standard care. Competitive element — ensure fair picking technique.
Data skills: % calculations; generational change; understanding natural selection mechanism.
Common errors / improvements: Not standardising time allowed for picking. Students consciously picking one colour — must simulate random predation. Not running enough generations to see clear trend. Using non-random initial scatter of moths.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Pale moths: cut ~30 discs per group from white A4 card (use 1 cm diameter punch or scissors). Dark moths: cut 30 discs from black card. Pale background: white paper. Dark background: black sugar paper or fabric. Scissors: 1 per group for making extra moths between generations.

Title: Antibiotic resistance simulation
Aim: Simulate the evolution of antibiotic resistance using dice or coloured beads to model random mutation and selection.
Key variables: IV: number of generations, antibiotic 'applied'. DV: proportion of resistant bacteria. Control: same starting population, same selection pressure.
Method: 1. Start with 20 beads: 18 white ('susceptible'), 2 red ('resistant'). 2. Apply antibiotic round 1: remove all white beads; double the red ones (survivors reproduce). 3. Add some new white mutants (2–3 per round). 4. Repeat for 5 rounds; plot proportion resistant each round. 5. Discuss: what happens if antibiotic is stopped mid-course?
Measurements: Number of resistant and susceptible bacteria each round, proportion resistant.
Analysis: Natural selection acts on existing variation. Mutations create new variation randomly — not in response to antibiotic. Key point: bacteria don't 'develop' resistance; resistant mutants already present are selected for. Misuse of antibiotics (incomplete courses) selects for resistance. MRSA example.
Safety: No significant hazard. Dice and beads only.
Data skills: Proportional change over time; mechanism of evolution; misunderstanding Lamarck vs Darwin.
Common errors / improvements: Students saying bacteria 'learn' to resist — address Lamarckian misconception explicitly. Not adding new mutants each round — resistance appears too quickly. Not discussing the difference between stopping antibiotics early vs completing the course.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 10 min. Beads: 18 white + 2 red per group in a small zip-lock bag. Dice: 1 per group. Recording sheets: print 1 per group. Calculators: 1 per group.

Title: Germination conditions investigation
Aim: Investigate the conditions necessary for seed germination (water, oxygen, warmth) and measure germination rate.
Key variables: IV: condition varied (water, oxygen, temperature). DV: % germination after 7 days, time to germination. Control: same seed species, same number of seeds.
Method: 1. Set up 4 boiling tubes with cress seeds: (a) damp cotton wool + air + room temp (all conditions); (b) dry cotton wool + air + room temp (no water); (c) damp cotton wool + boiled/oil-sealed water + room temp (no O₂); (d) damp cotton wool + air + fridge (cold). 2. Check daily for 7 days; record % germination (number germinated / total × 100). 3. Compare germination rates.
Measurements: % germination after each day, days to first germination, total % after 7 days.
Analysis: Water, oxygen, and suitable temperature all required for germination. Light not required (seeds germinate underground). Compare tube (a) vs (b)/(c)/(d) — only (a) germinates. Relate to enzyme activity needed for metabolic processes in germination.
Safety: Seeds — low hazard. Mould may develop — dispose of mouldy tubes carefully. Standard lab hygiene.
Data skills: % calculation; controlled experiment; negative controls.
Common errors / improvements: Not controlling seed quality — use seeds from same packet. Boiled water method for removing O₂ not thorough — oil layer essential to prevent re-oxygenation. Counting very small seedlings — define 'germinated' before starting (e.g. radicle > 2 mm).
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Cress seeds: same batch, same packet. Boiling tubes: 4 per group, labelled A–D. Tube C: add boiled (cooled) water + pour liquid paraffin seal just before lesson. Silica gel for tube B. Damp cotton wool: wring out until barely moist. Check after 7 days — photograph seedlings for classes that can't observe directly.

Title: Modelling vaccination and herd immunity
Aim: Model herd immunity by simulating disease spread in populations with different vaccination rates.
Key variables: IV: % of population vaccinated. DV: % population infected at end of simulation. Control: same transmission probability, same number of initial infected.
Method: 1. Create a 10×10 grid of students or paper squares. 2. Mark 5% as 'infected', 0% vaccinated. Roll die: if 4+ = transmission to adjacent unvaccinated individual. 3. Run 5 rounds; count total infected. 4. Repeat with 50% vaccinated (randomly selected squares blocked). 5. Repeat with 90% vaccinated. 6. Plot % infected vs % vaccinated.
Measurements: Number infected each round, total % infected after 5 rounds for each vaccination rate.
Analysis: At high vaccination rates, epidemic cannot spread even to unvaccinated individuals (herd immunity threshold). Threshold depends on R₀. Explain why some people cannot be vaccinated (immunocompromised) and rely on others. Link to measles (R₀ ~15, threshold ~93%).
Safety: No significant hazard. Paper/board activity.
Data skills: Probabilistic modelling; epidemic curves; herd immunity concept.
Common errors / improvements: Not randomising vaccinated positions — clustering gives unrealistic result. Too small a grid — stochastic effects dominate. Not repeating simulation — single run is very variable.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. Grid: draw 10×10 grid on large paper; laminate if reusing. Counters: 80 white, 10 red, 10 green per group. Dice: 1 per group. Coloured pens for marking grid. Recording sheets: 1 per group.

Title: Photosynthesis — effect of CO₂ concentration
Aim: Investigate the effect of CO₂ concentration on the rate of photosynthesis using pondweed and sodium hydrogen carbonate.
Key variables: IV: concentration of NaHCO₃ (0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0%). DV: bubble count per minute. Control: light intensity, temperature, same plant.
Method: 1. Place Elodea in boiling tube with each NaHCO₃ concentration. 2. Fix light source at constant distance (20 cm). 3. Allow 2 min equilibration; count bubbles per minute. 4. Repeat 3 times; calculate mean. 5. Plot rate vs CO₂ concentration.
Measurements: Bubble count per minute at each NaHCO₃ concentration.
Analysis: Rate increases with CO₂ up to a plateau (CO₂ no longer limiting). At plateau, another factor is limiting (light or temperature). Draw and interpret rate vs CO₂ graph. Compare limiting factor graphs for CO₂, light, and temperature overlaid.
Safety: Same precautions as BIO-05. NaHCO₃ — low hazard.
Data skills: Limiting factor concept; graph interpretation; experimental replication.
Common errors / improvements: Not equilibrating before counting. Bubbles varying in size — rate not truly proportional to O₂. NaHCO₃ changes pH slightly — potential cofounding variable. Not repeating — single count is unreliable.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 20 min. NaHCO₃ solutions: 0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0% — label clearly. Pondweed: as BIO-05. Lamp position: mark 20 cm on bench with tape. Water screen: fill glass tank. Thermometer at plant position: check temperature stability.

Title: Aerobic vs anaerobic respiration — yeast fermentation
Aim: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in yeast by measuring CO₂ production with and without oxygen.
Key variables: IV: presence/absence of oxygen. DV: rate of CO₂ production (bubbles/min through limewater or cm³/min). Control: yeast mass, glucose concentration, temperature.
Method: 1. Make two yeast-glucose solutions (5 g yeast + 20 g glucose in 200 cm³ warm water at 35 °C). 2. Tube A: open to air (aerobic). Tube B: sealed under layer of liquid paraffin (anaerobic). 3. Connect delivery tubes to limewater; count bubbles per minute after 5 min equilibration. 4. Measure daily for 3 days; observe differences in CO₂ rate and ethanol smell.
Measurements: Bubble count per minute, appearance of limewater, smell of ethanol (anaerobic only).
Analysis: Aerobic: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O (+38 ATP). Anaerobic: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (+2 ATP). Anaerobic produces much less ATP. Initial CO₂ rate may be higher anaerobically (fermentation fast) but yeast dies sooner. Compare energy yields.
Safety: CO₂ — not hazardous in small quantities. Ethanol vapour — mildly flammable; no naked flames near anaerobic tube. Yeast — low hazard. Handle limewater carefully (caustic).
Data skills: Rate comparison; equations; ATP yield comparison.
Common errors / improvements: Confusing yeast anaerobic respiration (ethanol + CO₂) with mammalian anaerobic (lactic acid). Paraffin layer not thick enough — some O₂ enters. Not equilibrating before counting — early readings too variable.
Technician preparation notes: Prep time: 25 min. Dissolve 20 g glucose in 400 cm³ warm water per class set. Dried yeast: 10 g per class set in small container. Flask A (aerobic): open to air via cotton wool bung. Flask B (anaerobic): seal with bung; pour liquid paraffin (~5 cm³) on top of mixture after adding. Limewater: 50 cm³ per group in labelled tube. Water bath at 35 °C: allow 15 min to reach temperature. Delivery tubes: check clear and not blocked.
